review_headline: Can't beat the price, but quality may be an issue after winter
review_body:
Thought I would share my thoughts on this antenna. I have had it installed for a couple days now.

- Do a YouTube search on Esky HG-981 and see the video of the unboxing video. The box came in good condition, but it looks like my 10 year old did the packaging of the antenna. No padding and just a couple rubber bands and a twisty. There were a few scratches and one of the antenna pieces was slightly damaged. Nothing severe but I would have expected a little Styrofoam or bubble wrap to protect the electronic pieces.
- The antenna was very simple to setup. Only issue was one of the pieces didn't click into the motor. The other piece in the same side clicked in so I don't have issues with it falling out.
- I live in Central Illinois and have concerns with the quality of the product. The plastic pieces doesn't seem very strong especially with the reflector coming out of the front of the motor. I think I could easily snap the plastic. Will it last with ice and snow hanging on it? I am keeping the box to return just in case.
- The instructions are a little lacking. It is just one sheet with little more than the installation instructions. It doesn't say anything about like if it is ok to turn the antenna when it is below 0 out. Or if there is snow or ice on it. It doesn't seem like the motor is strong enough for it so I am not planning to do it.
- As for the reception, I have the antenna pointed in the direction of the towers about 40 miles away. I get all the networks, but noticed the ABC station is sometimes breaking up. I have an alternate ABC channel that seems to be good without turning the antenna. I do live in the woods and have the antenna up only 20 or so feet up. That could cause some issues, but slightly disappointing considering the supposed 100+ mile reception range.
- The antenna spins just fine but understand some comments about it would be nice to know which direction it is pointing without a spotter. But I don't really plan turning it often. So that doesn't affect my opinion on it.

Overall for the price, I am happy about it. I now have the stations with no picture freezing that I want. Only giving it four stars because the little damage it came in the box. If the antenna is wrecked after winter, it is going down to two stars because I am thinking it is just a warm weather antenna.t I don't really plan turning it often. product_title: thinksound ts01 10mm In-Ear Headphone with Enhanced Bass and Passive Noise Isolation
review_headline: My ts01s fit so comfortably; the wooden cavity creates a really unique but ...
review_body:
I cannot speak more highly of thinksound as a company and their products. When my one-year-old ts01s began to fall apart (due to my own carelessness!), I emailed thinksound to inquire about if they could be repaired and how much that would cost. Ray Fournier emailed me back the next day informing me of a 1 year unconditional warranty; all I had to do was send in my old headphones. Less than a week later after sending my headphones to thinksound, I had a brand new pair waiting for me in my mailbox. And only a couple days after that, the president and CEO of thinksound emailed me personally to describe the damage to my old headphones and ways to avoid wrecking my new ones!

My ts01s fit so comfortably; the wooden cavity creates a really unique but stellar sound; and most importantly (to me) is that this company really cares about environmental sustainability. Their products and packaging are made with recycled materials. In fact, I stumbled upon thinksound by looking for a way to recycle old broken headphones. If you send in headphones (of any brand) that you want to recycle, you can get a 15% discount off of a pair of thinksound headphones (http://www.thinksound.com/recycle.php)

I think everything about this company is fantastic and I am really excited about the work that they do!

product_title: AUDIO TECHNICA Noise-Canceling Headphones
review_body:
I really want to like these noise-cancelling headphones but cannot. I will be returning them.

I bought these noise-cancelling headphones to replace an old pair from Sony which served me well for about 15 years and 250,000 miles. Over the last 1.5 days I've flown 5000-6000 miles and will be flying an additional 10,000 miles over the next 1.5 weeks.

I'm a very average-sized American male and these headphones are simply sized too small. My ears are a bit too large to fit inside the ear cups comfortably. I can almost live with that. Add to the fact that the headband will not comfortably fit over my head -- I need another inch -- and I find these unacceptable. When I get back home, They are getting sent back.

LIKE:
* Effective noise-cancelling
* Removable 3.5mm cord
* Sturdy storage/travel case

NO LIKE:
* Ear cups are too small
* Poor fit over the top of my head
* No volume control

review_headline: Great Sound. Warmer / Darker Signature. Excellent build quality!
review_body:
First, sound:

Great overall sound! When I compare this specific pair of buds to my Sony MDR EX110s ($25 on Amazon), these sound warmer in that they are somewhat bass and mid heavy. I don't dislike these, but when I compare to the Sony buds listening to the same songs with the same EQ (none) settings, these definitely have a different sound. Once you get used to the darker / warmer tone, you really start to like it. However, when compared to buds that have the brighter highs like the EX110s, I find I am wanting more with these. If you need to pick out the bass line or if you prefer a more bass-heavy sound, these are a great pick!

Build quality:

Best I've seen as yet in this price range. Metal 'cans' that shroud the buds, metal shroud surrounding the smart button (for smartphone stuff), and metal surrounding the plug, itself. The smart button works with my Android phone, Windows phone, and I'm sure would do the same with iPhone. It pauses music that is playing, resumes music that is paused, hangs up calls in progress, and when held activates the voice command feature of my Windows Phone (and I'm sure would do the same for everything else). The included carrying case is a great feature as well as it keeps me disciplined to properly wrap these up to store in the container. The case is almost exactly the same as the kind that comes with the lower end Shure in ear monitors, minus the wheel to wrap them around.

product_title: Etymotic Research 3-Flange Replacement Eartips - 10 Pack - Gray
review_body:
I bought these when the original tips would no longer stay on my Etymotic ER-6i's. Whereas the original tips held up for a few years, these ones are clearly more poorly made. After about a year of use, despite cleaning the mount with alcohol, these are already coming off, often remaining stuck in my ear. Perhaps a better sign of their poor quality is that they don't retain the original shape, easily becoming distorted -- a problem I never had with the originals.

Sound isolation is as good as the originals, which was the big selling point for me on the ER-6i, so I'll keep using the remaining tips until I run out. That factor and getting more use out of some expensive earphones are the only reason this gets 2 stars instead of 1.

Given the poor quality, these should be at most $1 a pair (so $5 for the pack). At the current price, I'd look into new earphones instead.

And if you happen to find a pair of earphones that are small and passively block out sound as well as the ER-6i did with these eartips, please leave a comment.

product_title: Philips HTL2160/F7 Philips Bluetooth Soundbar Speaker (Black)
review_headline: I would easily give if 5 stars
review_body:
Short answer:
If I could rate the sound bar only on size, appearance, sound amplification/improvement over television speakers, and value, I would easily give if 5 stars.

Now a bit more detail:
Didn't get from Amazon (unusual for me). I purchased a refurb unit from another site because at the time, it was considerably less than a new one on Amazon, but when looking for manufacturer's warranty information, I noticed that new units on Amazon Prime are now much closer to the price I paid for my refurb. Based on the current price, I almost could have bought a new unit from Amazon Prime for what I paid for my refurb + shipping + warranty. Granted, I have a 2 yr warranty vs. the 1 yr manufacturer's warranty, but the refurb didn't come with the AAA battery, whereas it looks like the battery is included in the new units, and the refurb didn't come with a connector cord (I knew that when I bought it, & not sure if they come with new units or not--I've read conflicting answers). All just observations to help those who are trying to compare, really, as I have no regrets about my purchase & already had the battery & the connector cable on hand.

Now the full review:
This replaced an old Bose 3-2-1 GS Series II in our bedroom. Other than the Bose's bumpin' bass (which I care nothing about for a bedroom), this system sounds as good as the old Bose--at least so long as the sound bar is not in surround sound mode. As others have commented, there's an awful reverb/tinny echo effect in surround sound mode. If you want true, booming, surround sound or are looking for a primary system for a large room, you might want to keep shopping. However, if you want greatly improved sound over television speakers for a bedroom, kid's room, office, etc., grab this sound bar & I think you'll be very pleasantly surprised.

review_body:
The only reviews to pay attention to are those that point out problems with the function and operation not related to sound quality. Most stereophiles love to throw out numbers and buzzwords to dazzle folks and to demonstrate just how much they can spend.

What you should do when choosing your gear is to go listen to it. Don't listen in demo rooms either. Listen to it in the store with lots of noise and bad speaker placement. This is closer to reality than a room set up by experts.
You will also get a good idea of the physical quality of the unit. If it's not missing knobs and the laminate is in good shape after dozens of people have played with it, it will certainly hold up in your living room.

Oh, and you don't need gold plating. That silliness came about when someone found out that high frequency signals travel on the surface of a conductor. You would have to be from Krypton to hear any difference. Just make sure the cable is well constructed. A poor connection at the plug will degrade the signal quality.

review_body:
You should join the lifestyle, its not a tabu, it works. I won't get technical, just give you the experience, simple and practical.

+ Save money recharging this batteries

CONS

= 10+ Engineering degree / field experience

review_body: Let's get one thing straight - there are no \\"magic\\" cables that will make a bad audio system good. But you can make an already good system deliver the most it possibly can with a quality set of cables. There are well-engineered cables, and poorly-engineered ones as well. Some insist that good sound can only be had after spending hundreds or even more on their interconnects. The Blue Jeans LC-1 cables are simply a revelatory product at bargain basement prices. I thought my old cables were good, and they were; but after installing the LC-1's, it was like a new experience. Admittedly, there was no A/B comparison. But I was acutely aware of the placebo effect; and as I spun up my first CD, I kept muttering \\"no placebo effect\\" over and over. I needn't have worried, because the overall impact was very apparent. No placebo here. It is hard to describe in words, but everything was clearer, more distinct and pronounced, even bass. I always listen for certain musical notes or effects in my music; and with the LC-1' s, everything had more presence. The harsh edges on highs and some instrumentals was gone without sacrificing any musicality. I had done some research before purchase as I have been aware that some snake oil salesmanship often accompanies discussions about cables. Everybody has an opinion. I recommend anybody interested in getting the straight scoop go to audioholics.com and peruse their articles on cables. They tolerate no BS. They also dislike snake oil cable merchants. Their own recommended systems have BJC LC-1's in them, including their ten thousand dollar, two channel system. The Blue Jeans website has good information too, and is also no BS, just straight talk and a little electrical engineering. Highly recommended.

product_title: Sennheiser Headphones
review_body:
I'm a real fan of these headphones. If you are looking for beautiful sound reproduction and a blissful listening experience at a (relatively) low cost then these are for you. Keep in mind that these are "open" earphones. They don't have a closed back so the music you listen to can be heard (at a lower level) by those around you and you will be able to hear things going on around you as well. This allows the headphone to produce a beautiful sound stage which means you hear the music around you rather than inside your head. If you are thinking about something to wear on a plane, around town or on the subway then these may not be the best choice. If you want a headphone that you can wear at home and that will make you fall in love with music all over again, then these are a great place to start.

If you like songs with great vocals, you will be very pleased with the HD598s. It has an amazing mid-range that really makes the singers pop. You get the sense that the vocals are right in front of you while the instruments are playing around the singer. A lot of people will say that the bass is lacking, but I disagree. I have found the bass to be tight and just what it should be to compliment the music. I have some bass heavy headphones and I never wear them anymore. The sound quality is great on my other phones, but the bass overpowers the music and muddies up the fine details in the music that come through so clearly with these Sennheisers.

Also, remember that your headphones are only as good as your music source. You want something that has a quality DAC (digital to analog converter) and enough power to drive your headphones. These HD598s are relatively easy to drive with an iPod or iPhone and will sound pretty good. If you want to unleash their full potential, look into a player like the Fiio X1, X3 or X5. A good quality DAC/Amp will remove the "noise" that you can get from lesser components and really let these headphones soar.nes soar.

These look nice. The shape is the first thing that people notice. They sure do look different then the bullet type headphones currently polluting the public. The build is made of sturdy plastic. it feels strong yet very VERY light. If you don't like heavy earphones, these will be fine for you.

The wire is just average and doesn't have any obvious memory effect. Likewise, they tangle like you would expect. One plus is that it is an OVER-EAR design. This means you HAVE to wear it with the wire looping over the top of your ear. This makes it harder to take off and put on BUT reduces cable noise(microphonics). It also has a nice sturdy L shape plug.

Another unique thing about the earphone that isn't shown very well, is that the wire close to the earphone itself has some kind of bendy wire over it. This makes it easy to shape that part into a c so you can easily wrap it around your ear. The problem with that is, it doesn't work very well. For me, the wire stuck up in an awkward shape and did more harm then good.

See that little hole in the earphone? Well that makes the earphone have such excellent bass. BUT in a windy situation, you will hear a LOT of noise from the wind blowing past that part. This can be avoided by simply taping that hole up but that does reduce sound quality.

So overall, Build quality is SLIGHTLY ABOVE AVERAGE for the price.

Sound

This is the important part. I didn't assume these needed an amp so I just ran them off my phone and my computer. The bass is definitely boosted in these. But in a good way. The second driver really helps make the bass rumble and tickle your ear(texture). It feels like you're listening to one of those big headphones that cover your whole head(circum aural)!

But, thats the only thing that is really special about it. The mids and the treble are definitely lacking. While the Bass is loud and very present, the mids and treble sound canned and distant. I'm not sure if mine was defective, but when the excellent bass is paired with the sub-par mids and treble, they really compound the balance of the earphone.

Some other things that audioethusiats talk about include soundstage, separation, and imaging. I personally don't know what imaging is really about but I think its something about clarity. For these, the bass really overwhelms everything. The mids and treble have poor imaging(clarity), separation, and soundstage. But the bass. Oh man, it has the soundstage. It feels like its out of your head. Very nice bass.

Overall, sound quality is sub-par if you are looking for a balanced headphone. If you like Beats, this will be good for you.

SUMMARY
So these headphones may not be everyone's cup of tea. Brainwavz is generally known as a competent headphone produces and I don't think they disappoint too much here. Its a ridiculously cheap dual driver headphone with a mic. The second cheapest dual driver headphone with a mic is the TTPOD T1s which is ~$45.

Should you get these? I don't know. Thats up to you to decide.

Thanks for reading!

review_headline: Great Sound, Functional, and Hefty Portable Boom Box!
review_body: I've been searching for a decent portable speaker to play my songs from my iPhone and laptop while at home or while at work.  I have owned the following brands:  iHome, Philips, Logitech, etc.  None have come close to the sound from this JAM Party Boom Box.  I listened to this speaker at my local big box store.  I liked what I heard especially being inside a big store.  Did not have to turn the volume up to hear the demo song.    I believe in \\"you get what you pay for\\".  Is this portable boom box speaker worth the price?  Yes!  It has two built in speakers that provides beautiful and enjoyable sound.  I've been listening to Maroon 5, Taylor Swift, Straight No Chaser (an a cappella group), Amy Grant, etc and I am enjoying the music from this speaker.    To hear a little more bass on my iPhone I have the music EQ set to \\"bass booster\\".    This speaker is hefty in weight.  It has a nice rubber-like handle that slides up and down along the sides of the speaker.  Underneath the speaker is a panel/kickstand that releases when pressure is applied to it.  It extends to support and raise the speaker (front) higher/angle.  The back of the speaker are two connectors that have a rubber-like cover.  There's a connector for the included power adapter and another connector for a 3.5mm audio cable (not included).  For me, I like having the capability to use bluetooth or line-in audio with my devices.    When the power button is pressed, a blue light comes on along with a short tone to let you know that bluetooth is searching for your device.  When your device is syncing/pairing, the blue light will blink for a moment.  After your device and the speaker is synced, the blue light will remain solid.  The on/sync light is on the left side of the box.  On the right side, the light is for recharging.    The volume can be adjusted via the boom box speaker and from your device (e.g. iPhone).  The speaker has the following buttons:  power on/off, track back, play/pause, track forward, volume -, and volume +.  This is a nice feature as I do not have to reach for my device (e.g. iPhone) to turn up the volume or forward to the next song.  There is a NOTE in the instructions that the track back and track forward does not work while the unit is using the line-in audio jack.    It takes around 3 hours to fully charge the speaker.  The battery should last around 8 hours via bluetooth and 12 hours when connected via line-in audio jack.    I'm enjoying my new portable speaker.    **  10/10/14  **    I've used this speaker with my MacBook Pro laptop via bluetooth while watching a movie.  Beautiful!  I turned on my bluetooth and in a few seconds my MBPro found the speaker called \\"Jam Party\\".    **  10/11/14  **    As a few others have mentioned in their reviews, there is an issue with the speaker dropping or fading in and out as the device (e.g. iPhone) is moved away from the speaker.  I've noticed it when I walked my iPhone away about 10 feet from the speaker.  I noticed it more when I walked behind something in the room.  Not too sure if I experienced an interference issue.  Still, not a huge issue for me.  Just confirming what others experienced.    **. 10/16/14. **    I saw an ad and review of the new Bose Sound Link Color.  I was intrigued with this portable speaker.  I visited my local electronics store to listen to this new Bose speaker.  Wow!  As in portable speaker size, colors, and mostly the awesome sound I was hearing.  I have to say the sound I was hearing from this speaker was truly beautiful.  I could clearly hear the lows and the highs as well as distinguishable bass.  With coupon in hand I purchased one in black.    Call me crazy, but I like both speakers.  They have a different function for my use.  I plan on using my Bose at home and will use my Jam Party at work.    I did notice that the Bose bluetooth signal is stronger.  I was able to walk away from the speaker with iPhone in my back pocket  about 25 feet with several walls between and theBose kept on playing...didn't skip a beat.  I did not have the same results with my Jam Party.    You get what you pay for.  If you can't afford the Bose, then I would go with the Jam Party.  If sound quality is key and you can afford $130 then I highly recommend the Bose Sound Link Color.  The next decision would be which color.    I have removed one star from my rating here.  That's in reference to the bluetooth capability/distance on this Jam Party.  It's now annoying that I can't walk away a short distance without it dropping the signal.  I'm spoiled by new Bose.    I will back to update my review to include battery charge and usage.  Stay tuned!

review_headline: Breaks iPhone 6 Touch ID (unless 2 USB devices are plugged in, or iPhone is out of case)
review_body:
Reviewing 2.1 amp 10 watt, 6-outlet version:

Odd: when iPhone 6 in a case, and is plugged into one USB port, the Touch ID does not work. When it is plugged into the small OEM charger brick or iPad charger it works with case on or off, but not when plugged into this unit with the case on.

BUT!
-- The Touch ID will start working when you plug in a second device. In this situation, both can be in cases.
-- The Touch ID will start working when plugged in with the case off and your hand/finger touching the metal back of the phone. (Yes, read that again.)
-- The Touch ID works when two devices are using both USB ports.

According to Belkin, the unit sends 2.1 amps to one USB, and when 2 devices are plugged into the USBs it splits the power. My guess is plugging in one USB sends too much power to the iPhone 6 causing it to turn off the Touch ID? Know that this unit's USB port is 10 watts, the Apple small charger cube that comes with phones is 5 watts, and the iPad is 12 watts.

Unplugging the devices allows the Touch ID to work again, and I never experienced the phones getting hot during charging.

The regular power outlets work fine, and have good tight connections. I also found that the distance between the outlets worked well and did not cause the plug clashing you can experience on other devices.

I my case, this unit is of no use to me since there are times only one USB device is plugged in and I like to use the Touch ID to log into the phone while plugged in. So, I'll be returning the units I bought.

product_title: AmazonBasics In-Ear Headphones with Microphone (Tangle-Free Cable)
review_headline: Entry-Level Earphones with Boomy Bass. Good for On-The-Go Use.
review_body:
The AmazonBasics brand strives to bring everyday items at a value, and from this perspective, the AmazonBasics Premium In-Ear Headphones are pretty respectable. Essentially, these are entry-level earphones that seem to be pretty well made, and they have some premium features such as a flat cable that resists getting tangled, an in-line microphone with remote, a choice of S/M/L silicone ear tips, and a black pouch with AmazonBasics branding.

In terms of sound, these are a bit of a mixed bag ~ low-end bass is significantly boosted while the mid-range and highs suffer from a little lack of detail. The strong bass makes electronic dance music and action movies sound pretty good, but the muddy midrange and treble make lighter and more detailed music sound flat. In the grand scheme of things, I don't think anyone buying these earphones expects sonic perfection ~ instead, they are looking for good functionality at a good price, and that's more or less what you get: punchy music is served up pretty well and the built-in microphone/in-line remote worked equally well with Android, iOS, and Windows Phones. (I tried a Motorola G, iPhone 6, and Samsung Activ S)

I compared these earphones to the Apple EarPods that came with my iPhone 6 and unfortunately, I can't say that the AmazonBasics were always better. While on the go, the AmazonBasics blocked significantly more outside noise and the strong bass felt rather fun and put a spring in my step. The EarPods have a more finicky fit and don't really block outside noise particularly well, but in quiet environments, they sounded more balanced and had fuller highs and mids.

Earphones are a very personal item and everyone has different preferences ~ If you're just looking for is some earphones to wear while doing stuff and want the ability to take phone calls and such, I believe the AmazonBasics Premium In-Ear Headphones aren't a bad choice.

Note:
1) These headphones really strongly emphasize bass. I listened to a few bass sweeps from 1Hz to 100Hz and quite amazingly, the bass can be felt at 20Hz and it becomes clearly audible at 30-35Hz. I repeated the tests with my [[ASIN:B009FRPMXY Audio Technica ATH-CKS99i]] earphones (which are part of their \\"Solid Bass\\" lineup) and they didn't reach the same bass loudness until 40-45Hz ~ the Audio Technica's have much tighter bass response and the highs and mids are significantly more clear. I repeated the same test again with my [[ASIN:B000XPG2QI Etymotic Research HF5]] earphones (which are recognized as being very accurate) and they didn't reach peak bass volume until ~ 55-60Hz but when it comes to mids and highs and clarity, the HF5's completely outclass both the AmazonBasics and the Audio Technica CKS99i's.sweeps from 1Hz to 100Hz and quite amazingly, the bass can be felt at 20Hz and it becomes clearly audible at 30-35Hz. product_title: Genuine National JDSLABS Objective2 Black Edition By NwAvGuy Headphone Amplifier JDS LABS (Made in USA)
review_body:
Wow, this product totally lived up to its reputation: got effortlessly robust and flawlessly neutral/accurate sound out of it ... powering my AKG K240s, which have never sounded better. Was using the Fiio E07K Andes before, and while that wasn't bad at all, I felt like I had to have its volume almost maxed out to get enough dynamics out of my AKGs.

With this O2 amp I get tons of headroom, never have to go past the 12 o'clock position...in fact most of the time I'm around 9 o'clock...and that's using 1.0x gain not the default 2.5 - 6.5 gain. Getting lots of detail and dynamics without having to crank up the volume or even use the high-gain button...this is the mark of true audiophile-grade equipment, being able to enjoy it at moderate or even low volumes rather than feeling like you have to blast it. Bass is authoritative, tighter and faster than with the Fiio, and treble seems more extended without any harshness...just good honest flat frequency response. Mids were good before, and sound even better now that the two ends of the frequency spectrum are more fully fleshed out, there is more of a coherent musical effect.

A note on DACs: they do make a difference! I started out using my cheap Turtle Beach Micro Advantage USB soundcard, which definitely had a thinner edge to the higher frequencies and generally seemed a little rough and hollow. I then switched to the RCA outputs of my NuForce uDAC2, which I had been using less and less as a USB headphone amp after buying the Fiio...definite improvement in terms of a fuller and smoother sound! Think I'll hold on to the uDAC2 for a while. I am looking forward to hearing how the Fiio sounds in its DAC-only mode, when my Fiio L7 Line Out Dock arrives in a few days...stay tuned for an update!

btw, I am extremely glad I ordered this directly from JDS Labs, for the following reasons:

1. 2. You get free laser engraving of an image or text on top of the case, by attaching an electronic image.

3. You get to choose which kind of AC adapter you want (different voltages for different geographical regions).

4. The lettering on the front is way, way more attractive...just go to their website to compare. My O2 looks like some kind of precision laboratory instrument! If you like the classic handsome looks of a black dial Seiko diver's watch like I do, you'll love it!

5. Their customer service, speed of shipping, and quality of packaging was truly impeccable. Wish that all companies did business like this!

6. They also sell very cool accessories like a 3\\" and a super-mini 1\\" C-shaped interconnect cable, quite reasonably priced.

7. They are extremely knowledgeable, responsive and helpful in answering technical questions about their products.

This very simple, easy to use, clock radio works exactly as I'd hoped it would. I noticed some previous review complained about some issues that this unit does not have. Specifically, someone complained that the display is not dimmable.. This unit (with two separate wake up alarms) IS dimmable. The snooze bar, when tapped, will toggle thru three different levels of brightness. Maybe the OTHER (similar) radio, with ONE alarm does not have this capability?
All I had to do to set it up, was to select the proper time zone (simple). THAT is the real beauty of this device, is that everything is simple to operate. Mechanical switches to turn alarms on and off and a mechanical (analog) tuner. I prefer digital tuners, but for a clock radio, the analog works great. The button to cancel the alarm is easy to find (on top). There are forward and reverse buttons to set clock and alarm times. Initial time was already set when it was delivered. Daylight savings time will adjust automatically... if it doesn't (at the end of this month) I will come back and add a comment to that effect. So far, it's been perfect... Oh, and... obviously, since this unit is a 4" cube, don't expect home theater sound to come from the speaker... this is a small clock radio, and sounds good enough to serve it's purpose.

product_title: Sony ICF-SCI Radio Frequency Scanner (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
The Sony ICF-SC1 was also sold in 1998 as the Sony ICF-SC1PC (the PC version having included programming software and cable for easy access to regional frequencies relevant to the user's interests - and locations). Powered by 4 AA batteries, the device was manufactured with a frequency range of 25-1300 MHz using AM, FM, WFM or NFM modes. There is a fabulous cheat-code direct keypad entry modification (that I found online) that enables extended frequency coverage for shortwave bands (at 5 KHz steps)! (Note: Once you perform the modification, Access to shortwave bands is only possible using Memory Page Bank 10. Also, the current memory banks MAY be cleared requiring you to reprogram the radio once you finish the Mod. But when I did mine, the scanner retained my previous frequencies... so I would assume the same for your procedure) Here it is:

*SHORTWAVE KEYPAD MODIFICATION - Enables reception below 25 MHz
1. Set the SQL (squelch) to MIN (minimum). Keep the volume level
whatever you like.
2. Power on the scanner.
3. Press the PAGE then key#1 and Key#10/0 and then EXE key to get to
page 10. You will hear a beep and display will show - - -.- - - for
few seconds and then it might bring some frequency on the display. It
depends if there was any frequency in the Intelligent memory in the
scanner. Don't bother at this stage that what Intelligent memory
is. You can read it latter in your manual.
4. Now go to preset 01. Press `PRESET' key then key#1 and
then EXE key. The display will be - - - .- - - with Page 10 on the
right hand corner and Preset 01 below it.
5. To put the scanner in the scanning mode press the SCAN key. The
bank / page number 10 will start flashing.
6. If any other page numbers are flashing, turn them off by pressing
the corresponding page number. For instance if both 1 and 10 are
flashing, press the 1 key. This should leave only the 10 flashing.
7. Turn the power off, then back on.
8. Press BAND then key#1. (Note you can press any key between 1 an 9
and this will work)
9. Cycle the power , off then on.
The result should be that the scanner is on 00.020 MHz and hasn't
scanned past it because the min squelch has held it there. Save this
frequency in any preset number / channel number in page 10. Follow
the procedure below.

Preset Tuning (PROGRAMMING A FREQUENCY INTO A CHANNEL)
1. Press SCAN, if necessary, to enter into manual mode.
2. The frequency 00.020 is already displayed.
3. Press EXE.
4. Press, and hold down ENTER, *NOTE* ENTER must be held down for the
remainder of this procedure.
5. Enter the number of the bank (PAGE) where the frequency is to be
stored. In this case press Key # 1 and Key # 10/0 to get to page 10.
(remember do not release the ENTER key until you finish all the
steps).
6. Press EXE.
7. Enter the number of the channel (PRESET) where the frequency is to
be stored. ( you can store the frequency between channel # 1 and 30
in Page 10).
8. Press EXE.
9. Release the enter key.

Out of production since about 1998, this scanner is getting very difficult to find. Keep in mind it is NOT a digital trunking scanner and will NOT seamlessly follow UHF, 800 or 900 MHz public safety systems in use by most police, fire and municipal services today. But I have programmed in all of my area's relevant 800 MHz EDACS/APCO frequencies by straddling them unevenly (out of numeric order) throughout one of the ten 30 channel banks (sony calls them \\"pages\\") - and this seems to work very well, as I can lock out or \\"skip\\" the noisy digital control frequencies and follow most of the dispatched radio traffic with some level of efficiency. The Priority feature is great, and can be used when listening to shortwave broadcasts and HF frequencies... as well as the normal reception bands. The radio is verypleasing to look at and handle. Sony's previous two scanner models (the Sony Air 7/8 and the ICF-Pro 70/80 had a red busy signal LED indicator (which I wish they had included on this model). But those earlier radios were limited to 10 memory channels - while the ICF-SC1 has 300 channels! More than enough for the basic scanner radio user's purposes! I love this radio and don't regret purchasing it at all (mine was like 'nib' from ebay for $130.00). Mark S. Bias KC9TSRodel). product_title: SENTRY Headphones
review_headline: Works Better When Correctly Installed And Not Connected to Crappy TV
review_body:
I got these from Big Lots. The transmitter can be plugged into an electric outlet to save on battery cost with a universal power cord found at Wal-Mart (among other stores).
If you have digital cable, it must be plugged into the digital sound ports. The guy who set mine up and a friend of mine both swore to me that there were no other places to plug the audio cables into but I asked her to look again (with a flashlight) as the guy said there were inputs for digital audio. All I could get were radio stations when the audio cable was plugged into the audio input.

Once the audio cable was plugged into the digital audio jacks, the tv station I had on came through loud and clear. However, if the volume on the headphones is too high, there is a hum.

I have owned these before, but was not all satisfied with them and tossed them due to the loud hum and difficulty in getting, and keeping a signal. Also, the transmitter had to be placed a distance from the tv and cable box that kept the short cord taut.

I decided to get another pair because the hum and constant static was better than listening my husband's constant nagging and shouting.

In the intervening months, I was given an HDTV and upgraded cable box.
Turns out the problem wasn't headphones, it was my ancient television. Also, the transmitter now sits in front of cable box next to the television, rather than on a shelf previously 3 feet high that kept falling. Oops.

If the headphones either fit over one's ears or in one's ears, I would have given it 5 stars.

Kat

review_headline: Online reviews were right. Great buy!
review_body:
While our in a store with my family, I was in the electronics department playing with the on display electronics. I heard how nice the Bose speaker box sounded, but thought the price was insane. I was willing to deal or pay for a full surround sound system, so I researched more on these sound boxes. I read that this one was even "close" to being audiophile quality. I bought it, hooked it up, played a movie... I was blown away. My living room isn't that big, so this model was perfect to fill my room. If you have larger rooms, you may want to check out the larger models. The Zvox is great for movies, listening to music, or just watching your favorite TV shows. It actually looks good sitting under my TV. If anything ever happened to this one, I'd buy another in a heart beat.

review_headline: Receive both UHF and VHF Channels up to 60 miles away!
review_body: I decided that I wanted to leave cable TV and go to over the air broadcasts.  I live 35 - 60 miles from the Tampa station antennas and 45 - 55 miles from the Orlando broadcast antennas. Not knowing much about what equipment to use I read a lot of manufactures information, articles and reviews about antenna systems and Antennas Direct came up with much positive information.  I decided to try the Clear Stream 2-V UHF/VHF antenna and the PA-18 pre-amplifier.  Our home owners association does not allow outside antennas so mine is in the attic.  I put the PA-18 mounted to the antenna mount and the power input 3 feet from the PA-18 with the lead to a 5 way spliter 6 feet from the PA-18 power input.  I used antennapoint.com to find the angle of both the Tampa and Orlando antennas and set the angle of the antenna more towards Tampa (the reception angle of the antenna also was adequate to receive most of Orlando.)  I tested the antenna and PA-18 on a table and received 22 channels and in the attic I receive 44 channels.  Picture and sound quality are better than with cable.

product_title: RCA RCR313BZ 3-Device Universal Remote Control
review_body: I didn't need anything elaborate to control a multiple of devices; I just needed a remote for my cheap, small tv that I got for free but didn't have a remote. So, I tried a couple of other basic remotes, and this was the only one that truly worked as it was supposed to, responding to inputs correctly. Additionally, coding was a snap - I only needed to enter the first code for it to work. Plus, it has a nice big 'power' button instead of the tiny power button that is found on nearly any other remote. That's a big benefit, to me.    It's worth mentioning that I tried what seems to be the most basic RCA remote ([[ASIN:B0056DR44Q Rca Two Device Universal Remote Control Oversized Buttons Hd Digital Sub Channel Support]]) but had no luck coding it. Whatever I tried, I could not get the channel select switch to work. It's too bad because that one had great big volume and channel toggles, the biggest I've seen. But, for the same price (or even less) this remote, the RCA313BR, has been great.    Another thing I rather like is the use of AA batteries instead of the smaller AAA. Maybe it's just me, but although it makes the remote slightly heavier and bigger, I just like the bigger batteries. If nothing else, they're a bit easier to find than AAA, the same price, and hold a bit more juice.    Although it technically has a backlight switch, it's pretty useless, only lighting up the circular control and power button.    I dinged it one star just for not being able to find the sub channel entry procedure in the instructions (use the '-' key to enter the '.' on the numeric keypad).    Note: There is an older, discontinued version of this remote,[[ASIN:B000FCSWX0 RCA RCR311BR Three-Device Universal Remote (Discontinued by Manufacturer)]]. The buttons aren't arranged quite as logically, as well as lacking the two, large volume and channel toggles on either side of the main, circular control.

product_title: APC Back-UPS Pro
review_headline: Per APC Tech Support, their Back-UPS PRO does not work with Apple iMac
review_body:
I've used an APC Back-UPS XS 1000 for years now. It didn't give me very much backup time, but the iMac worked properly when the battery cut in. Recently, the XS 1000 started to swap to the battery very frequently even with low sensitivity, so it was time to replace it.

I wanted a longer runtime for both the computer as well as the wifi and modem, so I went with a new APC Back-UPS Pro RS 1500G. It shows 1 hour of backup time with normal loads. All seemed well .. until I tested the backup function. When the iMac is on the backup battery from the new UPS, there is an odd fairly loud sound from the center bottom of the iMac. One of those sounds that makes one uneasy when it's coming from your iMac. Everything I've read states that the iMac doesn't need a pure sine wave. This is a 27" iMac that was new in May 2013, so it's a newer model.

So I spoke to both the main Apple Tech Support as well as the local authorized Apple Repair Tech Support. Both stated that the new iMac's can run properly on a step simulated sine wave. That they do not need a UPS with a pure sine wave to operate properly. Both Apple Techs felt it was likely a problem with the first APC Back-UPS Pro and recommended that I replace it as it was obviously defective.

I returned the "defective" APC Back-UPS Pro 1500 and got a new replacement. Both are/were model BR1500G. I setup the new UPS but hadn't had the time to check the backup function before we had a real power outage that lasted for several hours yesterday. I was using the iMac when the power went out and the iMac immediately started making the same loud, unpleasant, disturbing noise. I recorded the noise and shut the computer down. I was even more concerned when I realized that even with the iMac turned off, it was making a clicking noise .. the APC UPS battery was still supplying the wifi and router .. at that time I just shut down the APC UPS.

So I called APC Tech Support thisafternoon. As previously noted, the old APC UPS had no problems supporting my iMac and Apple Tech Support told me that the iMac DOES NOT need a pure sine wave UPS.

Well, according to the APC Tech Support person I spoke with, their APC Back-UPS PRO line no longer supports iMac and the only APC UPS's that will work with a newer model iMac are the APC SMART line. Not my words, theirs.

As I'm NOT going to pay $400+ for a APC UPS, guess this one is going back and I'll get a Tripp Lite.

So not only does APC not support Apple with their software, but now, per their own statement, they don't support Apple products with anything but their most expensive SMART UPS line.

Bye bye APC.

review_body:

The Charge 2 seems to be a bit brighter (more treble) than the Bose Mini. The Bose is warmer and it definitely has more bass punch and impact. I like bass punch and IMO the Bose sounds better than the Charge 2, but this is highly subjective. The Bose seems to be capable of playing a bit louder than the Charge 2. The Bose has a replaceable battery, but the Charge 2 will play much longer on a battery charge cycle. The Charge 2 supports speaker phone, social mode, and USB charging. The \\"phone\\" button on the Charge 2 can be used to pause, resume, and skip tracks. The Bose does not allow you to pause and skip from the speaker.

The Bose is a much nicer looking unit and it looks great sitting on a desk in my office. The Bose looks and feels much more substantial than the Charge 2.

product_title: Bose Solo 15 TV Sound System, Black
review_headline: Superb quality, treble a bit low, almost eliminates the need for a sub
review_body: Summary: Superb construction, Truly, short of surround sound receiver set-up, best all in one high quality super easy to hook up sound solution, better than a sound bar, and no need for a sub woofer. If you do not want the complications of a receiver and multi speakers, or if you value room aesthetics with minimal sound quality trade offs, this is the way to go. The trade offs are too mellow highs with no adjustment possible and no \\"simulated\\" surround sound mode. The THX sound test available on some discs sounds excellent. All of the speakers, including the rear, in the THX test, except the subwoofer provided output.    Details- Plusses  Looks good, solid, supports even 55\\" Samsung (see photo, 75 lbs is the limit), easy hookup with just two wires, power and optical sound connector.  The slight elevation from the TV siting on top helped out my viewing angle from the couch.  I did not give up TV sound (instructions suggest turning it off}, on my set you can simply turn it to zero. The combination of high end treble, and Bose low-mid range gave me the best overall sound.  The Samsung TV has adjustable SPIDF audio delay and I was able to sync TV and Bose sound perfectly with no echo. When I use both, I get a great sound stage with bass, and if I throw in some delay, it really sounds like a huge sound stage.  Turning on the cable box, TV, and Solo 15 all with one button push works great. The remote is solid, somewhat large.    Minuses:  You Give up TV digital control and effects such as Samsung Tru Surround Sound (it really opens up the sound stage and Solo 15 sounds narrow by comparison, when TV sound mode is set to normal they sound similar),  Auto level equalization, the TV when set to Normal does a good job of holding down overtly loud commercials, Solo 15 does not have an equivalent function  Great bass, and good midrange, so so treble  No equalizer, can use a little 5kHz-10kHz boost  By using the TV's only optical out you give up surround sound decoding in the receiver, I now use the optical from Blu-ray for that.  Should have pass thru on the digital out if you want to utilize additional speakers  The remote code for Yamaha did not work with my receiver. I had difficulty following the booklet code search instructions. The keys feel sticky and the bottom of the remote is rounded. Its the only remote I have where you cannot push a key with one finger while its lying down on the coffee table, the remote will simply flip over.    Neutral: Dialogue mode for me just sounds different, and not clearer, certainly sounds weird with some programs such as football games. The biggest effect is that it cuts out the low frequencies, where any boominess may obscure the dialogue.  In the past the Blu-ray fit between TV and the top of entertainment center. Now had to move it since it overhangs the speaker    Wish list: Speaker top on/off and volume buttons, LED volume indicator  Blue tooth connection with a possible Android/Ios app to control internal equalization.    I like it, certainly better than average, but short of five stars. With Bose this is a second generation Solo speaker (Solo 10 was smaller), perhaps with the next one they will add the app driven equalization and digital surround sound effects option for those that like them.

product_title: Sony NWZE38 Walkman MP3 Player
review_headline: Good non-Apple Replacement for a Zen
review_body: I bought this to replace a Creative Zen MX that finally bit the dust after 5 years of heavy use and isn't available anymore. The Walkman's operation is nearly the same, so that eased my transition, but the actual available space (14.4gb) is 0.2 less, which forced me into some unexpected deletions from my library (as I'd had the Zen pretty well stuffed). Had a few problems copying files (for which I used Windows Explorer): the Walkman sometimes insisted on duplicating one album's files in another's folder, overwriting the original. Don't know what was going on, but I finally got around it by renaming folders.    The sound is full and balanced, neither too much bass nor too much treble, so I'm well pleased. There's a \\"clear stereo\\" setting by which you're supposed to \\"obtain maximum effect\\" with the buds they provide, but I couldn't hear the least bit of difference; nor did I notice any difference between the preset equalizer settings, even with better headphones. (The ability to make these refinements never meant much to me even on previous players, so maybe I've got a tin ear - but if fine-tuning the sound matters to you, be advised.) One playback feature I love is the ability to shuffle all of an artist's tracks across folders, which the Zen wouldn't do. Another advantage over the Zen is that it doesn't need to be unlocked to advance tracks after the screen goes dark. You can also [supposedly] normalize volume across tracks. Maybe these features are common with newer players, but they were a step up for me.    My only mild quibbles are with the hardware: the headphone jack is at the bottom (a pretty stupid design choice, IMO) and the screen is so small that it wasn't worth importing any photos. (So, okay, it's a more compact device, but I can't imagine anyone using its video function.) I also question the logic behind the shutdown procedure: instead of actually turning off, it's left in standby mode for 4 hours, sipping at battery life. But I can't understand otherreviewers' confusion over volume control - it's just the up/down arrows, no problem.    So all things considered, for playing mp3 files - which is my only requirement - it turned out to be a good, economical choice in a shrinking market for such players (especially if you're determined to avoid Apple products). And thanks to Amazon for saving me a few bucks with a \\"warehouse deal.\\"    Update, 10/24/14    After using this for 3 weeks and still not being able to tell any difference between the equalizer presets (none, heavy, pop, jazz, unique), I thought there was a chance that I had a defective unit so returned it and bought another. I think I can safely report that it's not just my ears: there's really no perceptible difference between the presets. However, you can adjust the bass/treble on 2 \\"custom\\" presets and that does make a difference.

review_body:
I have a pretty extensive headphone collection, but I was in the market for a wireless set to use on my bus commute and came across an Amazon Warehouse deal for these. While definitely not perfect, the sound is the best I've heard yet from a wireless headset, especially when paired with an AptX supported bluetooth module (ex. - Creative W1). NFC pairing is great, and the 3 level noise cancellation is well done (just don't forget to turn it off when you power down the headset since it doesn't automatically do it.)

In terms of "cons," the side controls take some getting used to, and they're a bit hard to find just by touch alone. The headset has a premium look in pics, and it's certainly heavy enough to suggest quality components (too heavy on the head, though), but something about the overall look at feel isn't QUITE up to what I'd call premium. Finally, while I think the average person would find the sound to be pretty great, I'm a little spoiled by some of my higher-end open air sets, so these occasionally feel a little muted and claustrophobic. They're also LARGE (no folding or anything here). They will take up most of the space in your travel bag, but the nifty carrying bag they include is a nice touch.

Overall, I'm perfectly happy with the purchase. If you know what you're gaining and losing with wireless audio, and you don't mind the tradeoffs and the size here, I think you'll feel the same.

The earbuds fit in my ears very snug and there is no way those things are coming out. Noise isolating is correct! The over-the-ear wire prevents the earbuds from coming loose while running, etc. The memory wire could be a bit more stiff but it's good enough to get the job done, but even without the memory wire you don't have to worry about it because it's designed so well. The only time that the buds have come kinda loose is after I have been sweating for awhile, but I just gently push them back in and I'm good again. Most times that never even happens.

The sound quality is actually awesome. I've never heard better quality out of earbuds before. I have some cheap-o brand earbuds with a microphone for my phone when I'm in the car and it works ok but I would never be able to get the quality out of it like these. Even the bass is nice with them.

Cleaning is kind of a pain but it's good to do so that you don't get some weird ear infection or something. I wish that I had got the ones with a microphone so that I could take a call while running. I'm going to get a set for my wife for sure

product_title: APC Wall Tap Surgearrest Essential P6WU2
review_headline: Have several, all excellent, a few points to keep in mind...
review_body:
We selected this unit because of its simple neutral white color, and the fact that the plugs on the end face outward. Some wall surge protectors have the ground plug (the third round one) facing the wall, which makes the unit useless for any three prong power adapters. This unit is done right, looks clean, has easy to see lights that won't annoy you in a dark room, and is very easy to install. The included screw was long enough for all but one of our outlets, so we picked up a few longer machine screws at our local hardware store. After much research, we found these to be one of the top two or three best rated units out there. They are used in a lightning prone area, and since installing them, we have seen no damaged to our connected electronics.

KEEP IN MIND, that this unit has only ONE plug (on the back) that goes into the wall, and it goes into the top plug of the wall receptacle. Therefore, if you use this in a receptacle where the top plug is switched (meaning a receptacle connected to a light switch), that particular light switch will turn the entire surge protector on and off. Also, if your receptacle is upside down, then you will need to install this unit upside down as well, which is not as attractive as right side up.

product_title: Audio-Technica AT-LP240-USB Direct-Drive Turntable with USB Output (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
Overall, I am very pleased with this turntable. I currently have a number of vintage turntables including a Thorens TD 160 Super, Dual 1229, Marantz 6170 and Pioneer PL-112D. I also have a recent Pro-Ject Debut Carbon. I bought the Audio Technical AT-LP240 primarily to transfer vintage albums to digital format as a back up. However, I have found this to be a very solid and pleasing turntable for general playback too.

Sound: (Comments based on using the pre-amp in my Pioneer SX-980) I am using an LP Gear AT95SA cartridge on the turntable(TT). This is a good all around performer and has an upgrated Shibata stylus. It works well with the AT-LP240 table. So far I have about 15 hours on the new catridge and table. To my ears, this turntable sounds very good. It has very good mid presence and high end. The bass is solid, but not overly done. The bass response may improve as the cartridge breaks in. I was really impressed by the sound and quality overall considering the reasonable price.

Speed Control: The speed on this TT is servo controlled and seems to be very accurate. I have read several reviews saying that the speed as shown by the dot/strobe is drifting slightly (i.e., the dots seem to be slowly moving). I watched mine intently and at first I thought the other reviewers had a point. However, if you take pencil or a pointer or some sort and hold it steady as a reference point above the strobe dots at 33 rpm, the dots never moved at all. I think the drift noted in some reviews is sort of an optical illusion because the other dots for 45 and 78 move in the opposite direction. I have found the speed of my AT LP-240 to be very steady both by observation and by listening.

USB: I have only used this sparingly so far for recording and the sound is pretty good. I have not tweaked my recording setup yet, so I will post comments related to using the USB feature for recording later.

Other: The overall presentation of theturntable and arm is very high quality. The arm itself was easy to set up for the new cartridge. The phono cables provided were better than expected for this price point. The TT presents a very classy look (Not vintage looking, but very nice and clean). The TT came packed very well.

The main negative comment is that the TT cover is not hinged. It is sort of pain to have to mess with it. I understand the cover would be in the way for a DJ table, but since the 240 is geared for home use, a hinged cover would have been more convenient.

Also, the specs for this TT are not overwhelming from a performance standpoint and I do not have the tools to measure them directly. Even so, I expect them to actually measure better than stated in the literature. I do not hear any appreciable wow and flutter under careful listening.

The AT-LP240 is the version of the AT-LP1240 that is more for home listening and recording use and not meant to be DJ table. It has a cleaner more professional look to me than the AT-LP1240. The 240 does not have some of the more DJ specific features of the AT-1240, but I do not need those extra features at all. Otherwise, the specs of the two tables are the same and I suspect the 1240 would perform similarly well.

In summary, I have had many TTs over the last 40 years. Some are much better than others and my favorite is the Thorens TD-160 Super. Each of my other TTs has very good things to offer from a practical listening standpoint. However, the AT-LP240 really surprised me. It sounded much better than I expected. I have enjoyed listening to it very much and I think any person that wanted a spare table, a table for a second system, or wanted a good value in a TT to replace an older faulty TT would really like this unit. I have found myself listening to it frequently regardless of my other options. I like it at least as well as my other newer TT, the Pro-Ject Debut Carbon with the 2M Red cartridge.

review_body:
People who are shopping for this have probably already decided they want this small form factor 'on-ear' style (vs larger 'over-the-ear' or 'bud' style).

Two other earphones that I considered were the sennheiser on-ear momentum and the bowers & wilkins p3. I did not get the opportunity to listen to either of those, but I'd wager they sound, look and feel great. The professional reviews for these three are all over the place, and it really shows what a subjective issue headphone preference is. I chose the SOHO over the momentum because it was smaller and less 'flashy' and over the p3 because it was cheaper (used amazon marketplace vendor) and slightly smaller.

Though I can't compare the three i can assert the following about the sohos. (I currently have some decent JVC noise cancelling headphones, and various buds.) 1. They are extremely small. I expected small, but was in for a pleasant surprise anyway. 2. They are very well made and quite stylish. 3. They are very comfortable. The jvcs feel like a vise on my head. These are so light i barely notice them, even after a few hours. 4. Sound quality is really good. They are leaps and bounds better than my current headphones, or anything I've ever owned including some older sennheiser studio models. Many reviewers emphasize the technical aspects of headphone sound. All i can say is they sound great. Crisp, clear, accurate. Very pleased with this aspect. If the other two i mentioned sound better it would take a very particular or trained ear to discern it, I'm sure. 5. Sound bleeding out to surroundings is minimal. 6. External sound isolation is just so so. 7. The in-cup cable insertion and cable device controller are very clever and work very well. 8. The small, light, comfortable factor works against on head stabilty, but not terribly so.

If you have narrowed your headphone search to a few competing sets like i did, but cant test all in person, i can heartily recommend the HK. You will not have buyer's remorse. You will not find yourself thinking 'damn these suck! i shoulda got the b&w!!'.ot have buyer's remorse. You will not find yourself thinking 'damn these suck! i shoulda got the b&w!!'.

product_title: VideoSecu ML531BE TV Wall Mount for most 22"-55" LED LCD Plasma Flat Screen Monitor up to 88 lb VESA 400x400 with Full Motion Swivel Articulating 20 in Extension Arm, HDMI Cable & Bubble Level WP5
review_headline: Compatibility with Sony 40" and 48" W600B displays (KDL-40W600B and KDL-48W600B)
review_body:
I was very impressed with the build quality of this mount. The mount included all of the hardware (screws/bolts) I needed for installation. I used my own tools and wrenches.

I used this mount (VideoSecu ML531BE) with several Sony TVs (KDL-40W600B and KDL-48W600B) which both required a 300x200 mm VESA wall-mount hole pattern. This mount includes a large square plate that accommodates up to 200x200 mm VESA patterns, plus optional "wings" that can be attached to accommodate larger mounting patterns (including 300x200 mm). I used the four short 6mm screws included with the mount to attach the mounting plate to the TV.

Be aware that various outputs on the Sony W600B displays are positioned between the four VESA mounting screws. Only the side ports (HDMI #1/MHL, Analog/Headphone Audio Out, USB #1, USB #2) are easily accessible.

This wall mount bracket blocks the following ports on the back of both Sony W600B displays:

Digital Audio Out (aka S/PDIF)
Audio/Video In (L/R/Video)
Component In (L/R/Pr/Pb/Y)
Ethernet

You may be able to drill a hole to access the Digital Audio Out or Ethernet ports, but the other ports should be considered unusable. Fortunately, I do not need any of these ports. These displays support ARC and I am using HDMI to a receiver that supports ARC (Audio Return Channel), so I do not need the Digital Audio Out.

This wall mount bracket also restricts access to HDMI #2 (ARC), HDMI #3, and HDMI #4 ports and the "Cable/Antenna" coaxial input. There is enough clearance for these wires between the mounting bracket and the TV, but you *MUST* connect your HDMI cable(s) and your Cable TV cable to the TV *BEFORE* attaching the TV to the mounting bracket.

I attached several short cables to these ports so that I could easily swap cables without removing the mount. The cables must be at least 5-6" long to stick out of the small gap between the mount and the TV.

The following cables were a bit long, but worked well for me. If I need to move the TV, I can easily disconnect my HDMI and Coax connections without removing the mounting plate.

Monoprice 8-inch 28AWG High Speed Male to Female HDMI Port Saver
RadioShack 1-foot RG-6/U 75-Ohm Coax Cable (P/N 1500020) w/ RadioShack F-connector (coax) female Audio Coupler (P/N 2780477)and the TV.

The following cables were a bit long, but worked well for me. If I need to move the TV, I can easily disconnect my HDMI and Coax connections without removing the mounting plate.

Monoprice 8-inch 28AWG High Speed Male to Female HDMI Port Saver

product_title: Bose QuietComfort 25 Headphones (wired, 3.5mm)
review_headline: Not worth the upgrade from QC-15...
review_body:
My review is geared more towards QC15 owners wondering if they should upgrade. I myself was under this dilemma, debating whether it was worth it, and up until now there were pretty much no reviews comparing both headphones. So I gave in to temptation and decided to bite the bullet and buy myself the QC25 to compare to my QC15 so that I could use it on a long-haul flight that I was about to take, which I already took, which is why I am writing this review now. So yes, I have actually compared side-by-side both headphones on the battlefield. I think this is the best place to compare them, where they are meant to be used, as opposed to going in store and trying them on there. At least in the stores where I have seen the demos, there is no flight noise simulation, so I think that such trying out is useless.

Anyways, results? I think I am keeping my QC 15.

To be specific, here is why:

1) In the noise canceling department, I honestly could not tell a difference between the QC15 and QC25. Maybe some people claim that the QC25's noise cancellation is better than the QC15's (I've read quite a few reviews saying so), but I suspect that that is more of a psychological influence in which the NC on the QC25 is considered better just because the QC25 is a newer model than the QC15. This reminds me of a psychology experiment in which our professor held an opened small bottle with a special aromatic liquid inside, and told us that within a few minutes the whole room would slowly begin to be filled with its very powerful, but attractive aroma... She then asked us to raise our hands as soon as we smelled the aroma. A few minutes later when about two-thirds of the lecture hall had their hands up (about 120 students were there present) she revealed to us that it was just water in there! Anyways, I think you get my point here. Don't get me wrong, there is nothing wrong with the noise cancellation of the QC25...I think it is excellent! I just don't think that it is any better than that of the QC15. Btw, I was one of the students who did NOT raise their hands in the above experiment :-)

2) I am not an audiophile, but I was disappointed with the bass sound clarity of the QC25 compared to the QC15. I played one of my favorite tracks to test both headphones. Granted, I am in to classical music, so the bass for me normally comes in the form of the double basses and cellos. On my QC15, I can actually hear the individual vibrations caused by the sound of the bow hair pulling on the strings (if you have any experience with bowed string instruments, you will know what I mean). Not so with my QC 25. It was just a general generic sound coming from the double bass section... No bow hair vibrations as you would normally hear live inside a concert hall...or from the QC-15.

3) They eliminated the Hi/Lo switch on the QC25, and by default the cable is set permanently to the equivalent of the \\"Hi\\" setting of previous QC headphone cables. What does this mean? It means that you will find yourself having to constantly turn down the volume on your audio equipment, unless you don't mind the sound blasting in your ears. I was watching a movie on the in-flight entertainment system, and with my QC15 cable on the \\"LO\\" setting, I had an ample range of volume on which to adjust up or down on the aircraft's volume control. However, when I switched over to the QC25, I had no choice but to use the lowest possible notch on the aircraft's volume control....any notch higher and I would go deaf from such loud volume! And that lowest possible volume notch while using the QC 25 was loud enough as it was, but tolerable... I would have preferred to lower the volume further down, which was only possible in the \\"LO\\" setting of the QC15. For me at least, this was a BIG minus for the QC25. Btw, the reason I know that the QC25 cable is permanently set to the equivalent of the \\"Hi\\" setting on the QC15 cable is because during the in-flight movie, while I was using the QC15, in addition to testing it on the \\"Lo\\" setting, I also tested it in the \\"Hi\\" setting, and just like with the QC25, I had to use the lowest possible volume notch on the aircraft's volume control without going deaf. Edit: I forgot to mention here that I also tested both headphones on my iPhone, and got the same exact results. TO BOSE, IF YOU ARE READING THIS, BRING BACK THE \\"HI/LO\\" SWITCH!

Update 1: I've been reading other reviews complaining that sound \\"leaks\\" from the QC25 headphones...and I suspect that this is the very reason for this...considering how the QC25 cable is made to permanently function in the equivalent of the \\"Hi\\" setting of previous QC headphones, the QC25 are essentially loud headphones.

Update 2: Someone in my comments pointed out that the Bose manual states you can get lower volume output if you plug the QC25 using the airplane adapter. Since as of writing time (Oct 2, 2014) I already returned my QC25s without having checked this adapter feature, I was lucky that a colleague recently bought a pair and was kind enough to allow me to check this out on his QC25. Indeed, I can confirm that the only way you can get a \\"Lo\\" setting on the QC25 is by plugging the QC25 via the airplane adapter that comes included in the case. The adapter is double-pronged, but one of the prongs is retractable in order to convert it into a single-pronged adapter. This would mean that those of you who normally prefer to use the \\"Lo\\" setting on the QC15 (or other previous QC models) would have to plug the QC25 into your devices with the airplane adapter from now on, whether it be into the aircraft jack, your iPod, tablet, smartphone, PC, or any other listening device. When I tested this feature, the first thing I realized is that for everyday use, this would be a hassle in the long-run as it creates unnecessary bulk at the device jack of whatever it is you're listening. Moreover, with such daily use, I imagine the risk of losing or misplacing the airplane adapter becomes significant, which could eventually force you to buy a replacement adapter if you were to want to keep having the option of having a \\"Lo\\" setting. Yes, the airplane adapter is perfect for using on flights with in-flight entertainment if they require a double jack, but I would assume that for many of us, such flights are infrequent. Bose, what were you thinking? A simple \\"Hi/Lo\\" switch on the cable would have done the trick! Bose, I repeat, if you are reading this: BRING BACK THE HI/LO SWITCH! You don't even have to redesign the QC25 themselves, just redesign the cable so that it has the switch and voila! I suspect the cost to update the QC25 cable would be minimal.

4) The case of the QC25 is more compact than the case of the QC 15, which is good. My only gripe is that they decided to leave out the special zipper pouch that was common in Bose QC cases. That zipper pouch was always handy to store multiple spare batteries. Instead of the zipper pouch, the QC25 case has a slot that allows you to store one extra spare battery at a time. Apparently, it seems it is a common complaint about the QC15 that once you run out of battery that it stops working, but guess what? This has NEVER been an issue for me. I have always stored multiple spare batteries at a time in my QC15's zipper pouch... If a battery runs out on me, I immediately replace it on the spot. I have always made sure that I had no less than two or three spare batteries at any one time. But with the QC25, I am forced to have only one spare battery. Yes, I realize that it has that feature that allows you to play music without a battery, but I never intended on using that because I have always cared about not losing the noise canceling feature since I only use Bose QC headphones while traveling, which is where I need the noise canceling the most and the very reason why I purchased these types of headphones in the first place.

All in all, I have decided to give four stars to the QC25, especially because of reasons #2 and #3 above, and I guess I'll be returning or selling the QC25 soon. Many people are saying how the looks of the QC25 are better than that of the QC15, and I admit it was part of the reason why I considered the upgrade, but in the end of the day I give priority to practicality than to looks.

I am not discouraging you from buying the QC25... They are awesome headphones in the noise canceling department. They cut out the noise pollution of vibrations from engines, so they do exactly what they are designed to do. But this is a product that I would buy if I didn't have my QC15 already. So to all of you QC15 owners, you are not missing out much, continue to use your QC15s! For everybody else, go right ahead and buy the QC25! Besides, if this is your first time buying Bose noise-canceling headphones, chances are you have nothing better to compare them to... Just my two cents, and I hope this answers the question of whether or not to upgrade for QC15 owners, and thus helping you save money...

Edit: A few people have written to me saying that it seems my review is promoting the QC-15 as better headphones than the QC25, and yet I recommend buying the QC25 for those who do not have the QC 15 already. I would just like to clarify that my review assumes that the QC15 are no longer available for purchase. True, I realize that as of writing time it is possible to buy the QC15 in addition to buying the QC 25, but I don't count on this option lasting forever.

Also, one more thing, for those who already own the QC 15, keep in mind that the reasons stated above are what influenced me personally in helping me decide to keep my QC 15. Edit: A few people have written to me saying that it seems my review is promoting the QC-15 as better headphones than the QC25, and yet I recommend buying the QC25 for those who do not have the QC 15 already. I would just like to clarify that my review assumes that the QC15 are no longer available for purchase. True, I realize that as of writing time it is possible to buy the QC15 in addition to buying the QC 25, but I don't count on this option lasting forever.

Also, one more thing, for those who already own the QC 15, keep in mind that the reasons stated above are what influenced me personally in helping me decide to keep my QC 15. Perhaps the absence of the Hi/Lo switch on the QC 25, for example, may not be an issue for some of you, especially if you always keep your QC 15 on the \\"Hi\\" setting. But if you often useyour QC15 on the \\"Lo\\" setting, I suspect the QC 25 upgrade may be an issue. Personally, I don't understand why somebody would have their headphones always on the \\"Hi\\" setting. I've always found that sound volume has always been significantly loud on \\"Hi\\", and the few times I ever did switch to the \\"Hi\\" setting was because the overall sound of what I was trying to listen to was extremely low already, and the \\" Hi\\" setting was very helpful at amplifying such sound. In fact, that is how I have always thought about the \\"Hi\\" setting, as an amplification mode.

By the way, when you listen to your headphones on the \\"Hi\\" setting, the louder volume does help block more ambient sound around you... Could this be perhaps the reason why Bose markets the QC25 as \\"blocking more sound\\" than the QC15, considering that its cable is permanently set to the equivalent of \\"Hi\\" thereby outputting louder volume?

The ultimate purpose of my review for already existing QC15 owners is for you to be able to make an informed decision on whether to upgrade or not to the QC 25 by knowing ahead of time what differences to expect should you go through with an upgrade.

product_title: Fiio X3 Mastering Quality Music Player w/ Wolfson DAC WM8740 24Bit 192K
review_headline: Great sound, no fluff, bells or whistles.
review_body:
An excellent sound machine for individuals who consider themselves audiophiles, who crave the portability and elegance of a music player but are sick of flat touch screens and the mediocre music reproduction that usually plagues most modern portable music playing apparatuses.

You feed it music files and charge the battery through a direct, simple USB connection to any computer. File transfer is basically drag-and-drop. You may create folders instead of playlists (it does not have them). There is no wifi, GPS tracking or large touch screens to this contraption. You navigate files and volume control via physical buttons - a great feature slowly disappearing from current devices. The D to A converter and excellent pre-amp built in allow for playing almost any music file on earth, and allow for excellent sound reproduction even with high-resistance professional headphones.

The only annoying aspect of this thing has to do with the VERY SLOW charge time using the USB. Some will not like not having playlists - but as I have mentioned you may use folders created on the computer and dragged and dropped into the machine's memory - it will play your files by folder.

To sum things up: if you want to listen to music and enjoy hi-fi quality and you don't really need the bells and whistles of modern portable devices - this one is definitely for you!!

review_headline: Every home needs one of these ...
review_body:
This device is a bit hit and miss. Maybe it is trying to do to much maybe it is somewhat user error but i will detail my experience with it. It is tough to figure out with the enclosed instructions. I am just not the most technical person, but if you are, this would be a cinch to use.

Essentially it comes down to plugging it in and hoping you do it properly. I decided to use an SD card that had a few pictures on it and upon plugging it in Initially nothing happened so i reattached the device and hit the little button. The device connected and i was able to import some of the pictures on the card into the phone. I didn't test it with PDF or word docs but i would imagine that would be somewhat similar but would rely on the phone software to read the files etc. OK all good on that front at least with the Galaxy III used for testing.

Next i tried connecting the device to the HDMI output on my TV. I tried several times to have it connect and the TV just didn't recognise it as an input connection. The TV was an LG but i have had some issues in the past connecting HDMI devices so i tried it on a smaller Panasonic TV and it connected without issue and i was able to watch the short video i made for testing purposes. In part I put this down to the LG TV since it can be a bit finicky it seems on some devices but seems to work with most.

Some of the other stated functions i did not have the facility to test. I don't know what kind people would generally have 196khz audio files on their phones as it isn't a terribly common playback format but it may just be quoted as it is technically able to do it and this function may be of use to someone so i guess it can be noted.

It is a utility device - you may find one of its functions useful and at under $20 it provides value on that front if it works with your particular setup and devices.
