product_title: Sykik Bluetooth Stereo Headphone – Built Microphone Supports Wireless Music Streaming and Hands-Free (WHITE)
review_body:
It took me quite some time to ultimately decide on these headphones. I finally just went with it and honestly, I couldn't be happier for the price.

1) Bluetooth - they sync up to my Samsung 3 phone and iPad 3 with absolutely no issues. First time, every time. I haven't tried them on computers yet (my MAC or PC) but will update when I do.

2) Microphone - The only reason it gets 4 and not 5 stars. It's not great. Any loud noises, e.g. being on the bus, and the other person can't hear me. When I'm sitting at home or work, the microphone is definitely a nice feature. Sometimes they have trouble hearing me but for the most part, it's still easier then having to up sync the bluetooth. One thing to note though, I'm very loud.

3) Sound - I was surprised at how loud they can get and even more surprised at how well they sounded. Vocals are crisp and bass is pretty good, for a $25 pair of headphones. I listen to mainly Drum & Bass music and these work great with it. Noise canceling, lol, every time my boyfriend walks in the room I have to pull them off or flip 1 ear bc I can't hear a thing he's saying. You don't hear much besides the music.

4) Style - Not guna lie, they look silly. It's the first pair of over the head headphones I've had in years. They seem bulky and I feel like I look like I have a giant headband on my head, but I could care less. Having no wire was my number 1 necessity. I was a little sad when I got them and they were not foldable. They do not fold, the ears spin around so they can lay flat. I carry a backpack, and I'm worried they will break. As far as comfort, I find them perfectly comfortable. I have an industrial piercing and 7 others in my ears and they don't bother a one of em. They wear comfortably and even flipping 1 ear so you can still hear the world is surprisingly comfy.

5) Battery - So far, I've only charged them 3 or 4 times. I'm 3 days shy of having them for a month. I use them quite often but it's mainly for music. Rarely do I talk on the phone much less through these. I'm satisfied with battery life so far. It is very easy to forget to turn them off when your finished using them and I'm thinking that could affect the battery. Luckily, the flashing light reminds me so I've been good so far. One of my favorite things is that when they are dying, I can charge the headphone through the USB port and thorough an aux audio cable, I can plug it into my phone or ipad and still listen to music. The bluetooth won't work while charging, but the backup feature is a nice touch.

I would definitely recommend these headphone for anyone looking for a decent, cheap pair. If/when they break, I will get another pair. I just wish they would make them in different colors!!!

product_title: Amplified HD Digital Outdoor HDTV Antenna 150 Miles Long Range with Motorized 360 Degree Rotation, UHF/VHF/FM Radio with Infrared Remote Control
review_headline: its not to bad. Another problem I have had with it is ...
review_body:
This antenna almost deserves 5 stars.
My reason for giving it 3 stars is the rotator.

The rotator is supposed to go 360 degrees then stop and rotate in the opposite direction. However you never know which way it is going to as you try to rotate it. If you can watch it rotate while adjusting it, its not to bad. Another problem I have had with it is their have been times when it wouldn't rotate and I had to repeatedly push the button to get it to go again. (or manually move it to get it too work again.)

The antenna itself performs very well, I had no trouble picking up 24 stations in a 130 degree radius. with the farthest being 51 miles.
Now a little about my location
I live in a area with a lot of old growth trees which range from 90 to 100 + feet in height. The lot behind me has 9 of these trees. (which is the way my antenna is pointed) From past antennas I have found that I get better reception 6 to 10 feet off the ground. (most of the tree branches are 20 ft or more off the ground)

I did take this antenna to a friends house who lives a couple of blocks away and was able to pick up 29 stations with the farthest being 57 miles away. (6 to 8 feet off the ground) He has a better line of sight than I do.

One thing I have learned is that if you live in a area with lots of trees the location of your antenna can mean the difference of receiving 15 or 24 stations. (often times for me just moving it several feet over made a difference)

Also when installing a new antenna you should always use new coax, and don't split your signal to another tv until you have tested it. I have seen a lot of people complain about their shitty reception due to bad coax, splitters or improperly instlalled f connectors. If any of these conditions exist, the best antenna in the world is going to perform poorly.

Bottom line here is I am very happy with this antenna and wanted to give it 5 stars.

review_headline: Absolutely the most infuriating wireless speaker system (updated):
review_body:
Update:

I've been using these for several months now, and wanted to update a few key points.

Still no Amazon Prime music connection through the HEOS app.
Still cannot search or find the music actually saved on my phone, no matter what I try. It only pulls up two albums that I downloaded through Amazon but not the 50+ albums saved on my SD card.

And the most infuriating: After about an hour of listening, the app disconnects the device. Music still plays, but if I want to change anything, the app says 'DEMO' and no device found. I then have to manually plug in the phone and re-add the device. It is without a doubt the most infuriating thing about this. Also, adding insult to injury, I always have to log back in to the Pandora link through the app.

I am giving this one star since it frustrates me so much I am ready to just toss it. I use a Sonos wireless system at work and it works perfectly. I cannot say the same for this system.

The one good thing is that the system sounds really great. But I cannot recommend this system until they work out all the kinks.

____________________________________________________

The first and most frustrating thing I noticed about this device - you cannot use Amazon Prime Music (or the Amazon music cloud), Google music, or any of the music downloaded onto my Samsung Galaxy phone with the HEOS app.

I use a Sonos system at work, and that system does have more support and it can play music from my device. No matter how I try, I cannot get the HEOS app to locate any of the music files on my phone.

What it does support is Pandora (and a few other apps). It also has the ability to be hard wired in, but that defeats the purpose of the device. I can hard wire into my receiver - but very annoying for a wireless device to not have more options for streaming wireless music.

For now, go with the cheaper Sonos systems. The sound is comparable but the Sonos app supports a lot more 3rd party streaming services as well as easier access to music actually on the device. review_body:
Normally when I receive a review sample I can do a thorough evaluation and write a review within two days. This one took longer. The reason is that it took me a while to hear the differences in this model versus the [[ASIN:B00G4UQ6U8 Brainwavz S1 In Ear Headphones]], which also impressed me (and I also own).

After going through a pile of albums to try to understand what the product description meant by smoother bass I finally found an album that allowed me to hear it: [[ASIN:B00492ANTS Portrait In Jazz]]. When Scott LaFaro's bass came in on Autumn Leaves I started switching back and forth between this and the S1, and also hauled out some studio reference monitors. These phones are capable of going down in the 18Hz range for the low end, which is lower than most in ear monitors and phones that are usually in the 20Hz range at the low end. I am not sure my ears can discretely detect the differences between 18 and 20, but I was able to detect nuances that the lower end provided.

These also go up a little higher than more phones, which are usually in the 20 KHz range, Again, I am not sure I can truly hear sounds at 24KHz, but there is a discernible difference. I tested that end of the frequency spectrum with a few Ahmad Jamal albums since he tended towards the right side of his pianos.

One other thing that took me some getting accustomed to was the over-the-ear way of wearing these. I am use to in-ear or the old fashioned over-the-hear phones and I had to play around with these before I figured out how to place them in my ears perfectly. If you are use to over-the-ear you will probably not experience the learning curve that I did.

A few other features that I have come to expect from this brand are here: extra tips of different sizes, a hard case ([[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]]) and a 1/4\\" adapter. I love the flat, tangle-free cable that is tougher than it feels. And it has an adjuster like a chin strap on a cowboy hat that aids in keeping these firmly in place with the over-the-ear way of wearing them.

This is definitely a five star set of phones (according to my way of grading, anyway), and one that I will not hesitate to recommend to fellow musicians. We tend to spend a great deal of time listening to music and these do an excellent job of reproducing it. My advice, though, is to take your time when you first get them because their true power is not immediately apparent. product_title: Grado Prestige Series SR125e Headphones
review_headline: When "you want the only mud hitting your ears to be Muddy Waters."
review_body:
Updated: 2-1-2015

I listened to each Prestige headphone for at least 10 hours. The music I listened to was compressed in Apple Lossless format. I used my MacBook Pro with iTunes for playback. The differences in sound quality noted in this review were also heard on my iPod Classic with music compressed in AAC format at 256kbps VBR quality (iTunes Plus).

The Grado Prestige Series
===================
I've done hours and hours of research about the Grado Prestige Series. The following points lead me to initially purchase the SR-125.
- Numerous forums indicated that the SR-325 was too bright and caused listening fatigue.
- Although numerous forums recommended the SR-225 instead of the SR-125, a review from goodcans.com said that the difference between the SR-225 and SR-125 was noticeable only in certain songs and required well-trained ears.
- The Grado website advertises "The SRx25 will produce a sound that is pure Grado, with warm harmonic colors, rich full bodied vocals, excellent dynamics, and an ultra-smooth top end." on all SR-x25 headphones, which indicates that the SR-225 and SR-325 are refinements to the original SR-125 (original by order of price).

Below is the list comparing the headphones in the Prestige series and the Reference series. Please note that I have only listened to the SR-80i, SR-125e, SR-225e, and SR-325e. I relied on data from my research for the following differences: SR-60 vs SR-80, SR325 vs RS2, RS2 vs RS1.

SR-60 - entry level
SR-80 - improved bass
SR-125 - improved separation of horizontal sounds with a wider soundstage, more intimate soundstage
SR-225 - improved reproduction of space with a deeper soundstage, more intimate soundstage
SR-325 - improved look and feel, punchier bass
RS-2 - improved accuracy (warmer) with a smooth top end
RS-1 - improved look and feel, deeper and more intimate soundstage

-Prestige Buying Recommendations-

The SR-80 sounds really good for its price, but if you want a taste of the detail you've been missing without spending too much money, try the SR-125. The SR-325 is the real treat of the Prestige Series. It reveals even more detail than the SR-125, has an addictive bass, and a "look and feel" to be cherished. If you don't care much for "look and feel", the SR-225 will provide you more value.

-Reference Buying Recommendations-

The Reference series is notable for its warmer sound and smooth top end. The warmer sound will help instruments (like brass) and vocals sound more life-like. Those interested in Jazz and Classical music should give these serious consideration.

-Comparing the Top of each Line-

Prestige (SR-80) = Value Series
Prestige (SR-325) = Original Series (Improved Detail)
Reference (RS-1) = Prestige + Warmer Sound
Statement (GS-1000) = Reference + Bigger Soundstage
Professional (PS-1000) = Statement + Neutral Response

SR-80i vs SR-125e
==============
While some forums say that there is little difference between the SR-80 and SR-125, I disagree. When going from the SR-125 to the SR-80, there are obvious differences.

There is a much wider soundstage with the SR-125. Imagine a sector of a circle whose central point is at the back of the listener's head and the arc length is at the front. This area illustrates the space for sources of sound. The central angle would determine the soundstage width. The SR-80 would have a central angle of 110° while the SR-125 would have a central angle of 180°. For example, a sound that only plays on the left phone would sound like it's coming from the point 55° left of center with the SR-80. On the SR-125, it would sound like it's coming from the point 90° left of center.

The wider soundstage and improved intimacy result in more accurate sound with sufficient space for good separation of sound sources. In some songs, I can focus on just one track recording of the song; for example: backup singers become well defined like they are in a space all on their own, separate from the other sounds, as if there were recorded separately and then mixed in at that location (which is what happened). The SR-125 reveals this other dimension of production: how much work was put in the stereo mixing of the song. I have found that not all songs have such interesting production.

These improvements also make defects in the recording (hiss, pops, and clipping) less subtle.

I had to get used to such a wide soundstage provided by the SR-125. In the beginning, it felt like a different experience. Sometimes, I found it difficult to focus on the music as a whole because I felt bombarded with what seemed like stereo sources 180° apart. It seemed to require work to piece the sources together and felt a bit unnatural. Early Beatles albums in pseudo stereo were dreadful to listen to. More than ever, they became like listening to two completely different sources (which they are).

However, I found it more difficult to go back to the less intimate sound of the SR-80. The sounds become so distant that it no longer seemed like I was in the same room with the band, but maybe looking through a window. Now, I am used to the wide soundstage.

Another thing I read in some forums was that the SR-125 has less bass than the SR-80. I think that because of the improvements, the bass has to compete with the other sounds that now come into focus with the SR-125, which makes the bass seem more inconspicuous.

SR-125e vs Other Headphones
=======================
Interestingly, the difference in width of soundstage is not as obvious in other headphones I have such as the Koss PortaPro or the Sennheiser HD280 Pro. However, their sound quality is closer to, but not as good as the SR-80.

SR-125e vs SR-225e
===============

The SR-225 comes with L-cushions instead of the S-cushions that come with the SR-125. The difference in sound quality between the SR-125 and SR-225 is not as impactful as the difference between the SR-80 and SR-125, but I was surprised to hear that even more intimacy was possible.

The L-cushions increase the intimacy further, providing additional clarity and making details in the music are easier to hear. Vocals come closer to your ears. The reverberations of the lightly tapped cymbals are more easily heard; they can also be heard for bass drums. These reverberations give the sound a more musical feel. In addition, bass seems to be easier to isolate. When switching back and forth between the S-cushion and L-cushion, the intimacy is immediately noticeable; the details are easily noticeable in slower songs.

The SR-225 also has a slightly wider soundstage, but it's difficult to detect.

The headphones are slightly heavier, probably due to the larger chamber and different grille.

I enjoyed the increased intimacy of the SR-225. Again, once I had more intimacy, it was difficult to go back to the SR-125.

*No headphone amplifier was used for this experience. See section: The Case for a Headphone Amplifier.
*Also see section: Infamous L-cushions.

SR-225e vs SR-325e
===============

With the SR-325, we enter the area of diminishing returns with regard to sound quality. The SR-325e has a warmer tone - it's difficult to detect. There is also a punchier bass - can be detected, but not significant. I had to listen to songs back and forth at least a handful of times to understand some of the differences I was hearing. It also helps to be in a quiet environment and use quiet, slow songs in some cases.

The best thing about the SR-325 is the improvements to the look and feel of the line. The headphones are numbered (carved on the ear pad side of the chamber). The chambers aremade of aluminum and painted silver. The aluminum adds weight to the headphones, but it feels good. The headband is much improved (thank god). Pictures somehow don't accurately describe it. It is wider by 1/4", made of stitched leather with a rigid paperboard inside to support its shape, and lightly padded on the underside.

However, I do have some complaints about the look and feel. There were a few small defects in the paint. A small piece chipped on the first day. The exterior nubs of the plastic piece that holds the cans to the headband were not the same size. These issues might have been caused by the struggle to meet the spike in demand caused by the introduction of the E series headphones.

While I'm not sure the SR-325 is worth the full premium over the SR-225, it was difficult to give up the aluminum chambers and sturdy leather headband once I had them in my hands.

*No headphone amplifier was used for this experience. See section: The Case for a Headphone Amplifier.
*Also see sections: Infamous L-cushions, Long-Term Listening to the SR-325.

Long-Term Listening to the SR-325
=========================
I've been listening to these exclusively for about 3 months. During this time, I noticed some things.

Over time, the SR-325 developed a liquid smooth, airy bass thump (the so-called "punchy" bass). This gives an addictive quality to music. Just listen to the intro of Pink Floyd's Breathe in the Air... or Carpenter's Mr. Guder. It's so blissful; yet, such a tease because it leaves me wanting more. This "punchy" bass alone motivated me to upgrade to higher-end headphones (GS-1000).

I also noticed that I've been gravitating towards different music. I cherish music that was recorded better. Slow music that I previously thought was boring now became exciting. On the other hand, music with ambience, that I previously thought was exciting, became less exciting.

*No headphone amplifier was used for this experience. See section: The Case for a Headphone Amplifier.

The Infamous L-Cushions
===================

The L-cushions provide the biggest upgrade to the base sound quality of the SR-125e than the other upgrades that make up the SR-225e or SR-325e.

If the SR-125 was also shipped with L-cushions, the differences would be as follows.

SR-125 - base sound
SR-225 - slightly wider soundstage, slightly improved accuracy (warmer)
SR-325 - improved look and feel, slightly punchier bass, slightly improved accuracy (warmer)

Owners of the SR-125 may be tempted to buy L-cushions to get better sound. However, I found the sound to be too bright to enjoy for extended periods. Thus, revealing the greatest strength of the SR-225: not too bright with the L-cushions.

If you are looking to experiment with the S-cushion or L-cushion: moving to the L-cushion increases the brightness of the sound, which improves intimacy and tightens the bass (more defined); moving to the S-cushion decreases brightness, which reduces intimacy and loosens the bass (more boomy).

*No headphone amplifier was used for this experience. See section: The Case for a Headphone Amplifier.

The infamous drawback of the L-cushions is their comfort. When I used the L-cushions for the first time with the SR-225e, they were very uncomfortable to wear for more than 15 minutes. On some days it was not so bad, but repeated wearing made a bad situation worse. Even hours after I stopped listening, I would feel the pressure points on my ears. Below are tips on how to make them more comfortable.

- Rest the cushion on the upper tip of each ear. The biggest cause of my discomfort was caused by the upper tips of my ears rubbing against the driver. I discovered that the cushions became more comfortable when I rested them on the upper tip of each ear. This may change the sound.However, Grado has said that the best way to wear them is the most comfortable way. I also try to keep the headphone label buttons where my ear canal is so that the sound isn't affected too much.

- Loosen the headband. Loosening the headband will help by reducing the clamping force of these cushions on your ears. However, you will be shifting more weight of the phones to the headband. If it is not padded like the SR-325, the headband will become uncomfortable with too much weight.

- Don't move too much. Even with clamping force, these cushions do not have much grip on your ears, so they will shift easily when you tilt your head or widen facial expressions. The shifting increases discomfort. Try to use the headphones only while your body is in an upright position (ex: not lying down).

Using the the above tips, I can go 1 hour without needing to readjust the headphones. That's not as comfortable as the S-cushions, which I can wear for more than 2 hours without issue, but it is bearable.

The Case for a Headphone Amplifier
=========================

Headphone amplifiers built into devices such as iPods and computers are designed with power limitations driven by two goals: small footprint; safe universal operation. Unfortunately, high end headphones typically require lots of power to sound their best. They might sound OK without one, but they could sound much different when connected to a good headphone amplifier.

I was skeptical at first, until I bought Grado's GS-1000 and was disappointed by its bass performance. When I called Grado about this, they said that a headphone amplifier would help with bass performance. I picked one up and was blown away. Not only did the bass improve to a satisfactory level, but the soundstage completely transformed. It felt like another headphone. I was so impressed by the improvements that I had to try the amplifier with other headphones.

With the SR-325, the bass and soundstage was improved to satisfactory levels. The bass became louder, rounder, and smoother. The soundstage felt more spacious as instrument reverberations occupied more space, significantly improving the reproduction of ambience. The difference wasn't as dramatic as with the GS-1000, but the improvements are enough for me to justify making a headphone amplifier a requirement for the SR-325.

I no longer have an SR-225, but I expect improvements similar to the SR-325.

With the SR-125, the same improvements were noticed. The bass became slightly louder, rounder, and smoother. The soundstage became more spacious, mildly improving the reproduction of ambience. The difference is not as dramatic was with the SR-325. I would say that a headphone amplifier is not a requirement, but it would improve your experience with the SR-125.

With the SR-80, there were slight improvements, but not enough to justify buying a headphone amplifier.

*Note that headphones have to be broken-in to see the maximum benefit of a headphone amplifier.

Unfortunately, not all headphone amplifiers perform the same way. A headphone amplifier's job is not just to supply additional power, but also not imprint itself onto the audio signal while doing so. That's the challenge. The JDS Labs Objective2 is my reference headphone amplifier. I've compared it against the Fiio E12 and the Denon DA-10 and the Objective2 provided the best performance. You can check out my reviews for the E12 and DA-10 if you need more specifics.

*Note that a Gain of 1x (or 0dB) is perfect for Grado headphones and the Line Out of an iPod Classic (6G). However, this is different for Media Players without a line out, such as the iPod Touch (6G). In this case, I set the Headphone Out to 75% volume and use a Gain of 2.5x (or 7.5dB). With the efficient GR10e, a Gain of 2.5x gives me use of 50% of the headphone amplifier's volume knob for songs with a dynamic range of 14 dB. With the less efficient GS1000e, it gives me use of 75% of the volume knob.

Other Considerations
================
Since the headphones are open back, music can be easily heard by others and external sounds can be easily heard by you. External sounds will interfere with your perception of bass performance. This is typical of other sound sources open to the environment, such as car speakers.

The phone plug is 1/8" (fits in iPod) and comes with a 1/4" adapter.

The headphone cable is very thick, but sturdy. I feel like I need to be careful not to put too much stress on a 1/8" phone port. The 1/4" to 1/8" adapter from Grado may look like a solution to prevent stress on a 1/8" phone port, but the 1/4" adapter is thicker than it looks and makes the cord much heavier, making the situation worse.

PS
==
Relaxed, intimate, and emotional songs sound better with more intimacy. Examples:
K's Choice - Not an Addict
Spandau Ballet - True
Spice Girls - 2 become 1
Sting - Fields of Gold

product_title: FiiO RC-UE2 47.2" Cable for Ultimate Earsand M-Audio Headphones
review_headline: - price - solid connector with good wire strain relief Cons
review_body:
Pros:
- price
- solid connector with good wire strain relief

Cons:
- The individual wire sheaths are made of a hard plastic, which are then braided together to produce the wire assembly. The problem is that anything (that isn't soft) that rubs against the hard plastic wire sheaths will produce vibrations that will travel up the wire and you can hear it though your headphones! I walk 5 miles a day to and from work - the wires rub against my backpack/shoulder bag straps and will make a lot of noise that I can hear through the headphones. I managed to reduce it a little either by holding the wire away from the strap or putting the wire underneath my clothing. The vibration sounds are loud and cannot be ignored. Also, the wires will make a lot of noise at my desk because it rubs against the edge of desk. The product does come with a clip to quickly fasten it to something, but the chances of the wire rubbing against something is still there.

I honestly don't think I would buy these wires again, the vibration noise is a big problem. If you've bought the Triple Fi, you're obviously a person who cares about audio quality - so I would not recommend this to Triple Fi owners. To be honest, I was desperate for a wire replacement, but I should have just bought the OEM ones, even if they are expensive. I will do that next time.

product_title: Clip Plus 4 GB MP3 Player (Black)
review_headline: I love these little guys and typically buy more than one ...
review_body:
I love these little guys and typically buy more than one at a time (they're extremely easy to lose). I stick 64GB chips in them.

The good:
They're tiny. As in "clip it to you and forget it's there" tiny.
They're cheap. When I think what Apple is charging for a 64GB music player ...
They talk to anything. They mount up like any USB drive.

The bad:
They're tiny. Once you clip them to something, it's very easy to forget they're there. Which means you end up washing them when you throw your pants in the washer.
They're cheap. The front panel features are pretty much nil. It plays music. That's about it. The random function isn't that great. You can't play one album, unless that's the only album that artist has on the player. Otherwise it's Play All of that artist or play one song. Also, if you're on random and a song comes on that makes you think, "Hey, I'd like to hear that whole album," there's no way to easily click to that function. In other words, you get what you pay for.
And finally, the worst issue with these is that once in a while they get confused. You get these "NOT ENOUGH MEMORY...." messages and then it stops working. This problem often occurs with a constant need to "Refresh" the media. Then the only recovery is to reformat the Clip and reload all your music. Here's what I've found:

The Clip will ALWAYS refresh your media after you add songs. That's normal. But if you use your computer to recharge the Clip, depending on your OS, when you plug the Clip into the USB port, your computer will try and talk to it. Especially if you leave your computer's media player open all the time, as I do. It's been my experience that doing this will cause you to experience a LOT of the dreaded Sansa memory problems, since your computer is often meddling with it when it's plugged in. If you yank it out of the USB port when the computer's talking to it, blam.Dead Sansa Clip. This would happen to any USB memory device.

The solution, for me, has been to charge the Clip ONLY with a dedicated USB charger. The only time I plug it into my computer is when I'm adding songs, and even then I make damn sure my media player is closed before I do so. AND I make sure it's off before I unplug the Clip from the computer. AND I make sure to use the OS's "It's now safe to unplug your USB device" function before yanking it out of the USB port. Using these simple steps, I have gone from having to reformat and reload my Clips every other week to....almost never. I just had one screw up yesterday, first time in months. I reformated both drives (the local and the 64GB chip), threw my music library back on it, and we're back in business.

For the price, I don't think you can beat these guys.

review_headline: Good for its size and price
review_body:
I have had this little speaker for about a month and a half now and so far I have not experienced any problems with it. It's pretty light and easy to carry around if you need to. The thing lasts an extraordinary amount of time on one charge which adds to its ease in portability. It's also very easy to pair via Bluetooth. I have very little experience with Bluetooth but I did not have any problems at all pairing and repairing it. It can literally be done in seconds.

The most important part of any speaker is its sound and I would say that for its size and weight, this thing has pretty good sound. Of course it might not be as good as speakers 5 times its size or other Bluetooth speakers 5 times its price, but for what you are paying the sound is well balanced and clear. For those concerned with bass, I would say that it is more than acceptable for something its size. As far as loudness goes, I think that is substantially louder than my phone speakers and my laptop speakers. A good tip would be to connect your device directly via the aux in port on the speaker. This makes it noticeably louder when at its highest volume settings compared to bluetooth. I have tried connecting it to an amp to make it louder and while it can get substantially louder, it will also starts sounding a bit distorted and muffled. One complain I have is that when a device is connected through the aux in port, the volume buttons on the speaker stop working. This can be annoying if the device that is being connected to it does not have a volume button of its own.

Overall, I would say that I do recommend it for someone looking for an affordable bluetooth speaker.

review_body:
Bought these a month ago and have had no issues (even after dropping). I tested these against the $300 bose, beats, and any other headphones that were top notch at best buy. These were my favorite. If i had to pick a top choice it is between these and the beats pro (or executive, can't remember which). Keep in mind, headphones are all about preference. Comfort - 10/10 Again, preference. I'm very picky with headphones and how they feel. I thought these were very soft and light, so comfortable that you may forget they are on, they fit perfectly (For me, at least). If you like the feel of having headphones on your head, I guess you wouldn't really like these.

No disruption or sound quality going down after turning the music up loudly (disregarding the fact that you'll go deaf and music is not as pleasant as the decibel level increases). The lyrics are very clear compared to some headphones, and that is mostly because of the treble increased versus the bass. If you like bass, you probably won't like these... if you like treble, you'll probably do. note: this is with noise cancellation.
Without Noise cancellation - more like an 8. (All you need is batteries for NC)

Noise Cancellation - 9.5/10 Fantastic... kind of. If you are on a plane, bus, or the air conditioner is too loud, they block the noise out so that if you have music on, you won't hear the background noise. These are great for traveling. That being said, if everyone is literally screaming, you will have to turn up the music a little, haha. It's great at blocking all background noises,and most of the other noises from like TVs or conversations--- but not completely unless the volume is at a certain level (med). The level it needs to be does not bother me.

Value - 10/10 Most stores have them under $200, cheaper than most top headphones (usually $300).
Style/Design - 8.5/10 They're very basic looking.
Overall - 9.6/10 NC

product_title: Comply Comfort PLUS Earphone Tips
review_headline: Only worth it if the stock foam tips bother you.
review_body:
I tried these with a pair of Shure SE846 IEMs. For those who have comfort issues with stock foam tips and still prefer foam over silicone, these may be a significant improvement. If you don't have comfort issues with the stock tips, then don't bother.

These foam tips are initially much less pliable than the stock Shure foam tips. However, once warmed up, the foam becomes very soft and very pliable, much more than the stock tips. Prior to warming up, they're easier to insert into your ear because they expand much less rapidly, giving you more time to position them correctly once you compress them.

Supposedly, the only difference between the Comfort PLUS and the Isolation PLUS is the shape of the tip. The Comfort PLUS are rounder, whereas the Isolation PLUS have the traditional cylindrical shape you see with the stock Shure tips. The round shape may be more comfortable for some, but I found that the round shape didn't seal as well. This may force some to try a size up, which can defeat the purpose of the more comfortable round shape.

Some have complained that Comply tips change the frequency response or muffle the sound, but I didn't notice any difference. I do, however, always compress the top of the foam to the level of the barrel so that the top edge of the foam doesn't block the barrel when inserted.

These do have the built-in wax guard, but Shure has recently begun placing a wax guard in their stock foam tips as well.

These are a decent product for those who are bothered by the stock tips, but there is little to be gained for others.

review_body:

The new bar was installed in our condo in Florida and functioned beautifully for about 15 minutes. There was a small \\"pop\\" sound and the audio went away. The green light was still present, so we knew that there was power to the bar. We phoned the number for Klipsch Customer Service and spoke with Ryan. After several test activities, Ryan suggested that we send the entire system back to be replaced with a new one. He forwarded the UPS Shipping label the following day.

Within a week, we received an email that the replacement unit was ordered and the following day, the shipping notice came by email. So, less than two weeks to receive a replacement unit.

On the most recent trip to Florida, we installed the replacement unit and used it for over a week, with sources from \\"Dish,\\" Blu-Ray and Netflix (via Amazon Fire TV.)

Thanks to Ryan and the team at Klipsch Customer Service, what could have been a frustrating experience became one labeled, \\"There really are companies that pride themselves with excellent customer service.\\"

When you play these kinds of music thru it they sound bad a full volume. This is true for any portable sound system. My tip for people is don't turn the unit all the way up. There is big difference to "loud" and "loud and Clear"! You're ears will enjoy the music longer and with less fatigue.

I also have a JBL Charge which gets very loud but what JBL does is compress your music to the point that when let's say you have a bass drum hit then the rest of the song will dip down in level. So at very loud level the sound will fade in and out to the point where it's annoying. If you back the level down to where it doesn't distort then well you're basically at the same level as the Amazon (medium) version. I have a feeling that the Amazon engineers said lets not make this unit go to 11 and sound like crap, let's make it only go to 9 and have a better sound experience. I feel that the JBL engineers said let's make it so loud and annoying because that's what people want. It's like saying because my car is faster doesn't make it a better experience.
I say with all that then the Amazon (medium) wins hands down, for 3 reasons. Clarity, price and the one cool thing is that you can take a phone call with it.
If you were expecting more bass from either one of these or any of the other brands for this size and price then neither of these things are for you. Buy a Bose unit for 4 times as much. You will be happy but I tell you what, if I get the amazon unit stolen or accidentally left out in the rain or sandy beach, I won't feel so bad.

product_title: NXG Technology Pro Dj Headphones
review_headline: Seriously. BUY THESE NOW, While You Still Can!
review_body:
OK - I'm going to make this very simple. These are some of the best sounding headphones you can get this side of a C-note. I'm not kidding. I found these while researching for the (also excellent) Monoprice 8323, which are themselves well-regarded as among the best budget cans on the market. And they're right, the 8323s are amazing headphones for the price, their only shortcomings being the rather uncomfortable plastic ear cushions and headband padding. Many users of the 8323 replace these for greater comfort. These NXG headphones are identical to the 8323, but with upgraded fabric ear cushions and headband pads, and also feature an attractive, black and silver applique to the side panels which does nothing for the sound, but does dress the up a bit. They also come with cloth-wrapped cords rather than the rubber cords which ship with the 8323.

The sound of the NXG is nothing short of incredible for the price, comparing quite well with headphones costing ten times as much. The bass is full and powerful, the high are clear and the midrange is balanced and comfortable. The soundstage is adequate, though not as impressive as some higher-priced monitors, but again, you're only paying 1/10th the price.

Did I mention that they are only ONE TENTH the price of anything comparable?

These headphones do leak sound, however, so be prepared for those around you to hear your music. Probably not the best choice if you like to listen to hardcore gangsta rap while working in the office. Also, might keep your significant other awake if you like to listen to music in bed at night, but for just about anything else, it's seriously hard to beat these headphones.

Highly recommended!

product_title: Koss ESP-950 Electrostatic Stereophone
review_body: As an owner of several audiophile headphones, the 950s are my first foray into electrostatic headphones. If it weren't for the seemingly cheap materials used in the construction of these headphones, my rating would be off the 6-star scale. The clarity and balance of the sound, and the quality of the midrange in particular, are exceptional. But perhaps what really caught me by surprise is the bass: it's neither thumping nor weak (in fact not weak at all); it's just... satisfying, and ever present without distorting and distracting from the listening experience. It's like going back in time and listening to the first good loudspeakers you brought home. Actually, it's better than that, but you can't help but wax nostalgic with these headphones. Of course, as others have posted, they appear to be a bit cheaply made (though the carrying case is great), and for that they get a deduction from me.

product_title: Sony ICF-S10MK2 Pocket AM/FM Radio, Silver
review_headline: Best Radio Available for the Money.
review_body:
This radio is almost impossible not to buy at this price. If you're going to the beach and need something you don't have to worry about ruining in the sand, this is your radio. But it's more than just a cheap expendable radio. This radio is built solid. Tuning is smooth and stations are easy to lock in on. The reception is good on FM and phenomenal on AM. In fact, the AM reception beats my Sangean WR-11 table radio.

This radio is unbeatable for what it is: a cheap, analog, portable handheld radio. But if you're looking for additional features, you might want to look elsewhere. Some of its shortcomings include the lack of digital tuning and presets. The speaker is small so you won't get a big loud sound out of this unit. The headphone jack is mono and there is no external antenna jack.

The list of what this radio does have is pretty short. The on/off switch is built in to the volume wheel which feels solid and gives a satisfying "click" when toggled on or off. There is a very smooth feeling tuning wheel with enough resistance to make finding your desired stations easy. The frequency display is very accurate, especially for such a cheap radio. The antenna folds out and extends easily although most of the time, extending the antenna fully is not required (I live in an urban area). The downside to the antenna is that it does not rotate, but this has never prevented me from getting good reception. The AM/FM switch feels durable and easy to operate and all of this is housed in a sturdy plastic casing. There is a reason this radio makes it in to Amazon's Top 100 best sellers for Electronics. Not bad for a dying technology! Absolutely great for the park, beach, going to a ball game or just listening to news around the house.

Pros:

Great AM reception!
Solid construction.
Price.
Whip antenna feels less prone to breaking compared to other handheld radios.
Fits in shirt pocket.
Good sound for its size.
Great battery life.

Cons:

No weather band or short wave.
No digital tuning.
Speaker distorts when turned up too loud.
Whip antenna does not rotate.

review_headline: Fantastic DAP except for one omission.
review_body: Very nice player. Love the build quality and the incredible sound quality. Took a little getting used to the interface coming from an iPod touch.  I just updated to firmware 3.0 which is supposed to increase the audio quality even more as well as provide a nicer interface. Sadly, even though many users have asked for it, this player does not support replay gain. Replay Gain are tags that are calculated and stored within the music file that can be used by a player to have all songs play at the same volume level (or the appropriate volume for an album when playing the whole album). Yes, I can adjust the volume of the songs manually but it would be nice to be able to set a comfortable playing level and have the device play all songs at that level versus me having to frequently turn the volume up or down. My cheap Sansa Clip Plus has this capability as does my desktop audio player (Clementine). Hope that Fiio continues to improve this model and one day releases a firmware update that will add in this option. BTW, Fiio is a great company, I also have 2 of their amps and continue to be impressed by the quality of their offerings.

product_title: SONOS PLAYBAR TV Sound Bar/Wireless Streaming Music Speaker
review_headline: With a Simple Workaround, It DOES Deliver Dolby Digital 5.1
review_body:
Sonos' best feature is also their biggest flaw in regards to delivering a true Dolby Digital 5.1 experience through their home theater setup using a [[ASIN:B00AEMGGU2 SONOS PLAYBAR]], [[ASIN:B00834SIO0 SONOS SUB Wireless Subwoofer (Gloss)]], and either [[ASIN:B00EWCUK1Q SONOS PLAY:1 Compact Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music - (Black)]] or [[ASIN:B005441AJC SONOS - PLAY:3 Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music (Small) - Black]] as the two surround speakers. Specifically, that feature is Sonos' design and setup simplicity.

Sonos deserves a lot of high ratings for their simplicity of use and ease of setup. And with the latest release of their Sonos Controller app which includes universal search, Sonos hits high marks for many users - especially for those who use it exclusively to listen to music.

However, the issue that can be found on this Amazon board, along with countless other boards online, is the back and forth dispute that Sonos does (or doesn't) provide a true Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound experience through the Playbar.

I am here to tell you definitively that Sonos DOES provide a Dolby Digital 5.1 surround experience, but 9 times out of 10 you will not be able to get it using Sonos' simple setup of connecting your TV directly to your Playbar.

My home theater setup consists of the following components:

- [[ASIN:B00BBAFUQC LG Electronics 50PN6500 50-Inch 1080p 600Hz Plasma HDTV (Black) (2013 Model)]]
- [[ASIN:B00CX5P8FC Amazon Fire TV]]
- Comcast Xfinity Cable TV Cable Box
- [[ASIN:B00AEMGGU2 SONOS PLAYBAR TV Soundbar and Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music]]
- [[ASIN:B00834SIO0 SONOS SUB Wireless Subwoofer (Gloss)]],
- [[ASIN:B00EWCUK1Q SONOS PLAY:1 Compact Wireless Speaker for Streaming Music - (Black)]] (2X)
- [[ASIN:B001TH7GSW AmazonBasics Digital Optical Audio Toslink Cable, 6 Feet]] (2X)

Many TVs, including newer models, have only one optical audio output slot to connect to the Sonos Playbar by way of a TOSlink cable. And not all TV have the internal hardware that decodes the audio out of that slot to Dolby Digital 5.1. Many, will decode to Stereo, PCM, or another 2 channel architecture like Dolby Pro Logic. However, the Sonos Playbar will take these 2 channel inputs from the TV's optical out slot and convert them to a stereo signal correctly partitioned into a left and right channel and mix the center channel, left surround, right surround, and low frequency effects (LFE) channel into a decent, albeit not distinct, surround sound experience.

The Sonos Playbar has a design flaw that could be easily corrected with one (of many possible) fixes. If the Playbar allowed for multiple optical audio inputs instead of one, a user could easily connect their streaming media player, Blueray player, and cable box. The software could be updated to see where an active audio signal is coming from and would switch to the appropriate source automatically or manually if necessary.

When connected directly to my TV, the Sonos Controller registers \\"Audio Input: Stereo\\" for the Playbar under \\"Settings\\" -> \\"About My Sonos System\\". This means that the signal coming in from the TV is not decoding the Amazon Fire TV signal properly as Dolby Digital 5.1. However, when I connect the Amazon Fire TV directly to the Playbar, bypassing Sonos' instructions of connecting all of the components to the TV, the Sonos Controller registers \\"Audio Input: Dolby Digital 5.1\\" and the quality of the sound coming through all of the speakers is night and day. Playing the opening battle scene of Saving Private Ryan was much clearer and without a doubt pushed through 6 independent audio channels. Even the LFE channel pushing through the Sonos Sub was amazing.

I have doubled down on the Sonos ecosystem and fully believe that the products and service warrant the price paid. And the small inconvenience of manually switching the audio cable in to the Playbar input is a small price to pay to have one of the best, truly wireless, home theater setups in the business.

So, for those of you reading all of the reviews and wondering if you need a really expensive TV to get true Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound with the Sonos home theater setup, the answer is no. You can get true Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound from Sonos with a small, albeit inconvenient, workaround. If you are willing to manually switch out the TOSlink cables from the single optical input slot on the rear of the Playbar, you will be thoroughly happy with this purchase.

The current retail value of building a Sonos home theater system will run you between $1,796 if using Play 1s as surround speakers to $1,996 if using Play 3s as surround speakers. I am using Play 1s as my surround speakers in a room that is approximately 320 square feet with 9 foot ceilings and they sound great. Given that they will be used for the surround channels, I believe you may only need Play 1s and not the upgraded Play 3s for a home theater configuration.

product_title: Brainwavz ProAlpha In-Ear Headphones
review_body:
I think these are very good earphones. They were sent to me by Brainwavz for review and, like others of theirs I have tried, they sound great once they are properly adjusted, and far better than I might expect at this price.

They come with a very nice little carrying case and a good range of silicone tips for a good fit. The build quality is very good; the earphones themselves are made of aluminium onto which you fit the tips which suit you best, and a robust plastic sound-chamber. They have a good silver connecting cable with decent strain relief and the jack is gold-plated. This is plainly a well-made product.

The description says that these ProAlpha earphones are \\"tuned for bass.\\" They certainly are: the bass response is remarkable although middles are rich and there is a good, bright treble which is hiss-free even at high volume. I tried these with my Test Playlist which I use for audio products beginning with 15th Century choral music, ending up with The Rolling Stones, Leonard Cohen and London Grammar and going through most things in between. They are fantastic on rock and anything which needs a good bass kick, and Leonard Cohen's deep, creaky voice on Old Ideas sounds phenomenal! Just for fun I turned the low bass up 10 dB on my equalizer to see what would happen and the earphones responded beautifully, with the deep bass on London Grammar's Hey Now absolutely rolling round my skull.

The strong bass does make them a little unbalanced in classical music, with the violins in a string quartet sounding a little too mixed back, for example, so they may not suit everyone, but if you want a real kick in the bass the sound is great.

Correct positioning in the ear is vital with earphones like this. They come with a decent selection of silicone tips and a set of Comply memory foam tips so you will be able to find the ones which suit you best and it's well worth taking the time to get it right. Once I had got the right tips in the right position they sound was excellent and they were very comfortable.

These earphones (like all the Brainwavz headphones I have tried) are a quality product at a very reasonable price, giving excellent sound. They are well made by people who really know and care about sound and if you want a really strong bass response, I can recommend them warmly.the right position they sound was excellent and they were very comfortable.

These earphones (like all the Brainwavz headphones I have tried) are a quality product at a very reasonable price, giving excellent sound. They are well made by people who really know and care about sound and if you want a really strong bass response, I can recommend them warmly.

Bass. They've got it, and lots of it. These have the most bass of any earbud I have ever heard, and that bass is clean and clear. I read reviews touting how much bass they had, and those reviews were not exaggerating. Seriously serious bass. The highs and mids are clean and clear too, and never screechy or tinny or flat. Overall, the sound can be described as ample and full bodied.

Fitment is great, straight out of the box. They stay in my ear well even when I'm moving around a lot (exercising, working etc) and they block out a good portion of the noise from the outside world. I will note that some reviews said that the outer part of the earbud hurt their ears, so that could be a thing. I tried all of the different fitting types that came with the buds, but settled on the ones that came installed out of the box as they were the most comfortable, and so far I have not had any ear pain.

Cons:

Even though it has a flat cable, it still gets tangled occasionally. I have never had a set of headphones that don't tangle, so I have just accepted it as par for the course.

Conclusion:

Worth. Every. Single. Cent. Spent.

I would definitely buy them again, and I highly recommend them if you are looking for great sounding earbuds with lots o BASS.

product_title: Opti-UPS SS1200 Black UPS 1200VA
review_headline: About what you would expect for the price but for specific needs its a decent deal.....
review_body:
This is really a voltage regulator and buck designed to keep voltage fluctuations at a stable output voltage with a small internal battery. I suppose technically you could call this a UPs but I can't for the life of me figure out where they get the crazy VA numbers from. This will provide minutes (and not many) if used with a PC or laptop. I purchased this solely to provide stable voltage and some continuous power for a low draw wireless IP camera. We experience regular momentary \\"hiccups\\" from our rural power company, usually lasting a few seconds, rarely more than an minute or two. Considering the extremely low draw from the camera, this works out just fine. It powers the camera through the short brownouts and outages without which the cameras would auto-reset and cycle through their self tests, panning and tilting and trying to re-establish a wifi connection. This was annoying and required remotely logging into each camera to reset it to the desired field of view. This inexpensive solution solved that problem. For that limited scope, and the very low price, this is a good solution. Bought 2 will buy 2 more - same type of application. It also is useful for maintaining power to a POE injector that runs my outdoor Hawkings repeater and a small 4 port POE switch, again, extremely low power requirement for a very short period of time. Plastic case, SIX! outlets! typical low end Chinese build but again, for the application I needed it for and for $30 bucks, hard to beat. Voltage is indeed regulated up and down as verified with a meter and a variable AC (Variac) on the input side - regulation was surprisingly tight, actually better than expected. The Buck function did kick the output up 15 volts when I dropped the input to 95VAC but I'm not sure, and didn't want to find out, for how long. I suspect something would give if you had a low voltage scenario for any period of time. To be fair, 3 stars. YMMV.

* Update - I seriously don't believe there'sa battery inside this thing (I'll pop it up and check). I think I was seeing residual/quiescent power most likely from an internal cap but no way is this thing going to power anything if you pull the plug out of the wall outlet. It does, however, regulate the voltage. This shouldn't be advertised as a UPS. For that reason, dropped from 3 stars to 1.

product_title: NAD - VISO HP50 (Black)
review_body:
Yeah, that has been my best purchase in ears, pun intended.

I was always told about the soundstage of these cans and how much they sound like open-back cans. It is obvious they sound LIKE and not exactly as open-back, so it won't ever compete level to level with them.

However to people that do not want external noise and also that work in workplaces among other people, open-back cans are a luxury that cannot be used. These come in very handy. They offer that passive noise isolation all closed back should offer (and it is very well implemented in these) and a broader, fuller soundstage as the open-backs.

It responded superbly to amplification, minimum levels were enough to enrich music details. It has very little sound modification, I would say it enhances just a little, almost nothing, in the bass range. To me that is very important, I do not like headphones that completely distort the original music.

Using it solo with my iPhone it also responded very well, I didn't lose much detail, but of course with amplification is where all closed back should be. -The right (advance) button sends a stream of multiple presses every time. I use this a LOT for advancing to the next song in XBMC Music playlists, so this was the final deal-breaker for me.

-Keys on the keyboard often send multiple keypresses. It's annoying, but I could've lived with it. And I could not find a \\"backspace\\" button to undo them. I finally figured out Alt + Back arrow did a backspace, which is kind of cumbersome.

Well, back to my Logitech K400 keyboard, standard IR remote, and Music Pump XBMC (Awesome app! send him $) Remote on Android for now...

I gave 2 stars, 1 because the air mouse worked well, plus 1 more because other buttons, including the red Power on/off button, on the front seemed to work fine. The Power button worked right out of the box, unlike what other reviewers experienced.

review_headline: Budget Friendly Price, Sound Quality is fine-- BUT It doesn't stay firmly on my ear unless I hold it in place.
review_body:
I must have weird ears or something...

I bought this style because of the good reviews regarding the wear-ability of this device and because of my general propensity to break ear-hooks almost as regularly as the next occurring Tuesday. Another unadvertised perk was saying, \\"M-Pow!\\" like a Saturday Morning B-- Renegade Ninja movie...but that's a whole different script... ahem... back to the more pertinent issues...

It was received quite quickly, was delivered in a small, sturdy presentation box, with a selection of clear silicone buds (only the very smallest of which would work for me), a short USB cable, a USB wall adapter and a very cute little carry pouch that I will most likely casually misplace.

Personally, although the price was about equal, after using both, I definitely prefer the sound, fit and adjust-ability of Blue Ant to this, but was having device connectivity drops and was down to my last flimsy clear plastic ear hook when I ordered this one.

Anyway, even when the Mpow manages to stay in my ear, the sound quality is not a clear and crisp as the Blue Ant, (according to my \\"call-ees\\")doesn't noise cancel as well, and even though correctly inserted to my ear canal the device tends to \\"pop off\\". I've disconnected calls because of continuously using my hand to keep it in my ear. I used the smallest silicone bud (the larger ones make the problem completely unmanageable), but although the hook is semi-flexible the height is NOT adjustable and it does not rest BEHIND my ear at all, the curve is actually above the top of my ear. That aspect really takes away from the anticipated hands-free functionality I'd hoped to achieve with this purchase.

However-- Because the Mpow will likely stay in the basically one piece it came in and has not yet \\"ear-gurgitated\\" its silicone fixture, I'll probably wind up giving it away to someone sporting more generously sized \\"ear-pendages\\" and continuing my search for something more adjustable than the Mpow and less fragile than the Blue Ant style plastic hooks before it become the latest resident of my drawer full of scattered remnants of my previous attempts to fully realize \\"hands- free communication\\".

product_title: Grace Digital Rugged and Waterproof Case with Built-In Speaker for iPod, iPhone and MP3 Players
review_headline: Great Sound.  Sturdy Construction.   Haven't tried to drown it yet.
review_body:
I demand that any playback device gives me good sound. I hate cheap, hollow echoing, treble-blaring crap.
Even with only one speaker, this thing delivers. Crank up the bass setting on your mp3 player and enjoy.
I will say that you'll need to keep the volume under control. You can play it relatively loud, but at some point (well before max volume) it will start to vibrate and distort.... but what do you want from a single waterproof speaker? (Be realistic, if you want rugged and waterproof, it's not going to sound like a live show) To be clear though, it DOES PLAY LOUD ENOUGH CLEANLY.

The case is heavy duty plastic, with rubber at top and bottom to help stand it up without slippage. Seems very tough.
Has a little strap on the back that easily takes the average carabiner, making it easy to attach to almost anything.

It's pretty dern good on battery life. Using regular alkalines, cheap brand even, I've got about 12 hours of play time and still going.

The description claims it will float. I haven't taken it swimming, and probably won't. But it certainly seems like it would float if it fell in the water, and I'm pretty sure rain wouldn't be an issue at all.

My only gripe is that once the player is in it and it's locked shut, you can't control the player at all, just the volume. But again, if it's waterproof, sandproof, beerproof.... there's gonna be some tradeoffs. Long playlists = Solved.

product_title: ClearStream 5 Indoor/Outdoor HDTV Antenna - 65 Mile Range
review_headline: Excellent on VHF, not so great on UHF
review_body:
This is a very good VHF antenna, not too large, splits the UHF-VHF signal well, is broad directional tolerant, but for me was not terrific on UHF. If you have some other solution for UHF already and just need a pure VHF antenna, this is very good. But this does advertise as a combined antenna having \\"outstanding UHF capability\\" but in my experience it only got half the UHF channels in my area. Also it's pretty expensive for just VHF and no mounting pole. I ended up returning it and getting a model C2-V from the same company, which solved all my problems, a great antenna.

A basic problem with TV antennas is that even with the switchover to digital, some TV is on UHF, and while the helpfully the low VHF stations are gone, there are still quite a few on high VHF. This means that in any less than perfect reception area, you really need two different antenna designs to get them all. It's a shame the FCC couldn't take that opportunity to just use one band or the other for all tv, but there we are.

Now I live in north Metro Los Angeles (Pasadena). Half the major stations are High VHF (7, 9, 11, 13) and half are UHF (2, 4, 5, 28, 50). (No you can't tell by the nominal channel numbers anymore like you could in the past.) We're only about 3 mi. from all the giant transmitters on Mt Wilson. Great right? Wrong, I'm in the shadow of a couple mountains up against the foothills and even a decent indoor antenna gets little reception at all. Also, we are so close to the mountain with its spread of antennas that some are in one direction while others are off in another. Basically everyone here just gets cable or satellite. That's a drag because you can't just copy the antennas that your neighbors are using, cause no one in this whole neighborhood has one. I'm on my own.

I have been using a big old ugly Radio Shack UHF/VHF antenna on a big ugly tall mast with a remote control rotator. It looks like a big 8 ft long jagged arrow. It's an eyesore, and inour violent windstorms this thing has lost a couple elements, and the wind can rotate it, after most wind storms I need to fiddle with the rotator. Ugh. Well, the good news is, this is an antiquated design that probably no one needs to suffer with anymore.

I really wanted an antenna that's A) not so sensitive to direction pointed, B) is much smaller and lower on the roof, and C) doesn't fall apart in the wind. Oh yeah, and of course D) gets all the channels.

This antenna, now that I look at it, is clearly a VHF design. The good UHF antennas from ClearStream have the round coil design, either one, two, or four coils. This does not. It gets some UHF for me but not well enough to use. Ch 2, 4, and 5 don't come in at all. Essentially I would say you should plan on getting an additional UHF antenna. The good thing about this strategy is that you could point the UHF in one direction and this in another, this could well solve some directional problems in certain situations like mine.

Another plus is that I was able to mount this quite low on the roof. You might be able to just bolt it to a water vent pipe on the roof if it is long enough. Or your chimney. And if you need a pole, you will maybe not need a huge long stout one. Though that depends on how far you are from the transmitters etc. For that matter you could try to put it in the attic first, it just might work.

In the end I got the ClearStream C2-V which was cheaper than this, smaller, and actually gets every channel. And it comes with it's own adjustable mounting pole which is not very tall but works very well. I highly recommend trying that first if you think just one good outdoor or attic antenna would suit you.

product_title: Polk Audio In-Ear Headphones
review_headline: Great at first, not very durable
review_body:
I have had these earbuds for about 1.5 years now and will need to go with a new set in the very near future due to issues with the earbuds. It is nice to have an option of active noise canceling at a price much lower than Bose but really isn't worth the money. Issues with battery life and shorting out started to develop after about 9-10 months of use in my case.

Pros:
Relatively cheap active noise canceling earbuds
Base levels are great
Multiple earbud tip options
Listen-through capability
Buying parts for the earbuds through the Polk site is pretty easy to do though you will have to call in your credit card number
Tangle free cords are nice
Look good

Cons:
Noise canceling box has a lot of issues. Will listen through at times for no reason, will short out and now my right side is failing.
Noise canceling is great for low frequency but in some cases amplifies high frequency.
Too short, could really use ~0.5-1.0 ft of additional cord.
I have contacted the company twice about getting the headphones replaced or repaired. No response!
Shorting out started less than 1 year after buying (which means they should have been replaced... but once again no response)
Really most of the earbud attachments are completely useless.
Battery life decreased significantly as shorts started (as to be expected I suppose)
Noise canceling box/device is pretty awkward in shape/weight.
Battery cover is easily lost and name wears off over time.

Overall they start out and seem to be really nice. Just simply not durable enough, and don't let the durable looking wires fool you. The weakness is between the wire and the noise canceling unit (where the short starts to develop). Such an expensive pair of earbuds should last a lot longer and the company really should respond to their customers about a faulty product. I would probably bump this review to three stars if I even had a response from the company telling me how much they would charge to fix the product.

I would say that the active noise canceling isn't really as beneficial as one would expect. The active noise canceling really is not much better than simple noise reduction (blocking the sound by inserting the earbuds).

product_title: Sangean WR-12 AM/FM Analog Wooden Cabinet Receiver (Walnut)
review_headline: Not without problems, but in comparison to other products, near-perfect.
review_body:
The WR-12 is an upgrade insofar as size and and speaker array from the little brother, the WR-11. The WR-11 is a similar radio, but additional features exist in the WR-12, including binaural \\"stereo sound\\", and treble/bass adjustments. If I were being critical, I would give the radio a \\"4\\", but in comparison to similar devices, it really does deserve a \\"5\\". This device is for people who use radio in their listening diet; it would be unfair to purely grade this item as speaker-listening device (like an iPod dock). Also this radio shouldn't be compared to an awesome little workhorse like the CCRadio-2E; this is best used as a stationary radio, preferably connected to an external rooftop antenna. This last part is undoubtedly the kicker, because if you're looking for the unit to sit on your end table connected only via its power cord, you may not get all the reception you're hoping for.

My Use: This unit was purchased explicitly to serve as a kitchen radio/stereo over a corner sink nook. When I finish my installment I will post images. I selected this radio due to aesthetics (old school, no clock) and external radio hookups for AM and FM. Having a radio in the kitchen allows me to cook and clean, listen to news or baseball, all while my children play and/or watch programming in the adjacent family room.

FM Reception: I have this unit connected to an AFHD-4 by Pixel Technologies, mounted over my garage approximately 60 feet from my kitchen. That antenna is split three ways in my home using Pixel's MBS-4. The feed innervating my kitchen is bifurcated into AM and FM, with the AM loop wiring connected to terminals on the rear of the WR-12. Both Sangean's WR-11 and WR-22 claim AM reception, but some images for each of those radios do not show AM loop terminals. With an external antenna, FM audio is tremendous. However, my local NPR affiliate (KVPR) is fuzzy for reasons unknown. When a station is not perfectly in-tune with the radio, switching to \\"ST\\" (stereo) amplifies noise fuzz. NPR is not the best, but NPR still sounds quite good in standard FM with dial finagling. Other FM stations when tuned to \\"ST\\" are wonderful.

AM Reception: I primarily listen to KNBR 68, to the south of the San Mateo bridge in Redwood City... 290 miles NW of my location. While this reception is not wonderful, as the sun lowers the AM signal improves noticeably. I finished listening to a game last night during clean-up as my daughter watched television in the next room. Other, local AM stations are crystal clear (as good as AM gets). This includes AM Radio for 1340 & 940 (ESPN, Dodgers baseball), and 580 KMJ (Fox/Conservative programming).

***One major caveat to mention: I have 2 antennas on my home (TV and Radio, at opposite sides), but neither of these antennas are yet grounded (RF interference). There is a reason this has not yet been done, and I will revise this review once this has been completed. I currently have the radio in a temporary location (on a kitchen counter, but with antenna coax and the power cable in close proximity to each other. Power interference creates a lot of noise with an incoming antenna and this unit, so I had to elevate the power cable up and away from the resting coax to diminish (eliminate?) the effect.

***Caveat #2: I own a Sangean HDT-1X, currently connected in my family room system. I suffer similar problems with AM radio, but my NPR (KVPR) reception comes through on Hybrid Digital (HD-FM) and is flawless. I will revise this review in the future.

Choosing the right Sangean: The WR-12 was an easy choice for me over the WR-11, but the uncertainty of the loop configuration of the WR-22 and lack of stereo sound ultimately lost out in favor of the WR-12. The WR-22 has an enormity of great features, especially BT audio, but I use High Fidelity FLAC recordings through my phone, so the WR-22's USB low-def USB connection did not inspire me.

Aesthetics: Somehave mentioned the wood case differing from an appearance in some pictures, and only appears to be oiled. I agree, but this is a fine wooden case and the quality of the overall unit is bar-none. One can remove the case and apply a clear coat of varathane which would protect the case, provide luster, and deepen the coloring of the finish; I may/may-not choose to take this action in the future; I like the look of the unit as-is. product_title: Sennheiser On-Ear 926MHz Wireless RF Headphones with Charging Cradle
review_headline: Excellent sound and reception, mediocre fit and comfort
review_body:
This is a first impression based on a lot of use in two ways for about three weeks. One purpose was to use the headphones to enjoy Sirius received via a computer throughout a medium size apartment. The other was to watch TV and be free of the varying clicks, pops, and hisses that I have dealt with for years with my otherwise excellent Sony headphones.

From a reception and sound quality point of view, the 120s far surpass the Sony wireless phones. No noise at all when watching TV and excellent sound. Excellent sound when using the computer to enjoy Sirius as well. No interference anywhere in the apartment.

The downside, which could prove to be significant, is fit and comfort. The headband is adjustable, but I have yet to find a position or adjustment I could really call \\"comfortable,\\" and they tend to slip around. The Sony's were far more comfortable and stable on the head -- if you could stand the unpredictable clicks, pops, and hissing. In the end, sound is the key feature and the Sennheisers have been great in that respect for three weeks. I hope to get used to the comfort and stability issues.

I found them extremely easy to hook up to a Samsung TV.

At first it can be a little tricky to get the headphones to sit correctly on the recharging stand so that recharging occurs, but that passed quickly. Probably due to the excessive simplicity of the headband, it can't detect whether they are on a head or not, so you have to turn the unit on/off manually with a switch on the left ear cup. Another minor annoyance.

Another plus over the Sonys is tuning and reception. Unlike the Sony, there are no transmitter switch positions to set on the Sennheiser base, and no corresponding switch positions to set on the headset. All the tuning is done on the headset with a simple dial that works well. But since it's adjacent to a similar dial for volume, your finger will need to learn to remember which is which. If you can't hear anything or if volume is low, it can be either because the volume is turned down (obvious) or because the tuning needs adjustment (not as obvious).

In some respects this should be a 3-star review because of the level of fit and comfort. But all of the performance aspects linked to sound are so good that it would be cheating the unit not to give it a 4-star rating.

review_headline: Overall, the best headphones I have used
review_body: A Bose QC owner for many years, I tried other brands only after my QC15s failed on me three times. I bought Audio Technica ATH-ANC first; they had better sound but did not provide great noise-cancellation in flight. Along the way I tried noise-reducing ear-buds, which were better than I expected but not really comparable for sound quality. Then I tried and bought Beats Executive, which I'd put about half-way between the AT and Bose on both sound quality and noise-cancellation. I do a huge amount of transatlantic flying and I'd still be relying on the Beats but was attracted by a really low price offer of $240 on the Sony MDR1 RNC, which have received excellent reviews. I had seen that these were apparently to be succeeded by the cheaper and apparently inferior MDR10 RNC, so I decided to give the MDR1 RNCs a try while I could. Out of the box there were no connecting cables, but a call to Sony got that fixed without hassle. The first thing I appreciated was the superb build quality and comfort of these headphones - on both counts they left all the others far behind. On first listening, they sounded as good as the others but after a very brief burn-in they were also the best sounding - again by a wide margin. With great anticipation I took them on a flight and ... here's the surprise ... they have very good sound-cancellation, but the sound quality is altered when you switch it on - there's some loss of bass. The good news is that even without switching on the active sound-cancellation, they do as good a job as the others (except the Bose) because of the excellent fit over the ears. Bose are without doubt the best on sound-cancellation alone, but these are far better on sound quality, build quality, comfort, and can be used without power - they are also rechargeable. An excellent product. Note that many of the reviews are of the entirely different product MDR1-RBT, which has blue tooth but not the same noise cancelling feature.

product_title: ClearStream Indoor Antenna - 25 Mile Range
review_headline: Suits my needs well after some trial and error
review_body:
I've been using this antenna for almost a year, having ditched cable TV. What a didn't fully appreciate when I first bought it is that there is almost a science to the whole antenna-use thing. Where you live in relation to the broadcast towers, the topography of the area, and the placement of the antenna in your home are HUGE factors, among several others.
I initially placed this antenna in my living room very close to my TV and facing the general direction of the towers, and I had all sorts of problems -- missing stations, interference from people walking by, interference from stationary objects nearby (like a metal DVD rack) ... I would even find that the positioning of the antenna a centimeter here or there could make a huge difference, so accidental bumping led to a frustrating time of re-positioning for optimal signal strength. The use of the amplifier only made things WORSE, not better.
Then, after living with this arrangement for several months, I decided on a whim to stick the antenna in the attic, face it in the direction of the broadcast towers, and attach it to the TV via the existing (and unused) cable TV line. PRESTO!! It has worked great ever since!
I should note that I live in a major metro area and that the topography of the area is flat. That has a lot to do with why this antenna is working so well for me now. I'm sure that the shielding benefits of the high-quality cable TV line are helping also.
Bottom line: there is nothing wrong with this antenna. But it doesn't mean that it's the right antenna for you.
