product_title: Sony MDR-EX210B Earbud Style Headphones
review_headline: OKAY, I'M ON BOARD HERE. Fine Sound, Full Range, Sparkling Clarity
review_body:
With about 90% laudatory reviews vs 10% crabby outliers, I figured I wasn't doing a huge dice roll by ordering these.

I have some decent budget earbuds, including JLab JBud 3s, some really for-the-money superb 10-buck Panasonic RP-TCR5-Ks and some ungodly bass heavy V-Modas. The JLabs and Panasonics are nice listening earbuds, but both are a bit thin on bass (even though I am anything but a bass-head) and tend to get tinkly on treble, though most of time they are pretty pleasant.

So I wanted a reasonable upgrade, something that offered a fuller sound, more balanced tonal range, and still had what I value most in music: solid, clean mids and clear, clean highs, especially vocals. With their relatively-mega 13.5mm driver (vs 8-9mm on my other buds) and the many rave reviews and $30 price tag, I concluded these were the best bang for the buck buds.

Was i ever right.

Amazing audio, and not just with that \\"for the money\\" qualifier. Amazing, period. I got these two days ago (so I cannot yet speak to their longevity, but build quality seems solid) and gave them a test drive through a wide variety of music: pop, rock, folk, classical, jazz, others. The verdict on all genres was this: Winner.

Here's a route sampler.

1. Samuel Barber's 'Adagio for Strings\\" (that many of you know from the soundtrack of the film \\"Platoon\\"): A slow, measured haunting, sometimes soaring piece sublimely delivered to my ears via these Sonys.

2. Bob Dylan's 'Brownsville Girl\\", an 11-minute musical story with HUGE (totally atypical for BD) production values, including what sounds like a full orchestra backing him up, and all-female chorus on the refrain. All kinds of sounds here from Dylan's signagture rasp to the chorus' elegant harmony to the full-bloom orchestral backdrop. Best listening experience for me ever for this song. Sounds just swirling around everywhere, wide soundstage, crisp highs, potent mids, rich bass, eachsound discrete but still combining to create a radiant harmonic whole. I just love how this song sounds through these buds.

3. Morton Gould's 'American Salute', a veritable sound explosion; room (or head) filling, full-throttle, propulsive 3+ minutes of full sheer orchestral power----but with some crystal clear chimes jumping out at you early on. Absolutely majestic rendering through the EX-210s. I liked this so much that I hit repeat twice.

4. Leonard Cohen's 'Hallelujah\\" by both Cohen himself, and also K.D. Lang. VERY different sonic experiences. Cohen has this rumbling, powerful perpetual bass of a voice and it comes through brilliantly, set off and complemented by the rising mids and highs of the background chorus. K.D. Lang's version is, well, ethereal. No other word for it. Same song, but WAY different. K.D. Lang's, in particular, seemed custom-built for these buds, and what they can produce.

5. The live version of 'Tusk' by Fleetwood Mac. My god. A thumping, driving meld of drums, full brass section, and primal vocals. What a trip this is via the Sonys. Highs, mids, bass all tossed into one big bowl and tossed around, every sound separate but still unified. This may have been best of all now that I think about it. Hypnotic.

Also did some Springsteen, some Stones, Knopfler, main title from \\"Lord of the Rings\\". Oh, and some beautiful tenor with Tommy Fleming doing the Irish traditional 'Raglan Road'----a wavering, poignant masterpiece. Never heard this song sound more aching than through the Sonys.

A lot more. But you get the idea.

For $30, it's like listening to a nonstop live performance, no matter then genre.

So I guess you can infer that I like these.

review_body:

What this does is take HDMI video in and outputs VGA out and analog L/R audio.

I've tested this with a PS3, PS4 and a Macbook Pro laptop. Resolution, color, black levels are all very good. DVDs, blu-rays, games, and streaming video all work great. For me, analog L/R audio isn't even worth testing, so I didn't bother with it. You can continue to use S/PDIF digital output on the PS3/4 while using this device for just the video.

Does it come with a power supply? Mine did not, but some reported that theirs did. I would recommend a USB to 5V DC Type-M barrel adapter cable (e.g. http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B003MQO96U/) to prevent having to use up another outlet with a wall wart.

Is this product a knock-off? What I received was as pictured and has no brand or model # on it, it just says made in China, so I would guess that it probably is. Does it matter? Not to me if it works.

I gave this only 4 out of 5 because it didn't come with a power supply and only outputs analog L/R audio. It also seems a little oversized for what it does. It is a relatively cheap alternative to the more expensive HDMI to component video converters, though.

review_headline: Rocking me out of my Wet Socks
review_body:
I love, love the speaker I bought it to listen to music this past summer (Jul 2013) while at work or while running on the treadmill (headphones get sweaty and slide off). I’ve even carried it to the beach with me so I could listen while lounging in the sand. I carry it in my purse so I'm not without it. I love it so much, I bought several to give as Christmas gifts which gave me the perfect opportunity to see if two speakers would be better. I was thinking it would be cool for parties on the deck outdoors. I tried the Bluetooth connection with my iphone but I was unable to get the iphone to recognize more than one speaker at a time. I think that might be a Bluetooth limitation (one device at a time) but I’m not sure. Oh well. If you’re outside for a beer or something with several friends, one speaker is plenty loud enough, it's just not club loud, which my neighbors probably appreciate.

As for the charge, I’ve listened to music for several hours and not needed to recharge. Done it again, listening for a few hours over several days at work, and listened while working on the treadmill and still didn’t need to charge it. I really should see how many hours it can go but I’m sorry I can’t say that I know exactly how long it was in total. If I had to guess, I’d say maybe 6-8 hours. Overall, I have been quite pleased with how long it stays charged. It is certainly far longer than my iphone, that’s for sure. Thankfully, the few times it needed a charge, I had an outlet handy – it plays while charging.

When I was showing it off to a friend, they wanted to know how far you could get before the connection breaks so I left the speaker (which was playing a song from my iphone) in the room with my friends and walked into another room with my iphone and I’d say that I got nearly 26 feet away (out of line of sight as well) before the connection broke and it stopped playing but as soon as I moved a foot closer, it picked right back up.

This is a sweet piece of gear. I only wish it came with a velvety pouch to protect it from all of the other junk that floats around in my purse. I might share that even though it’s unprotected in my purse, and has been carried around (and used) for more than six months like this, it miraculously has no scratches and looks (and plays) like new which is a testimonial to the tough casing.
Just to make sure, this review was for model #V3-5CPB; SimplyVibe makes similar looking speakers that do not have all of the features I mentioned here. I know this because I accidently bought and then exchanged them for the correct models when I was getting those Christmas presents I mentioned earlier.t back up.

product_title: Clip Plus 4 GB MP3 Player (Black)
review_headline: Great Music Player With Many Options
review_body:
THE DESIGN:
This mp3 player is very small and lightweight, maybe two US nickel faces tall, one US 50¢ coin long, and maybe a stack of 12 coins wide, not counting the clip. This thing takes almost 0 effort to hold in the hand, and it can even be supported entirely by the earbuds in your ears! Despite this, I've dropped this thing many times at varying speeds and angles (on accident, of course), and the only visible scuff on the device is a small plastic chip on a corner of the device that is barely visible. This device is comfy in the hand, and every button feels satisfying to press with a *click*! The only bad bit about the design is that the buttons are too audible for use in a public setting.
-------
THE SOFTWARE:
The bundled OS that this mp3 player uses is perfectly serviceable. It has easy to navigate menus, but considering how few buttons the device has, there are menus within menus within menus. You can natively change the equalizer, delete songs, create a single playlist, control volume, skip tracks, and play/pause. When you connect the device to your PC with the included MicroUSB cable, there are different folders for you to put music, podcasts, voice recordings, and more in. There are plenty of options. Speaking of which, you can use this MP3 player to record your voice! Getting the sound files to your computer is too cumbersome to make this a microphone, but the mic in this is good enough for you to make quick notes to remember for later. Maybe you don't have your smartphone handy and some bully stole all your writing utensils. I don't know.
Browsing music is a breeze; you can browse by album, genre, artist, or just browse an alphabetical list.
There's also a radio built-in that I never use and there's also this thing called SlotRadio. From what I can tell, it was SanDisk's attempt to sell people $40 MicroSD Cards that connected to radio stations that only play one kind of music, such as rock or country. It also seems to havebombed hard, so don't worry about it.
-------
THE SOUND:
Don't be put off by this thing's size, it's sound quality is amazing! However, this device has no speakers. A con, for sure, but this keeps the cheap price cheap, and this is an mp3 player you would want for exercise or public listening, so you wouldn't want to play music over a speaker anyway. If you do want to do that in public, I suggest buying a Beats Pill and whacking yourself in the head repeatedly.
-------
UPGRADING THE STORAGE:
It's as simple as grabbing a MicroSD card and putting it into the slot on the device. It's great.
-------
OVERALL:
This device is amazing. A solid mp3 player that's the size of a Zippo with the sound quality of a good sound system, all for under $60. If you are an avid music fan, I can't recommend this enough.
-------
Edit: I've changed some terminology now that I'm more familiar with music equipment and headphone quality. Also, I added a section mentioning MicroSD card support

review_headline: Excellent speaker, with one little caveat
review_body: Compared to the previous version of this wireless speaker, this device has improved by leaps and bounds. The range has greatly improved, and the seemingly constant cutting in and out of audio has disappeared. The quality of the bass on the device is excellent, which is truly challenging for a small form factor. When turning the device on, it produces a low pitched chime that is still a bit too loud and makes it sound like the speaker is blown. Fortunately it is not an issue, and the sound is excellent once you start playing music. The phone capabilities are clear, but I'm not sure if I think they are useful. For me, anyway, I prefer to place the speaker across the room so that I have a fuller auditorium sound instead of sitting it 2 feet away. Because of that, if my phone rings, I either have to get up and turn the speaker off before answer, or shout across the room to use the speaker phone. After digging into the configuration on my phone, I was able to disable the phone audio going to the speaker and eliminated this issue. Once again, I could be playing music, my phone could ring, the speaker would stop playing music (as it should), and I was able to talk on the phone. Upon hanging up the call, the music would continue playing from where it left off. Perfect. If there is one thing I would change about this model, though, is the requirement to hold down the power button to both turn on and off the device. It seems like an unnecessary bother to have to hold the button in for a few seconds before the device will power on. It would make more sense to have a button that locks down when clicked, and pops up again when clicked again. This is not a huge issue, but it did give me some problems when I first started using the device. Like most people, I skipped the bulk of the directions and went straight to the bluetooth pairing section. Everything seemed to make sense, but I had trouble getting the device to stay turned on. I would click the power button, the LED would light briefly, and then go out. I did this several times thinking that I received a broken device. Finally I turned to the manual and read that I had to hold down the power button for a few seconds in order to get it to power on. This is counter-intuitive. 4.5 out of 5 stars.

I ended up with these by accident. Bought for someone else but ended up having to
keep them. So I thought why not pair them with my Dell Venue 8. These
sound very good working with the Venue and the equalizer on the Venue allows for
excellent adjustment of the ranges. Bass is not overdone but deep, midrange and treble are accurate.
They have a very \\"FULL\\" sound.
They are very light and I find the on-ear design more comfortable than I imagined.
I have a set of Ultrasone Pro 750's and while these are not in that league the sound
is way better than I expected for this price range.
The ability to \\"plug\\" these in with the supplied cable is a bonus. Decent pouch for
carrying and usb cable for charging.
One thing that to note. The ear pads are not as pictured. They are the pillow type
of pad instead of the smoother formed looking pad in the picture. Still I find these
very comfortable but I also have smaller ears.
The push button controls do not work with the Venue. I have a feeling this has to do with different types of devices and not the headphones. The construction seems solid and should last for many years with normal usage.
It will be interesting to hear what these sound like after \\"burn in\\".
Just to add I just received a Samsung Galaxy S3 with my new phone contract and
again the sound is excellent. The controls on the headphones work perfectly with this phone.
I have been able to walk about 35 feet away from my phone with no loss of audio.

product_title: Koss Headphones
review_headline: Bought them for bus rides and cold weather
review_body:
My Porta Pros broke (the lifetime warranty was so complicated and costly that I decided not to pursue the option) and I saw this as an opportunity to upgrade. I wanted a coiled cord because the Porta Pros broke from the base of the cord and presumably from tugging and twisting. Also the Porta Pros bleed sound quit a lot which is awkward in a bus and your ears tend to freeze a bit more in the -15 celcius weather. Thus I searched for closed, over the ear headphones. These ProDJ100s seemed to have a nice value for money and since I thought that (besides the very common flaw with the cord) my Porta Pros were of high quality and had served me well for 8 years inspite of suffering adverse weather, being stuck in purses and abused in various ways, Koss would be the brand for me.

How the ProDJ100s meet the requirements:
Comfort - Haven't had any issues with pain, but I do have a small head. They are nice and warm in the winter. Uncomfortable around the neck and hard to decide what to do with them if you want to hear what someone has to say to you since they are so big and awkward to maneuver.
Coiled cord - Fixes the problem with the tugging, but also is quite heavy and long.
Bleeding of sound - They do bleed sound, but a bit less than Porta Pros. Sorry fellow passengers, not much help there.
Quality of sound - Porta Pros were better. The sound in these feel a bit muffled and eventoned.
How they isolate noises - They are so noise isolating (while playing music) that I am in fear of my life as I think I'll get run over by a car or some similar situation where a noise can alert you to danger. Crying babies and loud teenagers in the bus definitely won't be a problem anymore. Instead, the clinking and clonking of the headphones themselves might drive me to insanity. And that is the most annoying feature with these headphones.
Looks - They look nice, a bit plastic.

I'm not in love, but I like them. Not the best headphones for onthe go. Better for indoors, static use (though I would get cordless for that). Still, not unusable and they give you plenty of value for money since they are cheap. 2-3 stars if they were 70 dollars, but for 40 dollars 4 stars. I'll continue use, but will persuade someone to fix my Porta Pros and use these on the side.

product_title: Onkyo TX-8255 Stereo Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Good replacement for 30 year old Technics
review_body: I had to replace a 30 year old Technics receiver/amplifier which handled the TV, DVD, CD, cassette tape, and phono (turntable), so I chose the ONKYO TX-8255.  The eight button input selection on the front panel is a very nice feature, and there was room to add an input cable to use with my iPad, laptop, or other device such as an iPod.  My sense is that the FM reception is superior to what I had, and the AM reception is also quite good. The A/B A+B speaker choice fits my existing system (15\\" Wharfedales) with a remote set of (12\\" JBL) speakers. There is no marked scale on the rotating volume control, but this is only a minor annoyance.  There is no \\"loudness\\" control nor high (hiss) or low (rumble) filters which are probably considered to be archaic. Wiring hookup on the back of the unit is easy to use.  The one criticism I have is the absence of a preamp for a magnetic (MC) phono pickup, but this seems to be typical of the stereo receiver/amplifiers now available. If it handled my magnetic (MC) pickup directly without the addition of a preamp I would give it five stars.

Be aware that there is another, similar device being sold here on Amazon. Reviewers of that other version indicate no difference between the two USB ports. This one does have the higher amperage USB port to charge your iPad (or more rapidly charge smaller devices).

As a frequent traveller, I'm always scouting airport gate/lobby areas for outlets. Some airports have not done much to improve access to AC, so people are often camped out near the wall outlets. With this compact unit, I have successfully accessed outlets that were already occupied. You just have to ask nicely.

When you get into your hotel, you find there are not enough outlets for all your electronics, or you have to go unplugging lamps around the room to free up more outlets. Not with this device.

product_title: Kinivo 501BN Premium 5 port High speed HDMI switch with IR wireless remote and AC Power adapter - supports 3D, 1080p
review_body:
This past November, I found myself in a situation that I think I shared with a whole bunch of core gamers. I had all of my game systems hooked up to my Onkyo receiver, and I was about to get two new game systems. I was going to have to either make some changes to my home theater setup, or I was going to have to give up on having all of my "current" game systems hooked up in one place.

I actually considered going down the path of getting a new receiver, with more HDMI inputs. But, honestly, the price point that I had to get to before the number of HDMI inputs would go up was pretty prohibitive. So, I started looking at HDMI switchers. Based on general review ratings, I bought the Kinivo 501BN.

My first approach was to keep the Kinivo facing forward in my home theater, and program my Harmony remote to manually configure the input based on activity. That worked, and the Kinivo was in Logitech's Harmony peripheral database, but it wasn't ideal. One of my biggest complaints about the 501BN is the brightness of the front facing LEDs. The Blue LED is a tiny, piercing point of light that I would illuminate my basement gameroom from all the way upstairs.

I considered covering the light with some semi-transparent film to dim it down a bit, but I took another approach. I gave up on the manual configuration of each input, and instead relied on the auto-switching priorities based on the numerical position of the HDMI inputs. The lower number inputs will take priority over the higher numbers, so as long as I wasn't trying to force some configuration where I needed a higher number to display without turning off a lower number, I would be good.

That approach worked pretty well. I ended up covering the blue LED with electrical tape, and I repositioned the 501BN behind my entertainment center, completely out of sight. I removed all controls for the 501BN from the Harmony, and rely entirely on auto-switching.

So, if this works so great, why did I only give it a 3 star review? Well, I have 3 devices going through the 501BN. An Xbox 360, a Playstation 3, and an Ouya. (Don't laugh at the Ouya!) That wasn't my original configuration. I had trouble with two devices syncing with my Onkyo receiver after passing through the 501BN. First, my 25' HDMI cable for my PC (Big Picture for the win!) wouldn't sync properly, ever. I moved that to my last direct Onkyo input. Second, my Xbox 360 syncs...most of the time. I'd say about one time in 5, I'll get a partial sync with corrupted display output, and missing audio. Sometimes it will recover when the system changes resolution. Sometimes not. I replaced all of the HDMI cables in use with the Xbox 360, and it seems like the problem is slightly less frequent, but it still happens. I plan on trying to insert some power on delays through the activity program for my Harmony remote, but I'm not sure if that will do anything. I have had no problems with the Playstation 3.

So, yeah, this is pretty good so far, but not perfect.

product_title: Coby 8 GB 1.8-Inch Video MP3 Player with FM Radio
review_headline: Avoid this item at all costs!
review_body:
I previously purchased an Apple ipod shuffle, but with a memory of only 1GB, I felt like I needed to get another. I'm a big advocate of film soundtracks and I'm constantly getting more, so with a little searching, I found this 8GB player for a VERY reasonable price.

But other than price, there's very few things I enjoy about this, and I ended up returning it to Amazon after a while.

For starters, I was warned of MP3 Players other than Apple, since I'm used to Apple's excellent quality. I should've looked closer. Once I received the Player, I was excited by the vivid blue color and small, thin size, but disappointed by the sensitivity of the controls. If you click slightly to the left of the actual button, it makes a loud, annoying 'click' and doesn't do what you want it to do. But, "No Biggie," I said.

The MP3 Player can be compatible with Coby Media Manager, but since I don't have that, I used the alternative method. Once plugged into the computer, it recognizes the MP3 Player as a removable disk and files can be copied and pasted into its memory. I have some of the few pros for this MP3 Player under this section. It's easy to transfer files onto the player, and you can create any folder you want to go onto the Player. These new folders can be accessed by visiting the browsing section. But I also have a con. Whenever I created a folder with a song in it, it made a duplicate of that song in the 'All Songs' section.

After I loaded all the songs onto my MP3 Player, there's some more complaints. For one, the only way to access music by artist is by going to the Browser section and clicking on the backslash that appears at the top of the list. For some reason, the artists (mainly Howard Shore!) of my music were recognized as 'Unknown," and so were the albums. I had to create separate folders under the browser section manually and load my songs on there. Another one of Coby's poor choices for this MP3Player is that in order to shuffle your music, you have to click the list button to bring up a menu. If you click on 'RandomAll', the music will be shuffled-sometimes. Not all the time.

Up to this point, I'm a little frustrated, but not too much. The sound quality is still good, and the Player works faster than another MP3 Player I owned a long time ago. But one day, it decides to skip the first few seconds of a song-and then another. The problem slowly grows, until the first few seconds of practically every song are skipped. I would have to manually start the song over in order to hear the first bit! So, my frustration is slowly growing, until one day, in the middle of one of my songs, it pauses, and then plays, and then pauses, and then plays, and then pauses. I start the song over, thinking it was just a temporary glitch.

Wrong.

I was ready to get rid of this MP3 Player, believing it defective, and my beliefs were confirmed when it locked up for about a day. I was unable to use it. Finally, we returned it.

So, as the title goes, I advise all those seeking a new MP3 Player to avoid this one specifically. And if you can, avoid Coby in general. No wonder it went out of business...

review_headline: Review of the Brightness of 5 Different Alarm Clocks
review_body:
Review of the Brightness of 5 Different Alarm Clocks

Executive Summary: I like my bedroom pitch black. Every alarm clock is too bright, even the ones I tried. However, with some window tint [[ASIN:B004YJWA74 Gila JS248 Peel and Cling Super Limo Black 35% VLT Static Cling Glare Control Automotive Window Tint]] (this is what I used, but I would suggest even darker tint) they can be manageable. I did not try any of the actual alarm or radio functions for any of the clocks.

I reviewed quite a few alarm clocks on Amazon before deciding to buy the following. The deciding factors were the design of the clock and the reviews in regards to the brightness. If the design appeared cheap I didn't consider it. If there were few to no reviews or if the reviews overwhelming or consistently said the clock was too bright I wouldn't consider it.

These clocks were to initially be placed on the night stand. However, they were all so bright I changed course and decided to place them on a ledge 25 feet away from the head of the bed.

Geneva 4584E Elgin Electric Alarm Time Clock [[ASIN:B000JPMH2K Geneva 4584E Elgin Electric Alarm Time Clock]]
The best of all the alarm clocks I tried. It's the only one I kept. Even though it had the largest display of any of the clocks I tried, it was only slightly brighter than the smallest display Sony ICF-C318. I have 2 layers of window tint on it and it's still a tad bright. The only negative is the LED lights used to light up the numbers are directly in the middle of each line composing each digit. As a result, the middle of the line is bright and the edge of the line is dim. At times this makes it difficult to read. Note: The first clock I received was broken. One of lines composing a digit did not light up. The replacement clock works great.

GPX, Inc. C353B AM/FM Clock Radio with Dual Alarms and LED Display (Black) [[ASIN:B00BCSYZKA GPX, Inc. C353B AM/FM Clock Radio with DualAlarms and LED Display (Black)]]
The brightest of all the alarm clocks I tried. My wife said \\"can you imagine placing that right next to your head? It lights up the whole room.\\" Even after 2 layers of tint it was still brighter than all the alarm clocks without tint. Also the size of the display was smaller than the Geneva 4584E Elgin Electric Alarm Time Clock so it was harder to read.

Sony ICFC414 Clock Radio [[ASIN:B001RB1XXY Sony ICFC414 Clock Radio]]
This clock is slightly brighter that the Geneva 4584E Elgin Electric Alarm Time Clock even though the display is smaller. Considering the clock is 25 feet away the display is too small to read.

Sony ICF-C318 Automatic Time Set Clock Radio with Dual Alarm (White) [[ASIN:B000MXWSYQ Sony ICF-C318 Automatic Time Set Clock Radio with Dual Alarm (White)]]
Not as bright as the Sony ICFC414 Clock Radio. However, even with 2 layers of window tint it was still too bright to place on the night stand and the display was too small to read from 25 feet away. The white plastic also stood out in a dark room.

Sony ICF-C318 Clock Radio with Dual Alarm (Black) [[ASIN:B000MXWSY6 Sony ICF-C318 Clock Radio with Dual Alarm (Black)]]
Same as the Sony ICF-C318 Automatic Time Set Clock Radio with Dual Alarm (White) except the black plastic did not stand out the way the white did.

Gila JS248 Peel and Cling Super Limo Black 35% VLT Static Cling Glare Control Automotive Window
First off, I would suggest even darker tint. The only way to have a dim alarm clock is to put tint on it. No one makes a dim alarm clock. They're all too bright. The tint itself is a tad bubbly once you put it on, but it stays on and didn't leave any sticky residue when I took it off.

product_title: Outlet Medical-Grade Power Strip 10
review_headline: This rated 5 stars until I opened it up
review_body:
One problem with surge protectors is they are like fuses, if you test it for its total protection, it self destructs. So the only way to know it will work is to examine the construction, test non-destructive parts, and then hope the rest work as advertised. I disassemble units and examine them before I even plug them in.

Pros
Ergonomics of the plug layout is very convenient
audible alarm
protection rating

Cons

On disassembly, the unit had a lot of excess flux, it was so thick in some parts its like vaseline. There were a few strands of hair inside. Its banks of protection diodes were soldered with unacceptably long leads, 2 of them were shorted. It didn't affect the protection since the polarity was correct, but it shorted two data lines together, sure enough the network jack did not work until I separated these diode leads.

The MOV grouped together were coupled to their thermal fuses with a form of tape. Unfortunately, One of them had unraveled so they were not coupled at all, this means had a surge happened the fuses were less likely to blow or would be delayed. Most makers use shrink wrap tubing to hold them together. Better designs encase the MOV in a small chambers inside the chassis to further contain debris and focus the heat on the fuse, but not this unit.

After cleaning the interiors, there were no problem with the sockets: power, LED annunciators, phone, fast ethernet and cable.

I'm not sure what the story was with this unit, but I returned it. If it was a fluke from poor quality control, then on my examination of the other components, this SPD could work. However, they MOV coupling is not optimal, the unit will get fairly hot before the fuse blows and likely melt the chassis before tripping the fuse. Sure enough, some user posted an image of a unit with a melted deformed chassis. Maybe Tripp Lite has improved this design since I bought mine, so given a benefit of doubt I rate it 3 stars.doubt I rate it 3 stars.

review_body: After admiring Bose for many years at friends and families homes, this is my first, entry level speaker into the Bose family.  I have had my Bose Soundlink Mini for a few months now and love it.  It is a hefty chunk of money for a portable blue tooth speaker but out of all the speakers in its price range and lower (which I tested for hours at Best Buy and the Apple Store), it out shined all of them in not only sound but build quality.  If I'm going to spend $200 not only must it sound nice, but it also better feel like $200-which it does.  It mainly sits on my kitchen counter and is used while cooking, or taken into the bathroom, or out in the backyard.  I have been a little reluctant to take it to the beach or camping because it is so expensive, but the few times I have, it worked incredibly well, and it is built well enough where I know it can handle some abuse.  I always get compliments on the way its designed, how heavy it is, and how impressive the sound is!  PROS: -Simple to set up and nice battery life! -The volume can be turned up WAY louder than you will typically need for lounging around the house or outdoors, which is nice. -This baby is is built like a rock. It's aluminum curved body reminds me of something Apple would design.  SOUND: I enjoy jazz, classic rock, and blues music and this speaker makes everything sound amazing.  Absolutely amazing.  It does really well with acoustic instruments-especisally on the low end: drums, standing bass,  electric bass, piano, and it pulls a nice low end out of voices like Frank Sinatra or Nina Simon.  All the instruments stand out on their own and don't sound like they are mashed together coming out of one tiny speaker.  I have heard little nuances in my music that I had not heard before in my headphones or car stereo.  CON: -My only complaint is this speaker is too small for the lower end or electronic and dance music. The Soundlink Mini does not do well with the quick bass beats of hip hop music.  This speaker ismeant for more of a relaxed sound and not club beats.  If you were mainly into Hip Hop, dance music or something more synthesized, I would maybe look somewhere else.  However, As someone who does play electronic music every now and again, its totally fine.  Its not a deal breaker to me at all; it is hard for any speaker in this size category to pull off that low tone.  My advice would be to play with one yourself before purchasing one.  Its so easy to find one at a store, link it to your phone and play your favorite music.  Try out a couple different genres and don't be afraid to crank it up!

review_body:
Good: These are heavy, solidly built, well featured speakers. Of what listening I did, they mostly sounded fine. Extreme highs, such as cymbols and the notorious vocal letter \\"S\\", sound smooth and controlled

Indifferent: A couple of things to note - the digital volume knob on the front takes multiple full revolutions to go from min to max. It is much more like a receiver-style volume. I was suprised to find out how much I had to turn this to hear anything. Pressing in on the volume knob switches between all 5 input sources on back. Placement is key for bass response with these units, and moving them mere inches could make it disappear. They are quite thick from driver to rear of the cabinet.

Unfortunate: The speakers do auto-timeout when source disappears for a time. They do not automatically turn on again. This timeout is not something that can be bypassed. There is a minor amount of zero-source hiss. During source output, I can definitely hear induced buzzing from both speakers--it is continuous. It sounds almost like artist-intended electronic distortion as it changes pitch with the output, but when my classical piano recordings played it too, that was a deal-breaker. I've tried 3 different sources, including iPOD, CD, and my high-end DAC's analog RCA outputs, going into all of the different analog inputs of the Yumis, and the results are the same. I tried a different power circuit and even a power conditioner to ensure this wasn't ground loop induced. It didn't matter. I truly wonder if this was a defect with my particular pair or if maybe the casual listener typically does not listen with their ears close enough (at low levels) to hear this distortion. At my desk, I sit less than three feet from the speakers and could hear it. Higher volumes drowned it out, leading me to believe it is in the preamp stage. I've been a mid-grade audio geek for most of my life, listening to music daily, so I am picky about quality.

I do not want to chance this being a design flaw, so I'm just returning them. I now plan to purchase a second pair of AudioEngine A5s, one of which I run in another room and they are simply excellent. I have an old pair of Paradigm Active/20s and the A5s, IMO, sound nearly as good! I hoped I could save a little scratch with this set of Yumis but they aren't at the same level as the A5s.

product_title: Yamaha RX-V673 7.2-Channel Network AV Receiver
review_body:
This is an amazing receiver. Unfortunately it turned out to be the wrong model for my needs. I wanted to be able to play the same music on my surround sound speakers and also on speakers scattered all around my house. I thought the 2 zones would handle that just fine. To get the second zone to play the same input as the main zone I just connected the stereo audio out to one of the unused audio inputs and set the second zone to use that. It worked but ... the main zone does all sorts of very fancy signal processing and that processing introduces a time delay of about a second. According to the Yamaha tech support there is no way to avoid the delay OR to introduce the same delay for zone 2. So if you can hear both the main speakers and the zone 2 speakers you get a very annoying echo. I ended up returning the 673 and getting a 773 (which has a special 'party mode' to solve this problem) instead.

Still, for the price it's a good system.

product_title: OontZ Curve Ultra Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker - Save 50% on the best Mothers Day and Grads Gifts that they would choose for themselves (Metallic Red)
review_body:
I wouldn't call myself a connoisseur, but tinny music drives me crazy. When my husband plays music on his iPhone 4S, it's like listening to proverbial fingernails scratching a blackboard. (I prefer earphones, he doesn't.) So I got him the Oontz Curve because it was easy to carry and not so expensive that if he broke it or lost it we couldn't replace it. He has an active lifestyle that includes splitting wood, driving horses, and running tractors. The likelihood of his breaking a portable speaker is high. The Cuve's sound is great, far, far beyond my expectations for thirty dollars. The other day he stopped at our neighborhood bar and grille for a morning cup of coffee. Now, everybody in the bar knew each other, so what I'd personally resent in another restaurant was perfectly fine here. The manager hadn't turned on the sound system yet, so he set the Curve and his phone on the bar and played some country music. The other customers were amazed at the sound. So when the manager turned on the sound system, they told her to turn it off--they liked his soundtrack and speaker better.

Maybe this will put the sound in perspective through written word. I bought a Jambox a few of years ago from Best Buy when the only color options were black or white. There were two levels, one around hundred and fifty dollars and the other close to three hundred. The difference in sound quality was so clear I had to buy the more expensive model even though that was not what I'd budgeted for. Had it been available then, I'd have bought the Oontz Curve instead because of its price and its sound.

Btw, the manager at the restaurant has ordered a Curve for her personal use.

product_title: The BEAN Personal Sound Amplifier by Etymotic Research, Pair, Frustration-Free Packaging, Brushed Gold, ER135-QSA-BG2-A BEAN
review_body:
I have ravaged my ears for many, many years. I adore loud, dissonant, distorted music. I've carried a Walkman or an iPod in my pocket for longer than I can remember. When I was at university, I went to see live music three or four times a week at both large and small venues. And since then, living in an urban area and using public transport subjects me to lots of noise daily.

Obviously, all this has taken a toll. Advancing age combined with a constant barrage of both intentional and ambient sound means that my hearing is declining. In social situations, I need to be paying attention to somebody when they're speaking. At home, family members dislike the volume levels I choose for watching TV or playing videogames.

The BEAN has been a good way to compensate for not being able to hear as well as I used to. I think the Bean is at its best when you want to amplify a single source of sound, such as a person speaking or when you're watching a movie, and there is not a lot of competing ambient noise.

What I like
*Easy set up. All you have to do is put on the eartips that you find to be the most comfortable and insert the batteries.
*Comfortable to insert into ears and to wear. I have a pair of [[ASIN:B0044DEESS Etymotic earplugs]] for concert use and the fit is very similar.
*Amplifies just enough so that people can speak more quietly to you or you can turn down the television a couple of notches.
*The kit comes with a good assortment of eartips and accessories.

Caveats
*It takes a while to get used to hearing EVERYTHING around you amplified. Your perception of the world around you will change when you use the Bean, especially when eating, doing things that create noise (such as typing on a keyboard or cooking), and hearing your own voice and breathing.
*The amplified sound has a \\"PA sound\\" quality to it. In other words, the trebly, thin quality that differentiates somebody talking through a microphone from speaking directly to you is present and noticeable. Consequently, I don't think the Bean is good for listening to music.
*There is audible hiss when your surrounding environment is relatively quiet. It's not that noticeable--at least to me.
*If you aren't careful about not putting your fingers near the Bean's mic when inserting or wearing it, it's very easy to create loud feedback. Not nice coming from something that's inserted into your ear canal.

Bottom line: the BEAN is a well-designed, easy to use device for dealing with some hearing loss. The sound it produces does take some time to get used to and it is not suitable for use in every situation, especially in crowded places or when listening to music. product_title: Audio-Technica-USB Direct-Drive Professional Turntable in Silver
review_body:
This turntable is sturdy, well designed, and very user-friendly. I have not had a desire to use the usb port, as I only bought this as a replacement for my old Panasonic table to play my albums on, so my review is based solely on the analog functionality. I also do not use the onboard pre-amp, because I like the phono-input on my receiver.

I am not an audiophile, but rather a lover of music...as are a lot of us. I do listen to a variety of styles of music, and at varying volumes, and find the sound quality of this unit more than pleasing.

I have tile flooring, and an old rolling stereo rack. I do not have issues with vibration through my floor, so I also cannot advise on how well the unit handles those vibrations...

I am not a DJ, but the reverse and pitch adjust are fun to play with and seem to work very well.

The turntable gets up to speed, and stops quickly. I like the 78 setting, because I clean my records, before playing, with a disc-cleaner while it rotates; this speed makes it a much faster process.

The cartridge that comes with the table is a player's cartridge, and it sounds amazing to my ears. They used to bundle a DJ cartridge with it, but changed that a couple (or a few...not really sure) years ago, and the tracking for this cart is perfect.

I set the table up via watching youtube videos (my last, and only table was fully auto), and it hasn't missed a beat. I don't mind that it doesn't stop automatically, or I would've bought a semi-auto table.

I would recommend this to anyone who is looking for a great player's-turntable and doesn't want to invest $400+.

product_title: TCC TC-750LC BLACK Professional Moving Magnet Preamp
review_headline: Doesn't last long, not very "audiophile", some design flaws
review_body: Mine lasted me about 7 or 8 months before it gave out. It doesn't ground very well, has some channel level imbalances and is prone to lots of RF and electrical interference. It also produces a ~50kHz hum about -4dB; you can see it very clearly over your music in a 192k spectogram. The design flaw I mentioned is that the grounding post that screws into the preamp hits and/or pushes and bends one of the microchip pieces directly in front of it. I consider this a design flaw because the piece is right there in the way of the screw's path, and there's really no way to stop it from happening unless you just don't attach a ground wire to it.

review_body: [...]    I bought the mount, and its fine.  For $26 bucks, if you want a mount like this, its not super sturdy, but it does the job.    Here is the problem though. Not the end of the world, but slightly annoying.  I contacted the seller, and they said \\"oh that model does not come with a Free HDMI cable and level\\".    I wrote back, explaining to them that the listing says it does, sending them a link to the listing, where it could clearly be seen that it said \\"Free HDMI cable and level\\".    They replied \\"nope, it does not say that\\".    what? i thought, so i took an actual screenshot of the listing (where it could be clearly seen that it said \\"Free HDMI cable and level\\"), and a separate screen shot of my order (showing that that was the exact model that i bought).    They then wrote back, saying that was not the model i bought.    Huh? they were just jerking me around, i sent another email to them showing my order page, my order number, and the exact item purchased, and they said \\"oh we used to include an HDMI cable and level, but we dont do that anymore\\".    I wrote back, \\"well all thats nice, but can you send me the Free HDMI cable and level listed?\\"  they replied \\"no\\" saying they would not do that.    So, i was like, wow, what a bunch of scammers,  i contacted Amazon, and they agreed with me.  Amazon apologized, and Amazon even refunded me the money, AND said i could still keep the TV stand.  So ultimately (due to Amazon) it worked out OK, but seriously, be very wary of this seller.    Also, not for nothing the customer service emails from Warehouseseller back to me were not only not helpful, but they were very rude as well.  AND... it says in the listing \\"Please report to amazon.com if you receive a mount without VideoSecu logo.\\"  TheTV Mount i did recieve works Ok, but it does not have the VideoSecu logo. product_title: Polk Audio Camden Square Wireless Portable Speaker
review_headline: Wireless premium sound speakers in a solid box
review_body:
The first thing I noticed is the stylish design of the Camden Square, clean, and at the same time, elegant. It would look great in nearly any room, regardless of being modern or traditional furnished. The leather covered sides allow to place the Camden Square in a vertical position, which originally I would have never thought possible.

Then I tried it, and I was surprised by the distinctive premium sound coming out of such a small box (comparing its size to the quality of the sound reproduced). Even during loud volume operation there is no sound distortion. The Camden Square, without any ostentation delivers fantastic sound. Both wireless or wired.

In addition to the quality streaming Bluetooth audio output, it includes the option to connect it to any other sound device that outputs audio to a 3.5mm Stereo input jack. It also comes with a rechargeable Lithium-ion battery that can go on for nearly a whole day without needing recharging.

There is a free DJ Stream app especially designed for the Camden Square, available both for Apple and Android devices, but it doesn't need to be installed on your device to pair it with the Bluetooth features of the Camden Square. I tested it on a Smartphone that no longer had any data service on it, and that doesn't have Wi-Fi, but it does have Bluetooth. And it paired perfectly with the Camden Square. I've been using this Smartphone only to listening to music. I copied all of my mp3 collection to a flash memory card and the sound has always been great, but now paired with the Camden Square, my music never sounded better!

For the kids or teens in the family this can be a really cool gadget, the mobility of it allows the parent to set the party in the backyard, or the back porch. And the kids can have fun playing around with the DJ Stream app. The app allows up to four people to control the Camden Square, but dozens of friends can use the app to vote for their favorite songs. A new way to add more entertaining to family meetings too. And since the Camden Square is sturdy, I don't worry about the kids doing any harm to it.

Because of its innovative architecture, exceptional sound quality and easy-to-use features, I highly recommend it.d more entertaining to family meetings too. And since the Camden Square is sturdy, I don't worry about the kids doing any harm to it.

review_headline: Did not work ..... at all..... in very average circumstances
review_body: I bought this after reading all the rave reviews as to how one could lose cable and use indoor HDTV antenna. As I only watch the nets and PBS, getting over-the-air signals to my tv - for free - was very appealing. I read the directions, set it up, did the auto scan, saw that 14 channels were available at my address but then, at the end of the scan, I saw nothing but snow. And the message weak signal/weak connection. I called from 1:30 until 5 PM for help - leaving numerous messages - no return calls. When I called at 5 PM, the message was that they were closed! That was Friday. So I had to reassemble all my cables, etc. and wait until Monday. I sent a couple of emails saying I was disappointed after reading about their great service. I called as they opened Monday at 8:30 am. The first woman who took my call verified that my address did indeed receive network channels and PBS stations. I told her about the scan and then the snow. She couldn't help me so connected me to a more experienced person. Both of these women were polite, professional but not sure about knowledgeable. The second one said I couldn't have my antenna near metal. As I had placed it slightly behind my drapery rod, I thought this was the problem. She said if that wasn't it that I would need to buy a converter. I told her I had a 2 year old Samsung HDTV TV and certainly wasn't in need of a box to convert analog to digital - something used for older, analog or older digital tvs. She couldn't offer any other help. I moved the antenna (very light and easy to move) away from the drapery rod just about 4 fee above the TV. Absolutely nothing. Read all kinds of articles on line. Went to TVFool and again learned that my address had plenty of broadcast towers within reception distance. Then, I tried the antenna in my bedroom - again with another newish Samsung HDTV (2011). Same thing - plenty of channels on the autoscan step but no channels due to "weak signal" . So the antenna was a complete failurefor me. And the service received from Mohu, while pleasant, was late, missing, unhelpful. Just thought I'd write this - not out of anger - but to give people another view of using indoor HDTV antennas. Not always a solution, unfortunately. By the way, I live in Asheville, in the city, in a one story house along a "normal" street lined with bungalows. Not a difficult site, one would think.

review_headline: Not HDCP compatible; Worked great for a number of weeks but then  . . .
review_body: The unit was working great but then I suddenly I was getting strange issues.  As a result, I don't recommend it but perhaps mine is just a lemon. Not High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection (HDCP) compatible which means when you are watching a premium movie, you get issues.      First the audio on my TiVo would go out and I'd get a warning message about my cables not being supported (something about licensing so not HDCP compatible).  I hadn't changed the cable from my TiVo but had merely hooked it up to this switcher rather than directly to my TV.  I got this intermittently but enough to change my configuration so the TIVo would be connected directly to the TV.    While using Google Chromecast and streaming Amazon Prime from my computer, I was losing the audio, not often initially but then it became more and more frequent; the video on the computer was fine.   Using Chromecast for YouTube and other apps was working fine.  Read that Amazon and Chromecast do not play nice together so upgrade my DVD player.  I got a newer smart DVD player that supported Amazon Prime streaming as well as 3D.  Again, there were no issues for quite a time and then suddenly, I was unable to see anything from the Blu-Ray player.  When I hooked up the Blu-Ray player directly, once again there were no issues.  Now I wonder if my initial issues streaming from my computer were also related to the device rather than Amazon and Google not playing well together.    Since the switcher is not HDCP compatible, there are a lot of movies out there end up having issues going through this switch.  I have therefore down-graded this device to one star.

review_body:
If you are reading this, I am going to go out on a limb and assume that you are probably much like me in that fitness and conditioning is likely very important to you. Otherwise, why on Earth would you be contemplating dropping over 2 bills for a set of sport headphones right?

Good, I commend you for your dedication to task. God knows the path we choose is not an easy one, and anything we can find to make our task that much easier is always something we are on the lookout for, be it workout gear, proper nutrition tips, supplements, fitness books and supposed \\"breakthroughs\\", and, of course, HEADPHONES!

Most all of us have probably been through more pairs of \\"workout headphones\\" in our tenure than their are stars in the night sky, and all of them have had their shortcomings in one way or another. Some sound great but are dead in month, some fall out of our ears, some have cords that like to short out on us, and others are a candidate for the trash heap not long after we take them out of the packaging. Why is it so difficult to construct a set of headphones that caters to our needs? This was my question for the ages until I discovered this particular pair, and while certainly not perfect, these babies do a better job than anything else I have ever tried (and I have tried TONS).

I will break down this review into a few simple categories and feel free to shoot me comments if you feel as though there is something I have overlooked. Fair ? Ok, let us get to it!

Sound-

Let me start by saying that if you are an audiophile these are not going to make you cream in your pants. I have numerous friends who are sound engineers and they are continually telling me how blown away they are by a particular pair or another. To me, they all pretty much sound the same in that price range. That said, I think we need to be mindful of our purposes here. We want music that is loud and engrossing enough to make us zone out and forget the 550 pound hunchback on the next treadmill over, yet isolated enough so that the hot girl doing aerobics nearby does not discover our hidden passion for Justin Bieber. This task does not require a set custom built for the president of Viacom.

With that in mind, these babies do the trick quite nicely. They sound great out of the box, and believe it or not they actually begin to sound better over time as they get broken in. Even the most annoying of the gym rat subculture are just a few taps of volume away from oblivion, and that my friends, is how I define audio bliss!

Fit--

This is really difficult category for me to make generalizations about since I have no idea what your head is shaped like. You could of been a stunt double in the direct-to-video remake of the Coneheads for all I know. However, suffice to say that barring some sort of rare genetic mutation at birth, you will probably not have too many complaints about how these headphones fit. They are fully adjustable, and nearly every one of my friends who I have let try these on have not reported back to me any problems (though many were hesitant to want to give them back). They also stay incredibly tight when you are doing activities that require you to lay flat (like bench press) or to contort your body in strange ways (I was talking about stretching you pervert).

They are comfortable to wear, and with the added audio bliss thrown into the mix, after awhile you will forget you even have them on. I have had more than a few Saturday's when I decided to go nuts and have ended up with a 3 hour session on my hands. Even during these sadistic, psychological, alpha male trips, I have yet to feel as though they were compressing me. Maybe I am just lucky and have the perfect shaped head, or, as is more likely, perhaps the engineers at Monster actually designed these headphones correctly. I'll let you be the judge.

Durability--

I have had these headphones for about 3 months now. When I first got them, I babied them to an incredible degree, but after the honeymoon was over, they have been abused like a Thai hooker. They have been drenched with sweat, dropped to the ground from a good distance, tossed in the backseat of my car when I was in a hurry, and generally used and abused like an ADHD 5 year old would his favorite toy. To date, I have seen no noticeable changes in either sound or fit and function. You can certainly tell they are not fresh out of the box from looking at them, but they seem to be no much more worse for wear.

If that changes, so will this review.

Functionality--

One of the biggest advantages of all of using this pair of headphones is the fact that they seamlessly sync via BlueTooth. I can't tell you them number of times I have been working out and got my headphones yanked out of my ears from the chord getting caught on a piece of gym equipment. I have even ruined a couple of pairs of headphones this way, so now you too can be like Pinocchio and rejoice that you \\"have no strings to hold you down\\". I use an iPhone 5, and it paired in seconds and I was good to go.

Most of you out there are probably technically savvy enough to figure out how to use all of the functions of these headphones in under 5 min, but to those of you who are not, it does come with instructions. As for me, I do not think I have bothered with instructions for any tech device or gadget in a solid 5 years.

The headphones are rechargeable and last about 25 hours or so on a full charge. I normally charge mine about once a week and have had no problems. It does also come with an adapter to run wired if need be, which is handy when you are either forgetful or stupid. I normally keep this in my glove box of my car in case of emergency and I am stuck at the gym with no audio. A fate worse than death in my book.

Summation--

Really, what more do you need to know? These sound fantastic, stay put while you are working out, do not have a glass jaw, and are technologically solid. They solve 99 percent of your audio related gym problems, with the only real drawback being their fairly high price tag. While I an certainly understand being hesitant about dropping hard earned cash on an item like this (I am a cheapskate also), ask yourself how much longer do you want to endure your gym audio situation sucking? I finally found my way off of that merry go round and I hope that you will too.

Now comes the truly hard part. Once you are properly outfitted to workout, you have to actually go workout. These bad boys will make that process much more bearable, but the desire to hit the gym has to come from within.

Got questions? Shoot me a comment and I will get back to you when I can.

Update----------------April 7th 2014

After a tad over 6 months of owning these, I thought I would stop by here and report back on my experience. In short, not much has changed from my original assessment. I have managed to go through 3 different girlfriends in that time period, but in contrast to the ex gf's, my Monsters have yet to be unfaithful to me or nag at me for drinking too much. After being jerked around by companies selling sport headphones for the entirety of my athletic life, it is nice to have some stability, as opposed to having to keep a pair of headphones \\"on deck\\" anticipating the inevitable failure of the current pair. Hell, I was so frustrated with one company in particular a couple of years back (who will remain nameless) that I was half considering abducting their CEO and fed-exing him naked to the Taliban.

I am a little surprised that the powers that be at Monster have not lowered the price on them though. They have been out now for going on a year after all. However, as a guy that also has more than a casual interest in home and car audio, I know from experience that anything youbuy from Monster is not going to be inexpensive purchase. They sell all of their stuff at an elevated price point, which I would normally be pissed about, but when the performance is exemplary, it softens the blow on my psyche and wallet. I might be cheap, but I am not a person that is hesitant to pay for quality. Especially for an item like this one that I am going to be using nearly every day.

I think Monster has really hit a home run with these headphones. I hope the company continues to carry this particular line so it can offer others a way to make their workouts easier. Some people claim to have some kind of spiritual epiphany during exercise. As for me ? My goals are far more narcissistic, at least by modern PC notions. If the desire to look good physically makes me vain or an awful person, then so be It. I doubt I will lose sleep over it.

The only major change I would suggest is to offer some different options as far as color. I mean seriously, lime green? Am I going to the gym to lift or suiting up for a gay pride parade in the Castro district of San Francisco?

Update ----- 12/04/2014

Wow, where does the time go? It's been now a year since I purchased these and they are still kicking out my loud EDM music as I grunt and sweat my way through the sociopolitical wasteland I call my local Planet Fitness. I have noticed that Monster has far more competitors for this type of device now than they did back in 2013, but competition is always a good thing. Competition keeps companies making devices like these stay on their A game, just as competition keeps me hitting on this Yoga instructor I see every other Thursday even though she has shot down every muscle head with the balls to approach her in the last year. {Note: She will be mine eventually}.

product_title: 4PCS RCA Y Splitter Adapter 2Female to 1Male For Audio Video AV TV Cable Converter by TheBigThumb
review_body:

If you think that you need this item, then you should really read how it supposed to be used - there are like 8 different products that look exactly like this one but have wildly different functions. In my case, this was perfect for taking the analog signal from my 1980's era NES and converting it to HDMI to play on a TV. (8-bit graphics on 1080p are not stellar, but look about the same as I remember from the 80s) This will not ever convert a DVD HDMI signal to analog, you need one of the other variants of this product to do that, probably the "HDMI2AV", not the "AV2HDMI".

Now on to the actual product: It is simple to use, pretty much always stays in the 1080p setting. (the 720p setting works, but why would I want to use that?) It failed from overheating once while sitting in an enclosed cabinet on top of a hot VCR and under a hot TV, I let it cool down and it began working great again. No failures since.

review_body:

This mount also says it will work with 16" stud spacing, but in reality you should not use it for that. I mounted a 55" Sony LED on this thing with the stud mounting at 16" spacing; and the back plate is now heavily bent between the bolting locations. Does not exactly inspire me with confidence.

Would not purchase again.

My TV has now been on this mount for several years, and it is still holding. However, the metal has sagged and bent enough to where the TV can no longer be moved around on the mount without a rubber mallet to "encourage" it (hitting the mount arms to move them). The backplate has held, but as i said in my original review it deflected from the wall by at least a half inch when mounted using 16" stud spacing. product_title: Arcam rLink Wired Coaxial and Optical DAC for rSeries
review_body: I recently purchased a used rLink for use with my Arcam A19 Integrated Receiver.  My application is as follows - Roku 3 into Samsung LN40A550 LCD TV via HDMI, Optical Audio out from TV to the rLink and RCAs from the rLink to the A19.  This setup allows the rLink to process every audio source coming out of my TV from the Roku to the Blu-Ray player to the Cable box.  Initially, I just ran an analog RCA out of the TV directly to the Integrated Amplifier.  This sounded actually pretty good, but I wanted a bit more.  I actually cross shopped this with Arcam's highly rated irDAC ($699 retail).  Whathifi.com really liked that unit, but having saved $85 on the rLink by buying it used made the value equation very tough.  In the end I decided that because the best quality I stream is Spotify at 320kbps, that the irDAC might just be overkill.  If you are the type of perfectionist that likes to burn your music in FLAC and check it for bit correctness using EAC, you would probably be more satisfied with the irDAC regardless of the price differential.  What I experienced with the rLink was better definition of the music, particularly in the lower registers like when listening to a standup bass and a wider, more natural soundstage. One other nice feature for Arcam A19 owners is the ability to power two of their DAC components via a 1/8 plug on the back of the amplifer.  That saves you a plug which in my case was very helpful.  Too many manufacturers like to use odd shaped plugs that inefficiently use up power strips.  At list price I would rate this unit a 4 star item - at the price I paid for it used I would say 5 stars.

product_title: Monoprice 108008 HDMI Over CAT5E/CAT6 Extender Wall Plate (Pair) with Built-In Backward IR Channel-Single-Port (1P), White
review_body:
I have a simple use case: run HDMI + IR 20' through a wall to an Xbox 360. It doesn't work.

When the device first arrived, I tested it with the 360 and two Cat5e cables (that checked out with a cable tester). I should have known from the beginning that I was in for trouble: when the 360 was set to auto-detect the display type, it reported DVI. As such, audio did not work. I had to force the Xbox to think the connection was HDMI and manually configure resolution. I was able to browse the dashboard and stream Amazon Instant Video at 1080p and Windows Media Center content, so I thought I could live with it.

After running ethernet through the wall, terminating, testing, etc, I reconnected the 360 and TV through this device and kicked back to enjoy my content. Windows Media Center and AIV still worked as they did before, but I discovered that when I try to play a DVD in the Xbox, it doesn't work -- just pops some default Xbox logo. Plugging HDMI directly to the TV (not through this device) fixed the problem.

To see if this problem was Xbox-specific, I tried my Samsung Blu-Ray player. That showed the boot-up splash screen but then went black when the menus should have come up. Again, plugging HDMI directly into the TV fixed the issue. I tried removing the units from the wall and going back to the shorter, well-tested patch cables but it made no difference.

I don't know whether it's an HDCP thing, a resolution thing, an EDID thing, need for better than my gigabit-capable Cat5e wiring (Monoprice recommends Cat6 but says 5e should work) or what, but some signals can be made to work and others simply can't. Do NOT expect this to \\"just work\\" like an HDMI cable. It does not.

One other significant design flaw: the IR transmission only works when the HDMI source (transmitter) is powered on, since that seems to provide the power for the IR. This, of course, means that you can't use the IR repeater to turn on the source (the Xbox 360 in my case). If your source is in a cabinet or otherwise out-of-sight (I would imagine the main use case of the IR repeater), you will need to physically walk over to it every time you want to turn it on.

I wish I had figured this out earlier, when I could have still returned it. As it is, I'm out the cost, plus the time required to run the ethernet wires through the wall. I've ordered long, separate HDMI and 3.5mm cables to run through the wall instead. More annoying and expensive, but hopefully it will actually work.

product_title: Bose SoundLink Mini Bluetooth Speaker
review_body:
In spite of a spirited debate with Eduardo while replying to Yano's 1-star review, I ordered a Mini as a present for my wife. At 12:04 AM she opened it and by 12:09 we were listening wirelessly to old school Jackson 5 Holiday songs via Pandora through her iPad. I am not here to proclaim the Bose Mini to be the "best sound money can buy", so you can relax Eduardo. However, I will say that my $200 was well-spent in my opinion. The little speaker is much smaller than one would think and it indeed has a heft to it. Is it worth the extra $100 when compared to other competitively-sized speakers? I think its worth goes beyond the decent sound it manufactures. The sound is probably known by most speaker buyers by now: a somewhat full wall of sound that is pleasant enough in the range between highs and bass. It's not directional - doh! What can you expect from a speaker the size of 8-donut box of Entenmanns? If I want separation of instruments and stereo sound, I'll find a good set of speakers, a nice Eames recliner and sit down for an hour or so. But the Mini fits the bill when one is moving about, in and out of a room while listening to Pandora knock out your favorite artists.

The extra $100 goes into a seamless (at least for us) Bluetooth connection, a simple charging system (for those that complain about making the charging connection to the plate, it takes what, another 5 seconds to seat it correctly?), and a solid build out of metal. That build goes a long way with me. I can remember Sony's first generation portable CD player being made out of a solid chunk of metal - it had the same heft this Mini does. Alas, as a lot of popular devices go, the move towards less expensive plastic is inevitable and so the Bose Mini is a nod to back to the day when something solid was preferred over something merely weightless. The Mini is still small enough to throw in a carrying case or the back of the car when one is spontaneous enough to hit the road for a quick getaway. I imagine this device will be working long after the cheaper plastic ones give up the ghost. I own an older generation SoundDock and it's been running flawlessly for about 6 years. Now my wife has her own speaker and won't have to deal with the audio cord while in the kitchen.

So whether it's listening to Mary J, The Young and the Restless, Dexter Gordon, or The Walking Dead, the Bose Mini makes for a worthwhile sound almost wherever you wish. And I'd say that's worth 200 bucks.

product_title: Sennheiser Headphones
review_headline: Very Comfortable, Good Sound, Good Value
review_body:
Sennheiser HD 558 vs AKG Q701

My initial impressions of the HD 558 was that it was neither significantly different from the HD 419 nor the AKG. The sound quality seems to be halfway between both of the headphones, and this was a reflected in its mid-way pricing as well. The HD 558 headphones without any burn-in had sufficient bass just like the HD 419 even though the frequency response graph in Headphones.com show a flatter bass response than the AKG. There was no distortion to the bass unlike the HD 419 even though the punch is the same. The 558 seems to clamp tightly onto the frontal cheek bone of the ear lobe, but after one night of extending it on the desktop, it is way more comfortable to wear than the AKG. It is not as light as the HD 419, but it feels invisible after a while. The AKG on the other hand makes me constantly aware that the headphone is present by causing slight soreness to the tender areas.

Comparing in detail:
1. Resolution & Transparency:
Flaws in the audio can be heard easily in both headphones. Noise cannot be detected. This is more dependent on source rather than headphones.

2. Freq balance & distribution:
AKG: Bass was lacking initially but after burn-in/ear cushions softening, the bass is satisfactorily good. Upper and mid freq range look more like HD 800.
HD 558: Bass is good, mids seems to be more forward but resolution of a violin does not seem to be as clear as AKG.

3. Layering:
AKG: This is more dependent on source rather than headphones. John Williams has good orchestra recordings while Hans Zimmer's music is created by combining multiple recordings which makes it sound stereo instead of 5.1. That said, instrument separation is very clear now in the AKG.
HD 558: Instrument separation is clear.

4. Texture:
AKG: In the Hillsong recordings which are done well, the female voice texture can be clearly heard. The background singers seem to blend in and harmonize with the main singer.
HD 558: In the Hillsong recordings which are done well, the female voice texture can be clearly heard. The background singers can be distinguished more clearly in the HD 558.

5. Color:
AKG does not seem to color the recordings.
HD 558 seems to muffle some of the sounds. Maybe it's the Sennheiser veil?

6. Imaging
AKG: Excellent soundstage in terms of depth and width, sounding worthy like a real orchestra. This excellent soundstage only appears in classical/orchestra music.
HD 558: Soundstage is smaller, like a band of musicians in a small room.

7. Air
AKG: Distance to each instrument can truly be visualized. This might be due to ample space between speakers and the ears.
HD 558: Instruments seem to be sitting in a single line. The speakers may be closer to the ears than the AKG.

Sound quality wise- it's quite comparable to Bose speakers. It's not perfect, but it's excellent. I also like how the sound fills up my apartment. I'll give it 4 OUT OF 5 for sound quality.

The risk of buying this product was worth it! Overall, this product is 5 out of 5. The quality is exceptional! And for just $79.99, you get an iPhone/iPod speaker dock, FMradio, speaker for other external devices and a digital clock. You get so much, it's so worth it. A must buy!

product_title: Sennheiser On-Ear 926MHz Wireless RF Headphones with Charging Cradle
review_headline: Functional but very expensive for obsolete technology.
review_body:
Positives:
Well these are defined as over the ear headphones, one can still pick up other outside sounds and voices due to the porosity of the ear foam pads (e.g. your wife commenting negatively on the TV show you are watching and being over the ear they allow you to pretend you cant hear....a great advantage).
Once I found the appropriate analog audio output and that manual tuning is required (see negatives) setup up was quick.
I like the convenience of the volume knob in the earpad.
The audio was crisp and clear and there was plenty of dynamic range, in other words I could adjust the volume to an uncomfortably high level well above my normal TV watching volume.
It comes with a couple of audio adapters but not a universal set, e.g. no RCA adapters..

Negatives:
This unit only accepts analog audio inputs (right and left) which are becoming scarce on 21st century electronics so make sure you have those available for your application.
There are 3 RF channels to choose from to deal with RF interference and those are manually selected and then manually tuned to with a dial on the earphones like an old AM radio. They us FM modulation, circa 60s. This manual nature of the RF interfaces surprised me and is not something I would expect in even 25 year old electronics.
After 3 minutes of no audio input (e.g. turn off TV) a loud hiss/static commences on the headphones. This means if you leave the headphone off the cradle and turn off the TV the headphone will hiss loudly until the battery dies. The headphone should turn off as well....poor design.
The charging cradle is a bit awkward to use in that if the earpieces are not set for equal length, then the headphone will tilt to one side and the conductors in the headset band will not sit flat on metal bars (you can see the bars in the picture) and the batteries will not charge.
The ear pad foam is very light duty and I would not expect them to last 12 months with normal use and wear and tear.
There are no RCA adapters included.
The charging light stays lit even after charging is complete!
Its awkward to plug in the power adapter. You almost need to used needle nose pliers as there is no room for fingers.
On occasion the tuner would detune and I would have to readjust the turning.

And the Darbee DVP5000

When I purchased my tv and bluray player I thought that was it. I thought the picture couldn't get any better than this, and honestly the picture was amazing. So I heard about the OPPO BDP 103D, I read the positive reviews, and I didn't know if it was worth dropping $700 on another bluray player. I watched an interview with Paul Darbee, and he said Darbee Vision actually sells the processor seperately as well. So I did more research, and watched testimonial videos on the Darbee Darblet, and I was sold. It arrived yesterday, setup was a breeze, my only gripe with the with the unit was that inputs should be on the front of the unit and the output should be on the back. Once it was setup, I popped in prometheus, and turned Darbee on to hidef mode, it was automatically set to 120%. At 120% the particle effect was pretty high, so I turned it down to 70%, and the picture looked AMAZING!. I saw scars on faces that I didn't even know were their before darbee, the detail in the tress and rocks looked unbelievable. You can watch comparison videos on youtube, but they just don't do justice, you really have to see it in person to believe it. I also tried it out with my PS4 and battlefield 4, and same results. The amount of detail in the environment just pops out at you. Most naysayers claim you don't need darbee, you can just turn up the sharpness and contrast, so I decided to try it out for myself. I turned up the sharpness, and I only saw an increase in jaggies at the end of objects. I love the darbee darblet 5000, it increases the depth and detail in the picture, and it was well worth the $260.
