product_title: Sony MDR-XB600 Extra Bass 40mm Driver Premium Headphones
review_body:
The SONY MDRxb600 EXTRA BASS headphones really punch the bass. If you're one of those people who would crank up the bass settings, or buy 15 inch subwoofers in order to feel the beat, you are going to LOVE these headphones. Obviously in some situations, with certain music, this might make the bass throb too much. Other music, especially music mixed to be reproduced by vinyl, or with lots of congas, electric and acoustic bass guitars, piano bass notes, etc, you are going to hear that music as tho for the first time. The pluses FAR OUTWEIGH the minuses, of owning a pair of cans like this. So, let me explain more in depth.

1. INCREASED BASS RESPONSE
I tested these with jazz fusion, reggae, psychedelia, and modern rock like Thievery Corperation, Porcupine Tree and Flaming Lips. I found that older music like the Rolling Stones late 60s albums, which hasnt been over limited, will sound VASTLY improved when played over the Sony headphones. After listening to Beggars Banquet, I took off the SONY headphones and listened to the Stones thru PHILIPS O'NEILL \\"The Bend\\" SHO4200bb headphones. WOW. The PHILIPS O'NEILL headphones made the music sound small, boxy, and weak, compaired to the Sony. I also compaired these Sony headphones to Philips CITYSCAPE headphones. The SONY still sounded far better than the Philips CITYSCAPE headphones. Jazz, reggae, and my 60s psychedelia, like Captain Beefheart, sounded VASTLY improved on the SONY headphones. The extra bass punch makes the music come alive. Its much closer to listening to music without headphones on, which is the goal, right?

2.HIGH SENSITIVITY XB DRIVERS
I find it amazing, that these SONY headphones are 30-40% LOUDER. In EVERY situation, I need to increase the volume control dramatically, to obtain the same Loudness on my other headphones, that I have with the Sony. This means it requires less electricity to produce the same degree of volume on the SONY headset...extending the battery life for your MP3 player. Overall, the increased bass is identical to turning on the \\"LOUDNESS\\" control on your amp. (AKA nighttime listening mode.) This setting increases the bass response to compensate for lower volume settings, which tend to diminish the ability to hear the music's bottom end.

3. DJ FASHION
If you check the photos of these SONY headphones, you'll see how the cans can swing up inside the headband, while swirling around 360 degrees. What DJs do, when they need to hear the current song with one ear, while lining up the next track with the other ear, is lay the cans on top each other, and then place the entire folded headphones in the palm of your hand, with the driver facing outward. That forms a tight package so you can place one can against your ear, without your headphones dangling over your face. For DJing in a loud club, or wedding, these headphones are perfect. Personally, I think the design is cool as hell. They're really modern looking, brown and black, with gold accents. Its rich, sophisticated styling.

4. COMFORT
These are far and away the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn. The cushioning over the headband, and around the ear is part of the reason, but the manuverability of the cans must be why they stay put on your head so well. No matter what size head you have, or how your ears are placed, these headphones create a firm, snug grip on your head, without creating any particular pressure points, or areas which are too lose. The tight seal over the ears, helps produce superior bass reponse as well.

5. FITS THE NICHE
There have always been people who bought 15 inch woofers for their home sound system, or master blaster subwoofers for their car audio, because they like to hear heart pounding bass. Almost all rock, R&B, rap, reggae, and jazz music sounds weak and thin, if the bottom end isn't kicking butt. I had no idea that headphones could even reproduce a fat bottom end, until I heard how poor my other two headphones sounded compared to these SONY. Now I'm spoilt.

AND IN THE END....its all a matter of taste. If you always fiddle with your equalizer to create thick, rich bass notes, then these headphones were made for you. Honestly, some music has so much limiting on it, and its mixed in the studio with the bass end so cranked up, that headphones like this might reproduce that sound too bottom heavy. I rarely heard that problem, tho, and only at high volume. If you listen to music at reaonable volumes, or even mild volumes, these headphones are perfect for you. Since they increase bass response, you'll still be able to hear the bass lines when the volume's turned way down. Since these are high effeciency headphones, it stands to reason your MP3 battery will keep its charge longer. Other big pluses are the cool DJ type design, and their comfort on your head.

product_title: Emotiva ERC-2 Differential Reference CD Player and Digital Transport
review_body: Yes, the a high-quality CD player IS essential to an \\"audiophile\\" stereo system.  Emotiva ERC-2 is a tremendous product (I had to buy direct from the company, because I could not buy through Amazon since I live outside of the contiguous United States, in Alaska).  I paid shipping, but most Americans should be eligible for free shipping.  Back to the unit: I own a very nice audiophile setup: McIntosh amp and pre-amp, and had a \\"good\\" 'reasonably-priced' carousel player, considered the high-end of the economical market, but I was frustrated by the sound.  I read reviews for the ERC-2 in several audiophile sites.  What they say, basically, is that they are astounded they can get the level of sound from ERC-2 comparable with players in the $1000-and-up category audiophile-level CD player.  I just received mine, and was stunned by the improvement in my system.  Some older CD's (pre-1990 manufactured) sounded fine (but, not much you can do about the 'lesser; analog source tapes). Newer CD's sounded absolutely great on ERC-2. Remember, you can buy an old McIntosh CD player for a lot of money in used condition, say, but that unit may not be capable of translating 20-bit or 24-bit, or SACD or SHM other modern formats, since it is old technology.  The cost-to-quality balance most definitely leans in the favor of this ERC-2 unit.  Drawbacks:  A quite slow-loading single-CD capable mechanism (no carousel), and while the remote is awesome (heavy and metal), to remove the batteries and replace, you need to remove and replace six tiny Phillips screws (so watch out you don't lose them).  Otherwise, this is a fantastic player for a VERY reasonable price.  Don't settle for a used 20-ish year old, used 'top of the end' model CD player, as good as they are, because there is really no way of ascertaining the cumulative wear on the product, or availability of parts, or finding someone to repair at a reasonable price if there is a repair issue. There is a 2-year warranty on ERC-2.

product_title: C2G/Cables to Go Cable Ties
review_headline: Wow! These cable ties sure did tie cables!
review_body:
I ordered the cable ties not really knowing what to expect. A cable tie is a very particular restraining device. I've had cable ties made of brittle plastic that snap in half when you tried to cinch them. I've have cable ties that refused to stay cinched after you cinched them. You might say that I am somewhat of a connoisseur of cable ties.

As a result of my cable tieing hobby when I needed to secure surface run ethernet cabling I knew there was only one answer.
Cable ties!

When I started searching for my solution I first came upon the surface mount cable tie anchors also sold on Amazon and figured these would work well together.
When I saw they were often sold together I knew I had found the right cure for what ailed me.

These cable ties arrived in a small plastic bag. While I didn't count them to ensure I had received single one of my valued cable ties I felt confident that the number would suffice.

I cautiously, carefully, opened the plastic bag by biting a corner off and sprinkled out a few samples to test for quality.

The material wasn't so stiff and brittle that I feared they would break when tightened.
The material wasn't so soft that I feared I would rip them in half.
As for stay cinchability? Well, I could only guess.

I decided to spend one of my cable ties on a practical test. I affixed the anchor to the wall and placed one of these cable ties through the anchor...

Breath baited I exhaled... then I cinched it. I cinched that cable good!
I cinched the hell outta that darn cable!

The cable tie did well. Once cinched, it stayed cinched.
It didn't break. It didn't fail.

I am pleased with these cable ties.
They sure did tie some cables!

product_title: Polk Audio PSW505 12-Inch Powered Subwoofer (Single, Black)
review_headline: Excellent Performer at a Reasonable Price
review_body:
This sub-woofer replaced a ten year old 200w/10\\" whose performance had been excellent, but suffered from RF interference from one of my radios, that no amount of choking and filtering could cure. The problem appears to have been direct radiation into the amplifier section that only major surgery was going to fix. The disturbing \\"thump\\" every time the radio was keyed (several times per minute) became quite annoying. Either the radio or the sub had to be turned off, hence my search for a new sub-woofer.

Enter the Polk Audio PSW505. I'm a strong advocate of buying behind the curve. Some of the best equipment I've ever owned was purchased with this approach. The PSW505 is not \\"current\\", but it is recent, and has a strong set of reviews at several sites (including my favorite, Amazon) The price is the same that I paid ten years ago for a 10\\" 200w unit, not near the quality of this Polk Audio product. The initial good news: no RF interference, no thumping, so it is clear that the RF shielding and bypassing in the sub-woofer's amplifier is well done. I even increased the power output from my radio from 5 watts to 45 watts, and no interference was present.

On to ease of use and performance:

Setup was very simple. One of three ways are used to hook up the sub-woofer to the system. The most common and no doubt popular is a singe RCA jack labeled LFE on the sub-woofer. This corresponds to a pre-filtered low level output present on most current Home Theater receiver/amplifiers. My Onkyo has such an output and a singe RCA cable connects the HT to the sub. Thee second means to connect the system is a pair (stereo) line-in jacks on the PSW-505. These are routed to a low-pass filter in the sub's amp, to set the cutoff frequency of the sub. Note: the LFE input on the sub assumes all filtering is going to be done in the Home Theater amp, so the sub does no filtering at all. Be sure to go into your Home Theater amp and set it up properly for a sub-woofer output. This includes setting the sub out to ON/YES, and setting the low pass filter frequency (100 Hz or so). The third method of connection is speaker wires. The same filtering is used on the speaker wire inputs as on the line-in inputs. There is a control on the back of the sub labeled 60/90/120 Hz. This looks like a three position switch, but I can't be sure. In any case, I didn't use the internal filtering of the sub, as my Home Theater amp (HT), did the filtering.

Performance is gratifying, to say the least. I did find the best match to my speakers was a setting of 120 Hz as the crossover from my HT to the sub. I used three methods to evaluate the sub-woofer, and one to measure. Firstly, I did some adjusting with a Sound Pressure Level (SPL) meter, and was able to observe the low frequency performance of the PSW505 with a swept signal source that started around 12 Hz and swept up to 300 Hz. There is a substantial amount of clean output starting at around 26 Hz. It drove the SPL meter to the peg and I couldn't hear it at all. Age can do amazing things to one's hearing! When the frequency sweep reached 32 Hz or so, I could both \\"feel\\" and hear the clean output of this beast. Frequency response was very reasonable (considering room acoustics play a gigantic part at these frequencies) up to the 120 Hz cutoff, and the main speakers handled things well from there. From a measurement perspective, the PSw505 amp/sub combo passed with flying colors.

Sound:

My test music consists of three artists:

Little Feat: Waiting For Columbus. Whoa. Fat Man in a Bathtub, Mercenary Territory and Spanish Moon were exquisite. The detail was most impressive and the raw amount of audio could be set anywhere one would like, from nicely balanced to shaking the room (tsste varies).

Papa Doo Run Run (famous Beach Brothers group that made a TelArc album with massive low frequency demads): Again: detail was astonishing, amplitude impressive.

Beethoven Violin Concerto in D: Opening tympani and orchestral crescendos were clean and LOUD.

The \\"con\\" is that they're not built to survive regularly being thrown down stairs or jumbled about unprotected in your backpack or chewed on by your dog or thrown across the room when you get killed in \\"Teh Haloes\\". Some folks may say this makes them \\"feel cheap\\". These same people buy the metal Macbook because they're careless and break the plastic ones. If you're not a doofus, you won't break these. The end.

TL;DR If you're smart, you're moving your mouse to the \\"Buy It Now\\" button.

You don't notice the difference so much when putting the Etymotics on for the first time as you do when you go back to the older headphones. But there is a clear difference in quality, and the Etymotics simply sound \\"pure\\" to me.

Review:
First just a couple of things that can make or break the purchase immediately
1. If you're contemplating buying these, I recommend noting what categories of music you listen to first: if it's anything extremely bass heavy (dubstep etc.) I'd stop immediately. These won't be able to provide that sort of sound. If your main music tastes are literally anything else (pop, folk, indie rock, alternative, etc.) definitely continue thinking about it.

2. These headphones take a good adjustment period and you have to be ready for that. You have to put them extremely deep into your ear. It took me about a week to get used to it and to, well, get \\"good\\" at it where I could get it well seated on my first try. Once sealed and seated correctly, you'll notice two things - the bass is a lot more noticeable, and you can hardly hear anything outside of your headphones - you can only hear the music. The noise isolation on these is bar none the best I've heard. I worked at a factory recently and was required to use ear plugs; the headphones actually do a better job than the ear plugs given at blocking out sound. (Noise isolation is great for a few reasons - 1. it let's you simply listen to music without any distractions, and 2. you can listen to music at quieter levels, while still hearing everything, which are less likely to damage your ears).

3. These headphones are not the most sturdy. The wires are very thin and it makes me nervous whenever I get my hand caught in them and pull too hard on accident. If you don't take good care of your electronics, I might recommend staying away from these. Also, as a side note, the rubber material used in two of the ear pieces has a similar scent to common dog toys, and after about a month I found my first pair ripped to shreds by my dog (a lot of other people have this problem specifically with etymotic due to the rubber). Just be careful in that regards. I have yet to break my second pair after 10 months and have had some strong pulls on them. The wire is still in tact everywhere.

If none of these bother you, and the price range is something you're okay with, then you're definitely looking at an excellent pair of headphones. As I said before, I am no audiophile; I don't have extensive knowledge of all of the headphones out there. My experience with playing and listening to music though makes me think that I can at least say when something sounds good and, wow, these headphones sound extremely good. I've listened to some songs over a hundred times and they sound completely different through these, in a very good way. I can't tell you how many times I've gone \\"wow, I didn't ever hear THAT guitar part before!\\" when using these headphones. And it's because they don't use cheap drivers to artificially boost the bass, but instead focus on keeping everything equalized.

I've never heard trebles as clear from these headphones. Music like Jonsi and Sufjan Stevens, as well as any instrumental piece I can think of, brings out every single treble note with breathtaking clarity. It's not just loud either - it's well balanced, and a very warm, pleasant tone.

I've also never been able to distinguish music played at 320 kbps and below it... I actually can with these headphones, which is extremely impressive in my opinion. (It does mean that I have to update my music to all be at 320 kbps so I enjoy it more... but)

While most negative reviews bash the bass, I really enjoy it through these. An ear for balance is something I learned in years and years of symphonic band, and music sounds much, much more balanced with these (again, the headphones HAVE TO be sealed properly in your ear). By lowering the bass, you really do hear quite a bit more sounds. Furthermore, the bass is no longer muddy, but really... \\"punchy\\" and \\"poppy\\". Dance and techno music sounded sweet, despite the volume of the bass being lower, due to the tone quality and articulation of the bass.

Their advertised \\"flat\\" response is completely true.

I notice things like dynamics a lot more, and find that it sounds like I'm hearing instruments right next to me due to their crispness and cleanness. review_headline: Very good, but was it worth the cost?
review_body:
It did provide a better signal. I get a few more channels compared to unamplified rabbit ears, and some feeble channels are more stable.
I'm using it with the USB input to the TV, which, for some reason, stays on even when the TV is off, which means the pale blue LED is always on, but that's a quirk of the TV, not the Leaf Plus.
Installation was effortless and could not have been easier unless it jumped out of the box, climbed up the wall and plugged itself in.
It didn't do any of those things, but it may have thought about it.
So, it performs well, is easy to use and is unobtrusive, but is it worth the $$$$?...
I have not compared it to other amplified antennas. Others are available for a fraction of the cost but I'm too lazy to bother trying any.
So there's your answer; If you're as lazy as I am, the Leaf Plus will get you a significantly better signal with minimal effort. If you're not quite that sedentary, you may want to try something cheaper first.

product_title: Sport headphone
review_body:
As a gadget junkie, my expectations of all stereo bluetooth headsets was low. Like the title says these little Exercise Freak's sound amazing and totally caught me off guard!
Let me explain why:

FIT - The fit was great. Yes, it takes a little time to work my large ears into the over ear grooves - but once in there its snug and tight. Don't have to worry about them popping out on a run. There are a bunch of other ear tips to fit people of different sizes. The ones that come pre-installed fit well and block out most noise around me. I can move my head around and rock out some head banging tunes to get pumped up and they fit comfortably.

ERGONOMICS - The button layout was nice and simple. Two main buttons and two volume buttons. Easy to make changes as you are moving around.

BUILD QUALITY - The build is really solid. I had checked out a few competitors and didn't experience the same level of quality of the Freaks. Looks like it can handle some serious sweat.

SOUND QUALITY - Ok, so here is where I am a nerd. After an initial charge, I ran a pink noise track on repeat for a full battery cycle to \\"break them in\\". (I do this with all speakers) Then I tested on some familiar tracks and compared them to my \\"wired\\" headphones. As for bass response, the low end exceeded my \\"wired\\" version (of a well known brand). I listened to Travis Barkers Knockin' and it was almost dizzying with the drum detail. The mid range is smooth and un muddied. Next, System of a Down's Prison was used for dynamics and range. Blew me away. Vocals are clean and smooth with out \\"breaking up\\". I also tried Aimee Mann's One, very smooth with flat response across the board. Downloaded the Denon Apps (Club and Sport) and made some tweaks with the EQ in the Club app. Like having a parametric EQ at your finger tips. Ran back through the songs again and was delighted as I \\"tuned in\\" to my hearing preferences. (Talk about the apps later)

BATTERY LIFE- They advertise 7 hours, but after a few charges it was only making to about 6.5 hours. (Not really a big deal, I do drive them pretty loud.)

BLUETOOTH PAIRING - Ok, so this was really fast on the iPhone. My Jawbone, Bose and Blue Ant devices took longer (especially the Jawbone). On my iMac it was fairly fast too, but I got caught up in setting all the preferences for I/O.

DISTANCE FROM SOURCE - This is where I got a little confused. On the iPhone the range was perfect with in 15-20 feet indoors. On the iMac it was almost 30 feet. Not sure why the difference was so dramatic, but when i am out excercising I'm not more than a few feet away from the iPhone.

CARRYING CASE - Very nice little canvas case with a matching carabiniere. Cool thing here is that when I am not storing the headphones, my iphone and ID fit in here and I can run or bike with attached to me or the bike. Very Nice.

USE WITH IPHONE - So here was the surprise, I did not realize that this was a bluetooth earphone with a mic. I got this thinking it was just a stereo headset. These things work great when paired to my phone and making calls. The people on the other end of the call think I am actually talking directly on the phone. The funny thing is that the headphones block out so much noise (with out electronic manipulation) that I talk quietly and have to remind myslef to speak up so that I am not whispering. LOL

USE WITH COMPUTER - The Freaks work great on the iMac. Great distance and sound quality. Used these for a few Google Voice calls and got the same results as I did with the phone. (You can hear the difference between VOIP and cell call.) As for music and movies, the sound was great. Took me a little while to get the sound EQ'd to my liking. (The Club app on the phone is awesome and gives you so many EQ options compared to the limited EQ with iTunes.) Please make a app for the Mac OSx that is like the iPhone app. Would use it all the time.

APPS - I love the apps! There is a variety to download, but I stuck with the sport and club versions. The club is the best music app for EQ on a iPhone that I have seen yet. Works with other products too. The sport is still new to me at this point, but it tracks my excercise routine and not overbearing like some other apps are when you are out.

Overall, I love these little guys. Very happy and satisfied. Price is very competitive and given the quality of the build and sound it should cost more in my opinion (but I am not complaining!) Would totally suggest these to others and hopefully you find this review helpful. Might have to reconsider my big over the ear headphones for some new Denon's (looking at the AHD-600) based on these little Freaks!

product_title: APC Audio/Video Power-Saving Surge Protector 8 Outlet with Phone/Network/Coax Protection, 120V
review_body:
The APC P8VNTG Power Saving Surge Protector is a great product, potentially impacted by inferior quality. The product itself is attractive, well, as attractive as a power strip can really be. The black design melds into most home theater decors. I personally like the blue LED lighting, but they are VERY bright. So if you don't have the power strip hidden behind something, the light may be distracting.

I purchased this model for the power saving features. My TV is connected to the master switch and powers off my receiver, Xbox, and Blu-ray player when turned off. This power saving feature is easy to configure (one button) and works well. I've only had issues with that feature due to my use of a Harmony remote that I can't seem to configure to wait between turning on the TV and other devices (to give them time for power to be restored, as it takes a second or two). Beyond that, the unit has met my expectations.

Where it has not met my expectations is in longevity. I purchased two of these, one died within one week. APC replaced it promptly under warranty (lifetime warranty), but I did have to spend money to ship the defective one back. The replacement unit is still going strong. The second one I purchased lasted about 6 months and met its end as well. I've just started my discussions with APC to get that one replaced as well.

Perhaps I was unlucky with getting two defective units, or maybe there was just a bad run. Either way, I have to dock two stars as I expect more from APC products (especially for the price). Should there have been no problems, I would have given it 5 stars.

product_title: URC MRF100B PowerBlaster For Use with MasterControl RF Series Remotes
review_body:
I spent a lot of time searching for a good remote control system that I could use from several rooms before I settled on Universal for several reasons. The remotes were easily programmable, even with macros, and I could clone one remote configuration to another easily. I could also easily use them without pointing the remote at the TV (or anything else), so I could keep my hands under the blanket on cooler evenings as well as use the remotes from other rooms.

There are two problems with Universal, and after contacting them, their basic attitude is, \\"So what?\\"

The first is about this booster/blaster. It dies. I've had two and they just up and die. They'll start being stubborn, not relaying signals for a while, then they'll just stop all together. Nothing has changed in my house, so it's not new signals interfering with this unit. It just stopped working. I can only wonder what kind of poor design or cheap components make an electronic device with no moving parts just quit so easily, but I'm looking for a new solution. I'm not going to trust them. Two units failing without reason is too much.

The other reason isn't tied directly to this base unit, but to remotes. I have two RF-20 remotes. Supposedly you can clone one RF20 to another.

Well, you can't always. If one remote is a later release than the other, you can't clone the configuration from one to the other. And how do you know one is a later release? You'll have to buy it and try it out!

This company uses substandard parts and is not concerned about customer satisfaction, so I won't be buying any more of their products.

product_title: Barnes & Noble NOOK Color eBook Tablet
review_body:
After having my Nook Color less than two months, I noticed a crack in the case at the charging port. When I called Barnes and Noble and explained and described the problem their first questions were: 1)Did you purchase an extended warranty? 2)Did you drop the Nook or do anything else which could have caused the damage? My response to both questions was \\"no\\" to which the woman responded \\"I am sorry, we do not warrant user caused damage\\" to which my response was \\"huh?\\"
I attempted to reason a little with her to no avail--\\"If your assumption was going to be that I caused the damage, why did you even bother to ask the question?\\" Well, the conversation went on for a little and it became clear to me that if one does not purchase the extended warranty, it is automatically assumed that any problem is the result of user damage and, in effect, there is no warranty at all.
A month or so later I decided to take the preschooler approach--if Mom did not give me the answer I wanted I should ask Dad--so I called again thinking something may have been in error on my first try. No such luck, same two questions, same response!
The nook works fine, but don't be fooled into believing that you have anything vaguely resembling protection against faulty workmanship. The purchase of a Nook is an \\"as is\\" transaction!

product_title: JBL J55i High-Performance On-Ear Headphones with JBL Drivers, Rotatable Ear-Cups and Microphone - Black
review_headline: Great Mid-Range Headphones That Delivers Many Excellent Qualities
review_body:
Audio is very important to me and it seems I've been on a never-ending quest for the perfect affordable headphone. Ever since my Sony noise canceling headphones croaked I've been searching but can't bring myself to spend $200 on headphones again. JBL is a very reputable company and they know how to do quality. I was a projectionist and can tell you that most movie theaters use JBL speakers in their auditoriums. I was excited to see what they would bring to an upscale headset. After using them for a few weeks I can say that they are decent but far from perfect.

They sound great for their construct. They have great sound replication and handle all ranges quite well. They may lack the \\"oomph\\" on the lows that some other headphones deliver, but I'm not a fan of bass heavy phones anyway. I listen to mostly film scores and they do a great job at handling intricate sounds and textures as well as the wall-to-wall sound of pop and rock. The sound isn't as full-bodies as I hoped it would be, but for the price it's pretty darn good.

The build is great as well. They are light and comfortable and easy to store. I'm an \\"over the ear\\" kind of guy but found these \\"on ear\\" phones to be pretty satisfactory. The cushions are comfy and the band doesn't put too much pressure on your ears. Even when they're stretched to the limit over my gigantic head. The set is sleek enough that you can carry it with you on the go and won't have to worry about looking like a doofus with giant headphones on. The built in mic is a nice added feature that can make it great to use with your phone and take calls.

So, in the end these are decent headphones. They lack that \\"oomph\\" that would make them the set I've been searching for, and the \\"on ear\\" design, while not my favorite, still is comfortable enough to wear for a long time. If you're looking for an in-between headset while you save up for a Bose or Sony noise canceling set then I couldn't recommend this one more. It's built sleek enough to take it on the road with you, but it really is meant for use in a quiet setting as you won't find much noise isolation with it.built sleek enough to take it on the road with you, but it really is meant for use in a quiet setting as you won't find much noise isolation with it.

product_title: Altec Lansing M202 Dual-Charging iPod Dock (30-pin connector)
review_headline: In smart, capable, expert hands, this dock is a giant killer.
review_body:
I was looking for a bedside dock stereo for my iPhone 4S (ios6) to replace my CD alarm clock radio. This review is a comparison between the AS-Octivo Duo and a Coby \\"Vitruvian\\" that I bought at around the same price ($30). I'm a hard-core audiophile, which means I'm an expert on what sounds good. So sound is always my top priority with anything audio.

On features, the Altec Lansing Octivo had an immediate advantage to me: it's very compact. That means more space on my bedside night table. Although I didn't think it could beat the Coby Vitruvian - a much larger, heavier unit, with a warm sound I like. And \\"straight out of the box\\", it didn't. But the Octivo has a suprisingly larger, better sound than belies its diminutive size. It reminded me of the Bose Wave. It's design appeared to be inspired by that, as though it might have comparable interior air channels that create a larger deeper sound than otherwise possible in such a sized unit. Well, I know it does at least have bass ports, and it does create a larger sound with deeper bass than you'd expect. Probably deeper than that of the Coby, but not richer (so, little upper midbass). Actually, it was pretty impressive out of the box, but eventually, after comparisons with the Coby, I wasn't crazy about the upper mids on the Altec. It gave the music a lack of body and roundedness. The Coby, a warmer, larger, bassier, richer sound was superior overall. One listen to the great Rev. Gary Davis' \\"Death Don't Have No Mercy\\" on the Coby made it crystal clear that the Octivo fell short, and at this point, it was no contest.

I figured and found out that the Octivo prefers being rammed into a corner. I mean shoved right up into the corner walls of a room, to where the sides are touching. This might mean the iPhone itself hits the wall a bit (if in Dock #1). This is what the Octivo was designed to do, and it reinforces the bass and adds fullness, making the sound much more palatable. The second thing I found that improved the sound much further in this direction, was going through the iPhone's headphone jack into the Octivo's AUX in jack. Now you're cookin'! Only problem here was, a bit of a background buzzing. This I discovered was caused by having the iPhone plugged into the Octivo by way of 30 pin connection. No matter if that connection was going through one of the docks, or the USB port on the side. It was improved by the use of the original Apple cable, but it was still present to some degree, and got louder when you touched the screen. The Coby did not have this issue, and the Octivo claims to be magnetically shielded for stuff like this! Third thing I discovered: Dock #1 sounds MUCH better than Dock #2. Oh well, good thing I only have one iPhone.

NOW ON TO THE TWEAKING: It wasn't 30 minutes into this thing, that I already started semi-seriously tweaking the dock, to improve its sound. I first tried stuffing memory foam into the bass ports. Now it gave the Coby some serious competition! It became harder to decide which to keep. The Coby still edged it out, though. But then I stuffed a pair of my black socks into the bass ports, nice and tight. And voila. That's the story of how the Altec Lansing Octivo became my new iPhone dock, and finally won out over the Coby. The effect this had was to significantly improve timbral textures. So while the sound may have reduced in size, it increased in quality and naturalness. In fact, it was so good, I was thinking there were stereo systems I've heard costing thousands of dollars, that did not acheive this degree of musicality! I still felt it held on to some traces of its former sound, but I could not complain, given how far I'd taken the Octivo, sound-wise.

FUNCTION-WISE: The little round remote is a clever design (like the rest of this unit), but will probably get lose easily due to its size! I found the controls perplexing to use in iTunes, but that's probably just a learning curve that's needed.I found the controls on the Coby remote somewhat easier to use, but it too didn't always do what I wanted or expected it to, in iTunes.

IN SHORT: It doesn't matter that the unit is light, if it sounds good, and can't move when wedged into a corner. So, stuff the Octivo right into a corner, use the headphone jack if possible, close the bass ports with something black and attractive, and you've got a really good little tabletop iPhone/iPod dock that looks nice, and sells for an amazingly low price and is a great value! I also like that it doesn't have a lot of bells and whistles (like the Coby's motorized revolving dock holder!) to break down, or a strong light (again, like the Coby's large blue lighted disc!) that disrupts sleep patterns.

product_title: Bose SoundLink Bluetooth Mobile Speaker II
review_body:
It's no surprise; this is the best Bluetooth speaker out there right now - and I know; I've tried them all. Literally. But here's the problem: It's too heavy, and just a bit too big. Of course, to get the kind of sound you get here, you need the size and weight - if not more! It does what it does well, in a small package, but in my side-by-side testing with the Monster ClarityHD Micro, (the new one - only available on the Monster website, I think - not the old one), the ClarityHD has sound ALMOST as good and is MUCH smaller and lighter. Half the size and a third the weight. I can put the ClarityHD in my pants pocket. The Bose would be hard to fit in a jacket pocket, and would weigh it down so much as to be really not an option.

The ClarityHD also gives you features the Bose doesn't offer: You can use it as a speakerphone - and an excellent one, at that - and it takes voice commands, (turn up volume, next song, etc). It has a wrist strap - because its light enough. And it gives plenty of volume without distortion. Granted, the Bose hits much higher volume, but think of the use-case... hotel room, picnic, outdoor on the patio... These places don't call for mega-volume - and the ClarityHD is much louder and less boomy than the popular Jambox.

So, its sort of like the digital camera paradigm: \\"What is the best digital camera? The one you have with you.\\". For most people, that is the camera in their phone, or the small camera in their pocket, purse, etc. When I travel, is it more convenient to throw my excellent Canon SX230 P&S in my bag, or my big DSLR with lenses? Same here. I was about to sell my ClarityHD and I started thinking about my use-case... When was I really going to use a BT speaker? At a hotel. At a restaurant, (maybe). Picnic? Beach? Around the house...? Maybe, but I have speakers and what not everywhere. Is the sound \\"good enough\\" from the Monster for these occasions? I'd have to say Yes. Is it even quite good? Yes. Is it as good as the Bose? No. But its the best I've heard for the weight and the size and the price. The next step up is the Bose, but I fear it will never make it into my overnight bag, fanny pack, or pocket. Also, I don't have to remember to carry the A/C adapter and chord... the Monster ClarityHD uses standard microUSB charging. Think about it.

To my mind, the Soundlink is good for a college kid with limited space that wants maximum sound that is also reasonably portable. It's 3 pounds; this thing isn't light. The ClarityHD is just under 1 pound. For those wanting bigger bass from the smaller units, like the ClarityHD, use an app like PlayerPro which has an equalizer in it. Pump the bass all the way up and you'll be surprised how well this thing handles bass, for its size. As good as the SL? No. But not bad at all, for $100 less and truly portable. Just sayin'...

EDIT: Some people are confusing the new ClarityHD with the old ClarityHD - the new one is twice the width and thinner. It's NOT available on Amazon. Best Buy has it, though. [...]

The one I mean came out in July, this year. It gets VERY loud - easily fills a room. A big room, even. I have both the SL and the ClarityHD on my desk right now, and spent hours playing them side by side; same songs, switching back and forth, adjusting the equalizer to suit each. I stand by my review totally. The point is, I'm about to pack for a trip to the east coast. I grabbed the SoundLink and thought, \\"Whoa... this thing is going to weigh down my bag quite a bit.\\". That got me started thinking about my use-case. I can throw the ClarityHD in my rolling laptop bag without weighing it down, literally, like a brick. A big brick.

It's GREAT for carting around the house; the sound IS clearly better than the ClarityHD. But I don't have a use for it around the house. I have speakers in my bedroom and office and my living room that blow away the SoundLink. It's all about travel, baby! And this thing isn't just something you \\"throw into a bag\\". It's a BRICK. The size is manageable, but the weight is too much.

And for the people who read the Best Buy reviews for the ClarityHD, realize that there are idiots in the world. They bought it and it didn't sound great OOTB. If they spent 5 minutes thinking about it, they would know that using an app with an EQ would have made the thing sound WAY, WAY, better. It handles bass FAR better than the Scambox, and gets FAR louder and cleaner, even with volume turned all the way up. In my (very large) office, I can't turn the thing up more than 1/3 the way before it's just too loud for the room. One reviewer said he had the NEW ClarityHD and that it was $100 less than the Jambox... Huh? It's the same exact price, unless he's talking about the BIG Jambox, which is HUGE, and not portable, (though not much less portable than the Bose). I suspect he's thinking the OLD one is the new one, because that one IS $100 less. Think about your use case, is all I'm saying. If you want the thing for around the house or bringing to the beach house, or for the patio, then fine. The Bose is best. If you want to use the heck out of it, bring it to work for con calls, throwing it in an overnight bag, or in your laptop bag, then I have to respectfully disagree that the Bose is worth the extra money or the extra weight and sound quality over the ClarityHD. And like I said, it charges using a standard microUSB - the same one I use for my phone and other devices. I should also note that I have had no problem connecting to it, or with ANY dropped connections. When I turn on my phone, the ClarityHD will immediately connect it - same as the Bose.to a bag\\". product_title: iHip Retractable Stereo Ear Buds
review_headline: Surprising sound for something so inexpensive
review_body:
I am NOT an earbud person at all - until now. Well, I still don't think I'm an earbud person, but am more than willing to use this particular product. I have 4 iPod/Shuffle products and never once used any of the earbuds Apple provides with them. Just looking at them my ears feel uncomfortable and as such I've always used headphones of some sort. Since I now have a small rechargable earphone jack speaker ([[ASIN:B0017LVU96 Macally Portable Stereo Speaker with Lithium Battery Silver TurboTune]]) that fills most of my listening needs I thought I would try out these earbuds after reading multiple good reviews of them. I travel a lot so I wanted something that would take up the smallest amount of room and not have cord all over the place. This product provides nice sound, is pretty comfortable for the price and they have extra pads for the earbuds. All in all, a good purchase for me - the product adequately fills my need.

Downsides: As another reviewer mentioned the cord on this is a bit short even at its fullest extension. This can be a bit problematic if I'm carrying my iPod since my arm can't relax comfortably at my side. I'm not a tall person - I'm 5'7\\", so I am knocking it from a 5/5 to 4/5 for this. Also, I'd think twice before I purchased this for someone who would be using them constantly since the wires are very delicate. I realize they have to be delicate in order to wrap around the center chamber and to be so compact. For someone like me who is using them a handful of times each month it will be fine. I know not to pull quickly and to treat it gently. I'm not sure the average teenager would be so cautious, however.

Overall I'd recommend it to someone with those caveats in mind. For the price I'm very pleased. I purchased this at a site other than Amazon only because it's on backorder here and I needed it before they would arrive. Once back in stock I may purchase a backup unless I can find something within a reasonable price range that has a longer cord and a cord that is a little less delicate.price range that has a longer cord and a cord that is a little less delicate.

product_title: Cheetah Mounts ALAMB Articulating Arm (15” Extension) TV Wall Mount Bracket for 12-24” TVs and Displays up to VESA 100 and up to 40lbs, Including a 10’ Twisted Veins HDMI Cable
review_body:
This mount appears pretty sturdy at first glance. It is much cheaper than others found at a store too. But I put a heavy old 32\\" on it (maybe 40 lbs) and I feel that this is pushing the limits. Something smaller or lighter would be more appropriate. I tend to like overkill solutions to weight bearing problems, comes with my engineering background. That being said, I don't think this will break per se but I am not leaving my TV extended out, I am keeping the arm close to the wall. I've adjusted the joints and what not and still it does not satisfy my need for stability. I've inspected much heavier TVs at full extension (in bars, gyms, etc) and they don't give or wobble as much as this one does while extended, so I don't think I'm being overly cautious. The steel is strong, but there is a lot of slop in the hinges which I think contribute to this even when tightened, unfortuantely at this price point probably not much you can do about that.

Also, the wall mount itself could use a few improvements. There are 2 slots that are vertical on the same stud. Very robust screws and metal there, I had no fear of it pulling out. But the first time I extended the TV, the mount rotated on the wall because of the slots, there is nothing to prevent this except more force/friction on the drywall. I already had it pretty tight, didn't want to strip the wood or crush the drywall so I put some finishing nails in a few grooves to keep it in place. That being said, something could have been done about this from the manufacturer relatively easy. Again, it might be overkill but I would have preferred to use 2 studs on this size TV, or at least have a 2 more holes to set it in place with a smaller screw once it is mounted and leveled with the slots.

Also, the tilt is not strong enough- no matter how hard you tighten, it will slip if you grab the TV to reposition the arms. No mechanism to lock the tilt, just a bolt and washer for friction.

product_title: iHome iP11 Spacesaver Alarm Clock for iPod and iPhone
review_headline: Good, but lacking a few features I would consider standard
review_body:
I just picked this up at the local department store. I paid $49.99. I intend to replace my old alarm/radio with one that I can play my iPod with and charge it at night. Turns out, there's no radio present, but with the iPod being internet radio capable (with wi-fi) it's not too big of a deal, but I do still wish I could tune-in to some of those better AM stations... Just preference. Seems like it will do just fine...
I'm using a 3rd Generation iPod (I think? with the curved metal back), and so far there are no issues of \\"this device not compatible...\\" blah blah.... So far, so good. Doesn't seem like it's going to happen either. Also, I don't know how every dock is, but I'm able to have my Belkin brand iPod case on while it is on the charger -- HUGE +. I forget the exact Belkin case it is, but it's very thin, and is mad of rubbery plastic that covers the back, and conforms the iPod, wrapping around with a small lip on the front.

Personal details:

-Small size and sounds great, at that.

-Minimalist in operation //
9 buttons on top: ALARM ON/OFF, ALARM SET, HOUR ADJUST, MINUTE ADJUST, ALARM RESET/UNIT OFF, PLAY/PAUSE/i(DEVICE) SELECT, VOLUME UP, VOLUME DOWN, and SNOOZE/DIMMER //
3 buttons on rear: DST +1/-1, EXB (BASS BOOST) ON/OFF, and TIME SYNC (with i[DEVICE]) //
You'll really only need 5 of those buttons for everyday use, so that's pretty neat -- keeping it simple.

-Snooze button is far enough away (1.5\\") from the iPod itself, so it seems like it's not too prone to me reaching over to hit snooze button, but accidentally breaking the iPod off the dock. I'm not too worried about it, really, i'm not known to be violent in the morning.

-Display is large and brightness-adjustable: Full brightness -> Dimmer -> Darker -> OFF -> Full Brightness -> ...
At this point in the daytime, it doesn't seem like it's going to be too bright at all at night. Even so, I sleep with the TV on anyway and I'd beSHOCKED if it was brighter than that.

-As noted above, the speaker sounds great. The volume output can get up there, but i'm upset that you can't adjust the volume on the alarm itself. I, personally, intend to have the beeper/buzzer sound more than waking up to music. It was kind of a letdown to not have that option. You will be happy to know however, that the beeps in the alarm go from single bleeps, (about 5 seconds go by) to faster bleeps, (5 seconds once again) and then the volume ramps up louder to continuous beeps that will continue for an hour (as per the instructions) before stopping by itself and resetting for the next day. The way I see it, the initial volume on the alarm is not very impressive, but when it starts to get faster and ramp up in volume, that's where I see my sweet-spot in getting up. It's much more....alarming... pun intended. This is where the preference comes in once again: If you are sleeping with someone else in the same room, it might be nice to have it be just loud enough for the person getting up at that time in particular, but for someone who sleeps alone, well... you see where I'm going with this. It's not very loud, but it gets loud within about 10 seconds. Not too bad.

-I'm upset that when my iPod is plugged into the dock, it will ALWAYS use the iPod's music as an alarm. The ONLY way that you can get the unit's onboard buzzer/beeper is by taking the iPod off. This is kind of a big deal for me because it would be nice to be able to leave the iPod on the unit and still have the buzzer go off. I'm not a big fan of waking up with music -- the song tends to get stuck in my head all day and then I get sick of it. Once again!: Personal preference.

-The unit features the music volume ramp up thing where when the alarm goes off, the music starts off low and gradually increases to the volume last selected. Also, this volume is independent from when just playing music. That is a great thing. What does this mean? You can go to sleep with one volume, but wake up to a completely different one. Who wants to go to sleep with the music as loud as when you wake up? Not me, i'll tell ya...
Also, while on topic, when playing music as you go to sleep, you can press the \\"SLEEP\\" button up top to turn on the sleep mode (like a Television sleep mode). You can adjust the timer from 90 minutes, 60 minutes, 45 minutes, 30 minutes, and 15 minutes, then back to 90. The volume will also go from the volume you pick, and gradually decrease with the time. Pretty neat feature if you ask me. Did you ask? Well now you know anyway. One weird thing is, once you press the \\"SLEEP\\" button to go into sleep mode, I don't know of a way to shut off SLEEP mode without pressing the POWER button and cycling the power off and on. I think it would've been nice if they had the sleep mode menu go like : 90, 60, 45, 30, 15, OFF, back to 90.
That makes much more sense, wouldn't you say? That's just one thing I would consider lacking. It's such a simple implementation and why it wasn't included, I don't know.

-The unit itself is very solid. Everything is compact and structurally sound. Nothing wiggles or creaks. Even the buttons have a very nice feel to them. I also like how the unit emits beeps when making selections. I really only heard it when finalizing my alarm time, but it's a nice feature that let's you know, \\"Hey, we're in this together, I'm going to get you up tomorrow morning. You don't have be like the indians and drink tons of water tonight so your bladder wakes you up. Hey, by the way, great song to fall asleep too. Goodnight.\\" Very good tactile feedback...

-The auto time sync feature is nice. Just press the button on the back and there you go. I kind of wish there was an option to have it reflect military time like my iPod does, but that's not a big deal. Time is time.

-The unit has a battery back-up feature that eliminates the power-outtage scenario. Don't let your boss know you have this alarm. You'll be limiting your options by not being able to use the, \\"but the power went out!\\" excuse when asked why you're late. I think the way it works (according to the manual) is the alarm will automatically sound if the power cuts regardless of the setting. I think the intention is to let you know that the power went out. I'm not sure, i'll have to read about it. Also, the battery is included with the unit. It's a replaceable watch battery that you must install in the rear by unscrewing a cover and installing it. Simple. Don't have a screwdriver? You might want to add a philips screwdriver to your cart along with this. It's about that time if you were holding out.

-The bottom of the unit has little rubber \\"feet\\" so it won't slide like my old one did. Good stuff.

So, my main complaints are that you can't adjust the alarm volume, there's no AM/FM radio tuner, and you can't have the onboard alarm go off while the i(DEVICE) is plugged in and charging. Not big issues, but I like options!

Final verdict is that I would recommend this alarm clock. It's quite nice, and not bad for the price. I may have felt better paying $35-40 for it though. I Don't think it's truly worth $50, but hey, it sounds good and is VERY solid feeling.

Ok, enough rambling, I've got to go listen to this great 50's blues station. Sounds fantastic on this speaker. I hope this review helps!

product_title: Denon AVR3312CI Integrated Network A/V Surround Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: A nice AV receiver for a good price
review_body:
For those who don't know this - Denon puts out a new generation of receivers each year, and the year is encoded in the product name: AV3312CI means the 2012 version of the \\"33\\" model with \\"CI\\" (custom installation) features. In general, unless you need some feature that just arrived, you can save a fair bit getting last year's model. That's how I bought the 2012 model instead of the just-arrived AV3313CI (yes, like car model years - always ahead of reality), at half-off the list price.

This is a nice AV receiver. It sounds good; it's flexible; it looks decent; and its remote integration is better than average. Like its brothers, it is primarily focused on handling HDMI connections, with analog audio and video up-converted to 1080p format. Like all its brothers, it refuses to down-convert anything digital - your HDMI inputs will not show up on composite or component outputs, for either video or audio. There are S/PDIF inputs but no outputs, so at least we're spared an open refusal to transcribe HDMI audio to those. If you want to feed analog outputs, you better also connect analog inputs. I find that annoying but I'm not counting it against this particular model - they all do this, because the HDMI Gods have declared war on the \\"analog hole\\" and are bullying all major manufacturers into these restrictions.

The main user interface is your TV (only through HDMI output). There is a two-line LED display up front that shows, essentially, the current and next line of whatever's on the TV menu. It's serviceable in a pinch, but I wouldn't use this device for pure audio switching - it's fairly annoying to set up if you can't see the TV menu.

There are three zones (Main, 2, 3). Zone 2 and 3 can steal a total of two amplification channels (bumping the main zone to 5.1), or stay unamplified and leave the main zone to 7.1. In addition there is one analog recording output that can be switched separately. There is no HDMI output for zone 2 (that's the New Thing for the 2013 model). There is no composite audio input, so any surround game sound needs to be encoded through HDMI or S/PDIF.

Surround processing is good and is checking all the relevant boxes. Audyssey's letter soup (\\"MultEQ XT blah blah\\") works well and seems happy to create a virtual center speaker simply by noticing that there's no center speaker connected. There are more modes and trims than you'll ever bother to figure out. The dynamic compression (for movie watching without upsetting the neighbors) works pretty well.

There is an alphabet soup of internet audio services all ready to play (assuming you connected the Ethernet plug to the internet). The associated user interface is (surprise) on the TV screen, and it's not particularly good or easy to use. Personally, I'm plugging an Apple TV into my Denon and using it for all those fancy internet things. But I suppose the Denon would serve in a pinch.

Among annoyances, there is a total inability to route audio to its HDMI outputs while actually driving its speakers. It's completely either-or, for both HDMI outputs. This is both silly and annoying, because it makes it hard to use HDMI for distribution to multiple rooms, and I see no reason (even legal) for this. There are minor annoyances with the way the receiver responds to serial or IP commands. There is a loud clacking noise (a relay) whenever the main amplifiers switch on or off, even for muting (you can work around that). None of these rise to a major objection, but you should be aware of them.

Four stars for \\"I'm glad I bought this, it's good enough to drive my house, even if it's not (even close to) perfect.\\"

product_title: Creative ZEN Style M300 4 GB MP3 and Video Player with Bluetooth and FM Radio Playback
review_headline: Decent for built-in music. Useless for expansion.
review_body:
I bought the Style M300 to replace a Sansa I lost recently. It looks like I'll be looking for that Sansa just a little bit harder.

The physical design of the M300 is great and certainly lives up to its name. It fits comfortably in jeans or pants and is pretty comfortable to hold and operate. The capacitive buttons are a nice touch. Its sound quality is quite good, but that's standard for devices from Creative. Unfortunately, that's where its positives ended for me.

It seems that Creative really wanted to tout the little colour screen it has, despite it not being good enough to comfortably handle most audio and video. Album art is displayed,in full, on the \\"Now Playing\\" screen with no known way of turning it off. It looks pretty bad and adds no functional value, but that doesn't stop it from making the track information in white font completely unreadable at times. What makes even less sense is that one can change the font colour for the entire system...except for the \\"Now Playing\\" screen!

I didn't have any Bluetooth speakers or headphones to pair it with, but it's annoying that I cannot transfer tracks to it this way.

Despite these flaws, the ultimate dealbreaker for me was its completely inane design for handling microSD cards. While it's capable of supporting up to 32GB of removable storage, actually *using* those 32GB on this player is an exercise in frustration. It takes up to ten minutes for it to scan the card and display it contents. Transferring music to the card (not the internal flash memory) is much, much slower than using a reader. Worse, these contents are NOT indexed into the main library and can only be accessed from its own separate section. (It seems that this also prevents you from creating playlists from songs on the card too.) Worse *still* is that this scan is *not* permanently indexed, which means that the card must be re-scanned every time the unit shuts off! While the head designer of this unit might be fine with waiting ten minutes for his or her music to load, most people would probably not be okay with this.

These problems would be palatable if I could flash it with Rockbox, but its 512KB of on-board RAM will probably prevent that from happening.

The 2GB Sansa Clip is $29.99. Given this, I cannot possibly recommend this to anyone.

Another plus is how compact they are. The folding feature makes them much easier to tote around, which I have actually been doing since I can't decide where I want to use them the most, in my cube at work which is noisy, or my home office when I work from home.

There are two dings. One is that I can't wear them for very long. I can't wear them at all when I need my glasses on, which I wear while working on the computer, but that is not the fault of the head phones. They start hurting my ears after an hours or so. That just may be my own issue though. I have become accustom to wearing ear buds and my ears are large.

The second is that the invisible mic does not pick up as well as other headset I own. Testing it with several others we found the voice pick up on these comes across muffled. They are fine if you can talk louder than normal, but in a cube environment this won't work well.

So I find these great listening headsets when you need the noise cancellation. It makes them being uncomfortable tolerable for longer periods of time. The down side is I would not use them in a cube environment to answer the phone because you need to talk louder.

My recommendation is that if you find wearing full size ear phones comfortable and you are going to use them in an environment were you can speak up the are definitely a great purchase.

First the elephant in the room: the durability. I agree my original Chrome did not last past a year. The build at the time had the straight cable design at the jack that was definitely prone to breaking much like the pictures people have posted. V-moda eventually redesigned this now have a 45 degree angle jack. It even has a head that lets you push down the jack without applying pressure to the cable at all. I picked up the Nero with the in-line mic over 2 years ago and until yesterday the L side started to fade(they were yanked out my ear probably for the 1000th time). I'm convinced the Nero with its mesh cable is more durable than the original plastic on the Chrome model. Unfortunately it seems these headphones are discontinued. When I got them they were $100 bucks, and now they're $30. Even with the issues I think they're way more durable than Klipsch S4i I tried to replace them with. At $100 I was very disappointed with the S4i. The cable was skinnier than the V-moda with no protection (the Nero and Chrome both had their primary cable lines covered somehow, plastic or mesh). Also the Vibes are metal! Not plasic on the Klipsch. The mic placement wasn't thought out well as they hang near my chest as if you wanted to hear my heartbeat. The Vibe Duo hangs closer to your mouth and should you have the over ear clips they'll be closer on the right side. So definitely the S4i went back to best buy and now awaiting my 3rd Vibe duo. product_title: Terk VR1 Automatic TV Volume Controller
review_headline: Does a resonable job, not an excellent job.
review_body:
I listen to Internet radio and got tired of continually adjusting the volume to compensate for volume and loudness differences. I ordered this product to connect my Grace internet radio to my M Audio powered speakers.

My assessment after a week is that this product does a reasonable job of controlling volume changes on a particular 'net stream I tune in to. But, as other reviews have stated, it is not a solid 'loudness' controller---so yes, overly compressed and processed commercials still sound 'louder' than the other program material on the stream (stream = Internet radio stream). I don't know the design details of this product, so I don't know if it is correct for me to expect it to control loudness AND volume----these are different concepts. Average volume is not the same as loudness. On 'net radio there is one commercial in particular that is very annoying, due to how it is processed and compressed, and this product does not diminish the sound of this particular commercial. But, on talk shows, it does a good job of keeping the talk show (callers, host) balanced. I don't know how it would perform on a TV.

The idea of 'loudness' control is one that hardly any technical company has dealt with---and those who have are broadcast equipment makers, such as Orban, and the defunct CBS labs (As in CBS TV and radio). Alas, I lack the thousands or hundreds of dollars to use these products. Given this, this Terk/Audio Vox is a darned nice product for what it can do at the small price. Maybe adding TWO of these---in series, might help, I don't know. Just be aware that volume control is not the same as loudness control. I think this product is a volume controller, not a combined volume and loudness controller. We need a product that does both.

I recommend this Terk/AudioVox, just don't expect it to do a solid loudness control job for you---volume, yes!

product_title: Audio Technica ATH-CKM500 BK | Inner Headphones (Japan Import)
review_body:
A quick intro, I'm keanex on Head-Fi I regularly review headphones and other audio gear. I'm here to give you a quick review on these.

Bass: The bass is well extended, very clean with no signs of distortion whether it's through my iPod, laptop, or O2+ODAC combo. The bass hits hard and is quick, but the mid-bass is a bit pushy, this may change with burn-in though.

Mids: The mids are intimate, clean and smooth. These are the most realistic mids I have come across in my endeavors for an IEM.

Highs: Well extended, no added sibilance, and balanced really well with the overall signature.

Instrument Separation/Soundstage is one of the best I've heard in an IEM. I feel as if I'm in a small club that is tuned to provide a clean sound. Instruments have room to breath even in the most complex parts of songs I've heard that even sound a tad confusing at time on my Audio Technica Ad2000.

I know I'm saying clean a lot, I can not stress how crystal clear the sound on these is. A lot of people praised the Fostex T50RP for their black background, well I think these may even be cleaner sounding.

The comfort isn't the best, the IEMs don't fit too comfortably in my right ear, but they IEMs stay in and form a good seal despite the semi-shallow insertion. The build quality is top notch, you can't ask for better at this price, again Audio Technica sets the bar for IEM quality.

So that's my quick review after 3 days of ownership and about 20 hours of listening. Yes, 20 hours. These IEMs have made me want to re-listen to every song I own over again, which is something next to my Meelectronics A161p and Audio Technica Ad2000. These are the headphone to beat under $100 and I'd be impressed if any company could build a driver as clean as this for their IEMs even at double the price. There's my gushing mini-review, these deserve every bit of praise they get.

review_headline: You get what you pay for
review_body: As impressed as I am with the fact that I could get a 25' HDMI cable overnighted to me for under ten bucks, this cable is very 'meh.'  I'm using it with the HDMI-out port on the new retina MacBook Pro to connect to an HDTV.  The initial impression is great -- perfect quality video on the screen, and perfect quality audio. Except I have two problems with this cable: about 15 minutes into using it, the audio becomes really muffled and tin-like and I have to disconnect and re-connect it.  Then, about every 5-10 minutes my TV cuts to static momentarily and goes back to the video.  I first thought it was because I was moving my laptop around and the cable was coming lose, but even without touching it the same problem happened.  I moved the location of the cable to make it less twisty, and it seemed to help.  I don't have this issue with two other shorter HDMI cables with the same HDTV and computer, so I'm assuming this is just a poorly-constructed China-made cable... you get what you pay for.

review_body:

The controls are very straightforward and easy. Power volume is handled by pushing down on the \\"legs\\" of the unit. Having buttons placed in such a way enhances the sleek design of the zx100 and keeps things nice and tidy; no ugly switches or big buttons to fuss around with.

One benefit over iHome iHM60GT is that the ZX100 has a built-in aux jack. With the iHome iHM60GT, one has to carry around an aux/usb combo jack at all times. The ZX100 does come with a combination aux jack/usb--for charger and adding on a second speaker--but you can also just leave that jack behind and just plug into your computer, phone, mp3 player, etc. with just the built in jack, which is about 3\\" inces long. Very sleek and handy!

Overall, a very good purchase. The strength of the unit is its sleekness and durability. In terms of volume, it's good enough to fill a room or backyard (I have found that I use it a lot for BBQs and grilling), and it's small enough to bring anywhere. For the price, I couldn't be happier.

product_title: Panasonic ErgoFit In-Ear Earbud Headphone
review_body:
... better sound! I bought these to replace my Skullcandy Ink'd earbuds ([[ASIN:B003KN2K20 Skullcandy INK'd Earbuds S2INCZ-040 (Pink)]]), which broke after I lent them to my seven-year-old brother. (Not doing that again.) I loved my Skullcandy earbuds for their good sound quality for the relatively low price, but then I saw that these [[ASIN:B003EM800S Panasonic RP-HJE120-S In-Ear Earbud Ergo-Fit Headphone (White/Silver)]] had a better price and better reviews. Better earphones for SIX DOLLARS?! I didn't believe it, but bought them anyway.

When I first tried them out, I was disappointed. The sound was tinny and soft compared with the Skullcandies. (I was able to compare them side by side since the Skullcandies work if I hold the wire at exactly the right angle.) But then I tried them out with the largest set of silicone buds that came with them -- the difference was amazing. Crystal clear sound. Defined bass. The Skullcandies sound fuzzy and muddled in comparison (the Skullcandy bass might be slightly more powerful, but it's definitely a great deal less clear).

I want to emphasize how important it is that you use the proper size silicone bud -- try them all out to be sure. The ones that fit me with the Panasonic RP-HJE120 earbuds are nearly twice as big as the ones that fit me with the Skullcandy Ink'd earbuds.

An added bonus of the Panasonics is the L-shaped plug. I've read that this reduces wear on the wires at the connection, and thus will prolong the life of the earphones, but I haven't owned them long enough to know whether this is true.

The only way that the Skullcandy Ink'd earbuds beat these is that the Skullcandies are more efficient earplugs -- they fill your ear more tightly and thus block more background noise (at least with the shape of my ears). But the significantly better sound quality, plus the extremely low price, make the Panasonic RP-HJE120s totally worth five stars, and in the long run they are overall better earphones than Skullcandy Ink'd.

product_title: Ultra High Performance HDMI Switcher, 3to1 Switch
review_body:
Every time I turn on my Xbox I wish I had found this little gem sooner.

I see that some reviewers had trouble getting what they wanted out of this switch so I want to get specific about how it works for me.

There's room for 3 inputs on this switch but I'm only using 2 of them. My two inputs are an Xbox 360 and a Directv/Tivo receiver. They are both hooked up to an LG flatscreen TV through this HDMI switch.

The Tivo box is always putting out signal and the HDMI switch sends that straight to the TV. As soon as I turn on the Xbox, the HDMI switch transfers the Xbox signal to the TV, instead of the Tivo signal. I don't have to do anything, just turn on the Xbox. As soon as I turn off the Xbox, the HDMI switch goes back to sending the Tivo signal to the TV. I love it!

If I want to watch some TV and take a break from the Xbox WITHOUT turning the Xbox off, I just use the little remote and select the other input.

Some reviewers noticed changes to their image once this switch was hooked up. The Xbox 360 needs to have some settings changed in order to take full advantage of the HDMI connection.

My Xbox defaults to a Screen Format of NORMAL (4:3), so once I set that to WIDESCREEN that got rid of the stretched image. It also defaults to a Reference Level of STANDARD. Changing that setting to EXPANDED fixed the washed out colors. The improvement to the image over using the older composite cable is definitely noticeable.

There's a few other points to mention here.

This HDMI switch has an optional power supply which I didn't need and you probably won't need either. The switch runs on power supplied through the HDMI cables from your equipment. Some older equipment doesn't supply power through the HDMI cable and only then would you need that optional power cable.

Also, when I first hooked up the HDMI switch, I got picture but no sound. I unplugged the HDMI cable from the Tivo source, plugged it back in and everything was fine.

Lastly, when the HDMI switch changes from one input to another, it takes 7 seconds to switch the source. This doesn't bother me at all. I only mention it so you know that it isn't instantaneous.

This is one of those purchases that I'm happy with every time I see it work. I only wish I found it sooner.

product_title: SONOS CONNECT Wireless Receiver Component for Streaming Music
review_body:
This is my first review on Amazon, because I think Sonos has earned it, and it is a way to thank Amazon and posted reviews that helped me buy and set up what is now a four zone Sonos system at my home in India.

If I could give both Amazon and Sonos more that 5 stars, I would.

That said, there are some things that a potential buyer should know, and hopefully, this review will help.

This review isn't just about the Connect, but the entire Sonos system of which the Connect is just one part.

Some background: Before Sonos, I had decent hifi systems in three rooms, with the main high end system in the living room. Music replay was via many CDs, and I wasn't aware of internet radio to any large extent. But I was well versed with high end audio equipment, having owned different systems for over ten years. There is even a turntable in the system, although it isn't used much since Sonos came into the home!

I had heard about Sonos, but did not know much about it. When I moved to a larger home a little over a year ago, I started researching Sonos and the Amazon reviews were of great help.

But what was even more helpful was the User Forum on the Sonos website, a treasure trove of useful information, with very helpful members. When I ordered the first of the many Sonos units I now have, it was without having seen or heard it, because there is no distribution in India. A leap of faith.

Since there are quite a few unhappy posters here, that aren't satisfied with Sonos, I must accept that the system may not work as advertised or sold out of the box. A certain knowledge of home wifi and routers helps. But what helps even more is the truly world class Sonos support, that is available for free as long as one needs it, and the referred forum. It is easy to register on the forum, and start asking questions, that are usually answered very quickly by other Sonos users with a lot of experience of the system. And when that fails, it is easy to invoke support from Sonos directly. In my case, I had a glitch when the system was new, a year ago, and another one a few days ago. The first was a little complex, but Sonos support did all the handholding needed to resolve it. The recent one took just one email to have it fixed. It doesn't matter where in the world the system is, as long as it is connected to the net, Sonos can \\"see\\" it, and troubleshoot. In my mind, it is these two forms of support that elevate Sonos to the rare product that fully delivers on all it promises.

It also affords the flexibility of choice, based on budgets, and the kind of systems one already has. For instance, my high end system that sits in the living room, is now driven by the Connect. This way, I hear music of the same quality as always, but now I do not need my many CDs, or the CD player. All the CDs are copied to a hard disc, which is a one time investment of time and effort that needs to be made. Having done that, I can select any of my CDs from scrolling in the Sonos controller that is an app on my ipod touch. I can make playlists, play select albums, play tracks in sequence or in random. Apart from the sheer convenience, this means that I am listening to many more of my CDs a lot more often.

Then, there is free internet radio. Many stations, that offer good quality music streams, deliver music that sound as good as CD replay. Internet music services like Pandora or Spotify aren't available in India as of now, so I can't comment on these.

What this means is that I am now listening to music a lot more often than I did before, and music from all over the world, as well as my CDs. And all in high quality stereo.

For other rooms, there are other units that are more suitable, depending on the kind of systems one has there, or doesn't have.

And one can add these to the system whenever - depending on budget availability or the mood. Once that is done, one can play the same music from the same source in all rooms in perfect sync, or, play different music in each room. In my case I now have music via Sonos in the living room and balcony via 2 connects, in the bedroom via a Connect Amp, and dining room via a Play5.

It is a year since I installed the system, and it remains a source of continuing delight.

If I were to be looking for multi room audio again today, I would buy Sonos all over again, no hesitation.

My only grouse is with Amazon. I got 6 different units from Amazon, all shipped to India, from the US. All were delivered to my home in India, within 10 days of the order click. Perfectly packed and therefore, no damages. And all of them are working fine. The grouse is that I find that Amazon no longer ships Sonos to India, and I hope that changes soon.
