review_body:
This item improved my TV quality immensely. I was using an RCA 10 dB amplifier (inside), and was having trouble picking up FOX, most of the time it would be NO SIGNAL or it would be spotty. I got this and installed the main box to antenna pole, and plugged in the cable going from the antenna to it and plugged the other one going to the house into the other port. This device also supports using separate VHF and UHF antennas, I was considering buying an additional VHF antenna for this item, but the quality without the second antenna was so great I just kept my current antenna by itself. Once I had the main box installed outside, I came inside and took the house input cable and plugged it into the power part (the small plug that powers the amplifier outside), and scanned for channels. All of my channels, were coming in great and and I had two FOX inputs (one from my location and one from Tallahassee, around 90 miles away)! And they looked perfect, no static or breaking!

In the end I am very happy with this item, it has given me all the channels I wanted in perfect quality! It was easy to install and works perfectly! Highly recommend!!

Just to let you know, I tried using this amplifier with my old amplifier, however, I got a lot of interference on the screen, so I am just using this one. Also, I tried using this device inside the house (not installing on the pole) and had spotty service on FOX, so I installed it at the antenna and it worked perfectly!! I also have it set to combined input (one antenna input) and FM Trap On. Just FYI.

product_title: Digicom PMA-5031 40-70-Inch Universal Tilting TV Mount
review_body: I did a lot of research and read a lot of reviews.  This product had a good amount of up and down tilt, which I felt at the time would be important.  Most reviews said they did not change the tilt once it was set to where they wanted it but I wanted the option to move it as I needed.  The center of my TV is about eye level when standing, so when doing exercise or playing active video games, I wanted the TV facing forward (no tilt) and when sitting on the couch, I wanted to tilt it down.  This mount allows me to do this without messing with the tilt knob adjustment (but I could tighten it if I wanted to). I could easily tilt the TV with my hand, which is what I had hoped for.  One site I visited that reviewed various mounts mentioned that they could see no reason why somebody would need to tilt a TV upward.  Really?  There may actually be people out there that may want to get off the couch and do aerobics or play active video games that require you to stand once in a while.  If you have a TV that is at couch height, you will get the best experience if you tilt it up towards your eyes when you stand; not that you have to, but it is a nice option to have.  Tilting up also allows you to access the cords easier if they are in the bottom half of the TV.  The long length made it easy to place it where I wanted it and still hit studs.  However, if you have a small TV, the mount will probably stick out.  Mine is 55\\" and the mount is almost visible on one side due to where I placed the TV on the mount.  The mount seems strong enough; the weight rating was well above the weight of my TV, so I feel comfortable with it.  I didn't have any problems with the lag screws like other reviewers had.  Just make sure you don't over tighten them and the heads shouldn't snap off.  The mount came with all of the necessary screws of various sizes, and spacers for rounded TV backs. Nothing was missing from the box and the product was in perfect condition.  The mount came in the original box,but I was surprised to see that it was shipped only in the original box with no plain outer box concealing the contents of the box that is dropped off on my porch.  Not sure how many TV mount thieves there are out there, but you never know.  As most reviewers noted, don't trust the leveling bubble as it is not accurate.  Use your own level.  The instructions weren't the best, but good enough to easily install and mount the TV.  They didn't say much on how to adjust the TV once it is mounted, and I think it wasn't clear where the adjustment knobs went.  It was obvious the instructions were translated or English was not the primary language by the last statements in the instructions, which stated: \\"Thanks for choosing our products.  Enjoy the using.\\"

Philips now has, at last count, fourteen different docking speakers, ranging in price from around $70 to $300. I've had a Philips DS3000, which is near the bottom of the Fidelio line, for about a year now, and I've been pretty satisfied with it. It has acceptable sound for a small box, and has given reliable service. It currently sits on my nightstand, where it recharges my iPod Nano and provides musical alarm clock functions. The DS7650 costs about twice as much as the little DS3000, but promises bigger sound and portability. So how well does it deliver on these promises?

Pretty well, I think. There's much more bass extension in the DS7650. It's not in the same category as the [[ASIN:B002QQ7TLY Bowers & Wilkins Zeppelin Mini Docking Speaker for iPod]] that sits on the shelf above my computers, but then it only costs half as much. The battery function is a particularly nice feature. I haven't tested battery life to see how close it comes to the advertised \\"up to eight hours\\" of playing time, but I've had it on since dinner- that's been four hours so far- and it's still playing loudly.

The DS7650 comes with one of those single sheet, multi-lingual \\"quick start\\" guides, but I prefer to do the real consumer test- just start playing with it. I plugged in the charger and looked for the docking connector... which was nowhere to be found. Hmm. Aha- the unit actually unfolds, with the protective cover becoming the base. Very clever. plugged my iPod Touch it the docking connector, and switched the unit on. My iPod immediately lit up and told me I needed the Philips \\"Fidelio\\" app- and asked if I'd like to install it now. Sure. I pressed the required keys and a minute or two later music was booming out of the 7650. I say booming as it was a bit heavy on the bass- sort of the 70s boombox sound. But the Fidelio app lets you fine tune the EQ, so I switched it from extended bass to flat, and it immediately sounded more natural. (As an experiment I tried placing the unit on the floor, right up against the wall, to see if that enhanced the bass more naturally. It did, as you might expect.)

Controls are simple- on/off and a volume rocker that sends control signals to the iPod. Everything else is done from the Fidelio app. There's a 1/8\\" stereo jack as well as the iPod docking connector, so you can use it with just about any modern portable audio device. I tested mine with a battery powdered LCD TV, and had no problems.

Of course it's still not hi-fi sound, and the stereo image is not as good as you'd get from headphones or a pair of speakers placed a few feet apart. The sound is nothing like you'd get from a proper stereo system. Nonetheless, it's very good for a portable system. Volume is impressive- there's enough power to make it almost uncomfortably loud in a 12x20 room. The combination of ruggedness and battery power makes it a natural for backyard use, dorm parties, travel, and anywhere else you need decent sound. I think mine is going to move to my basement shop, where it'll provide music while I tinker with robots.

Update: After a year and a half of occasional use, it stopped working. It still charged an iPod affixed to the connector, but it stopped producing sound, either from a directly connected iPod or from a device connected to the audio jack. I tossed it.ing the unit on the floor, right up against the wall, to see if that enhanced the bass more naturally. It did, as you might expect.)

product_title: New-Samsung Blu-Ray Disc Player - BDD5700
review_body:
My fist \\"Smart\\" TV purchase. Not having other similar devices to compare it to I can only tell you what my experience has been as a newbie. When purchasing I recommend doing research on-line as the product boxes and sales staff weren't very helpful. For instance, one might assume (I know, I know) that the various manufacturers would make access to the most popular suppliers of on-line video available. They don't. If it doesn't SAY Amazon on the box you likely aren't going to get Amazon access. Such is the case with this device. We have an extensive Amazon collection of video material and can't access it. Why wouldn't Amazon be included? I can think of absolutely no good reason.

Second, this BBD-D5700/ZA would not work with only three bars of WiFi signal and what's worse is neither the device nor the support staff know or share this information with you. You may be left thinking there is a compatibility issue with your ISP (as did the Samsung \\"tech.\\"). Their advice was to call my ISP.

Before making the final decision whether or not to return this item I took the unit and placed it 6 inches from the WiFi router and it worked.

The look and feel is much like a smart phone only with with a less responsive user interface. You are presented with on-line access to Samsung Java apps (none of which as of this writing include Amazon) that you can download and install.

Netflix is available and while nice when it works, falsely reports that you have no Internet connection when the signal is apparently not what it wants to see. It frequently buffers also.

Hulu offers one of the best experiences running much more smoothly and robustly although it too will complain about the connection even when you have the thing a millimeter from the signal and all bars solid.

Picture quality and features (home network and USB access etc.)are nice.

As of three days after purchase I think we will keep it. I did have to buy a WiFi repeater ($70.00) to get full signal to the BD-D5700/ZA (as I said, it STILL cries about signal and connection in certain apps). I opted for this as running a hard wire was not an option and the additional signal penetration was useful anyway.

This device replaces a Toshiba laptop we have been beating to death for years (one gig ram, slow processor) in service as our streaming source. On the whole the experience with the BD-D5700/ZA is less problematic than the lap top had become (due to higher bandwidth streams etc.) and so our hope is that Samsung develops an Amazon app SOON!

PS Check for firmware upgrade availability after your purchase as these can often remedy many issues (that is if you can connect).

UPDATE: I have found that a hard wire from my WiFi repeater to the device works best. I still get connection errors but fewer. It would would seem the WiFi receiver functions poorly in almost anysituation.

UPDATE UPDATE: Returned. This thing made my wife and I want to pull our hair (well, her hair) out! Back to using our old lap top, we can access everything and it connects perfectly to WiFi every time. If you've never used a computer before you just might... Nah, forget it. I just plain sucks.

product_title: Logitech Harmony 700 Rechargeable Remote with Color Screen (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Not what they used to be
review_body:
I've happily owned 4 different Logitech Harmony H688 remotes since 2002. I recall I paid $150 for the first one, and around $80 or $90 for each since that time. The remote was great, it handled up to 15 devices! My two year old (now 8 year old) could operate it. Heck, even my wife routinely got solid use out of it (that's saying something).

But the bad news is Logitech doesn't know how to leave well enough alone and just keep cranking out a solid product. Instead they discontinued the 688 some years ago, and have replaced it with a series of marginally functioning or largely crippled 'improved' versions: Color screens that frequently broke during falls; rechargeables with malfunctioning charge-cradles; and supported-device-counts that were a fraction of the older units, for a lot more money. And none have delivered even the 2002-era 688's stability, capabilities, or value.

Now, 688's are getting rarer than hen's teeth. Yea, you can continue to get them from 3rd party vendors that have been sitting on old stock, but they're harder to come by. So when I found the 'Tivo' button failing on my last 688, for my next replacement I decided to try out one of Logitech's newer offerings, the $95-$115 700 remote (vs. the ridiculously expensive balance of the line - $250 for a basic non-touch-screen remote? Are you kidding? You're getting into Ipad territory there!).

Well, here I am trying to get the settings migrated from that old custom-programmed/learned-code 688 config, and finding that the 700's lobotomized 6-device limit is too small to even begin to get a basic rig configured anymore. I've reduced the device count to 6, and am finding that I still can't fit the config into the remote's capacity. It's ridiculous. I spend $10 more for a doorstop that handles less than half the capabilities of what I bought a decade ago.

Not batting 1000 there Logitech. Between the debacle they've made out of the SlimP3/Squeezebox MP3-player headunit and it's current software (that I also own, and recently upgraded), and now this. I'm really considering moving away from Logitech products completely. My latest Logitech trackball is about the only well-made/well-engineered product in the bunch.

Update after six months of use (Sept 2012): We've been using the Harmony 700 as our primary AV remote now for awhile (along with an old TiVo peanut remote). As I mentioned above, I had to lobotomize the heck out of my five year old 688 remote config to get it to fit into the new remote. In addition, I had to avoid logitech's 'preferred' downloadable config app and instead had better luck using the older harmonyremote online configuration site. I also had to completely start over from scratch building the config: Adding each device definition to the profile one-by-one to an empty config, and avoiding use of my prior 'learned' commands, all aimed at keeping the memory footprint of my config from exceeding the newly-reduced capacity on 'modern' harmony remotes. There's no way I'd consider the 700 to be an 'improvement' over the 688.

The 700 works OK, after all the frustrating monkeying around (which was never required on prior device upgrades). So I added one star to the score (bringing it to a whole '2'). But on balance, I'd still buy a 688 over the 'improved' 700, without a second thought (I'll probably go back to buying up old stock when I find it). Heck, I'd buy just about any decent option I could find. Sadly, most choices in the niche are either brutally expensive (for home theater geeks), or very complicated to configure.

COMFORT - Speaking of the ear cups, these babies are among the most comfortable over ear headphones i've ever worn. I'm not sure if they're more, less, or equally as comfortable as my Razer Electras. But, even though it's plastic, it doesn't look cheap. The matte black head band, glossy black leatherette ear puffs, and silver highlights give it a classy look.

SOUND - I only received them int he mail earlier today, so i haven't given them a proper \\"burn in\\" yet. But, the bass is definitely there. Definitely not as BOOMY as I expected, but perhaps letting them break-in will change that. I did play with some EQ settings on my laptop and ipod though, and it helped tremendously. I plan on purchasing a Fiio headphone amp soon. But, as i said, the bass IS there. Everything sounds crisp and clear, but a little bassy due to the nature of the headphones. Some people may not like that, and hate how the mids and highs are \\"muddied\\" but I actually like that in a headphone. I also game a lot and watch a good bit of films, so the extra bass comes in handy there too. As some one who listens to a lot of bass intensive music (hip hop, rap, techno, dubstep, etc) i'm satisfied.

product_title: SONOS P5 Color
review_body:
We bought our first over 2 years ago. We now have 4 of these in 3 different rooms: 2 in a paired stereo set-up in the living room, 1 in a bedroom and 1 in the kids' playroom. We also have other Sonos components. If you already know everything about Sonos, skip down to where I summarize my view on the sound quality of the Play 5.

If you're new to Sonos:
Sonos is the perfect system if you like to have music playing around your house for several hours a day, and you like to explore music. Set-up is a snap. Although you can use this exclusively to play music from the internet or music you have stored on your computer or NAS external hard drive, we use it more in conjunction with internet radio, Rhapsody and Pandora. Rhapsody has a monthly subscription cost, as does Pandora for it's commercial-free/higher \\"bit rate\\" version. But we listen to way more music than we watch TV, so the $15-20 a month we spend is a bargain compared to our ridiculous cable bill. MOG is also a very good subscription-based service. Again, you don't have to subscribe to anything if you don't want to. (Note: many professional sports teams blackout their local radio broadcasts from internet streaming---MLB sells a subscription, and a handful of rock bands from 60s-80s don't make their music available via on-demand subscription services.)

But you need other stuff with the Play 5:
1)Unless you plan on attaching the Play 5 with an ethernet directly to your modem or router, you need the Sonos Bridge [[ASIN:B000X1TS54 Sonos Bridge Instant Setup Solution For Sonos Wireless Network (BR100)]]. One of the great things about the Play 5 is the portability. I haven't bought these for the dining room (we don't use that room often) and back deck (the Play 5 isn't weather proof), so having the Bridge really is a necessity. We can bring one of the Play 5 units to wherever we are. Linking to the Bridge is very easy.

2)A Sonos Controller [[ASIN:B002GU5YBM Sonos CR200 Wireless control of your Sonos Multi-Room Music System]] OR the free Sonos app. We use both the Sonos controller and the free apps for IPhone and IPad (also available for Android). I like the Sonos Controller, but it's expensive. I wrote a review on differences.

3)Optional: a NAS drive to store your music. If you store your music on your computer and it's hibernating, you won't have access to it. Having a NAS drive solves this problem.

4)Optional: If your stored music fits on an Ipod or IPhone, you can buy the Sonos dock [[ASIN:B0047T7AGM Sonos Wireless Dock 100 for iPod and iPhone]]and stream it from there. I reviewed the Sonos dock and made a couple of suggestions if you have heavy duty cases on your IPod or IPhone to make sure it fits on the Sonos Dock.

Sound quality:
Short review-it's very good. I find the sound crisp and the bass is good. My wife and I listen mostly to jazz, classical, 70s-90s rock. My kids listen to everything from Raffi to hiphop. The Play 5 does a very good job on it's own in medium-sized rooms (15' x 15' and 12' x 16'). In another room (14' x 16'), where I want a more pronounced stereo effect, I've paired them (left and right). Sonos has a paired stereo setting for this use and it works perfectly.

Long review-once you start compressing audio into MP3 files and streaming it around your house, there's going to be a slight loss of fidelity. I think it's minor, though many audophiles would disagree. I've been listening to MP3 files and streamed music for so long, I'm not sure what I'm missing, though I do notice a slight difference when using subscription-based servces that offer a higher bit rate. Sorry I'm not doing a good job here of talking about compression and streamed files. But for most of us who don't have the ear of an audophile, the bigger issues are the room (size, windows, flooring, etc.), quality of speakers, and speaker placement.

Besides my Play 5 units, I have Polk (good,value-oriented) and PSB (better, higher-end) speakers, hooked up to Sonos Zone Players, amped [[ASIN:B001CROHU4 SONOS CONNECT:AMP Wireless Streaming Music System with Amplifier for Speakers (ZonePlayer120)]]and un-amped [[ASIN:B001CROHX6 SONOS CONNECT Wireless Music Streaming System for Home Theater or Stereo (ZonePlayer90)]]. The Sonos Play 5 definitely holds it's own when comparing streamed music to those set-ups. The Sonos technology makes speaker placement less of an issue than for traditional speakers. Of course the sound is better coming from a higher-powered amp and more-expensive speakers. But that doesn't mean you'll get a poor quality sound from the Play 5. You're just not going to be the man in those old Maxell ads sitting in front of a speaker getting blown away (apologies to those not old enough to remember those ads). Instead, you'll get a very good audio experience.

Sonos has been one of those life-changing products. It allows you to experience so much. It helps you make cool party playlists, even if you're not cool. Never have had a regret.

product_title: Audio Technica Solid Bass
review_headline: Read this before you decide to purchase BEATS STUDIO
review_body:
For those who don't want to read the full details go to the very bottom for short review

DETAILED REVIEW:

First of all, i have compared the two headphones. I USED to own beats studio headphone before I purchased this and all I can say is that the bass itself is not some VIBRATING HEADPHONE NON-SENSE. Let me give you an example. Beats Studio headphones vibrate when you have massive bass songs; however that's all It is good for. Beats headphones are NOT bad headphones. They have very good bass response, and pretty descent mids and highs, but it doesn't have the satisfying audio quality that most audiophiles love. NOW LET'S TALK ABOUT ATH-WS55 SOLID BASS headphone.

These headphones DO NOT VIBRATE WHEN YOU HIT BASS like the beats studio. One thing that is a turn off for many bass headphones are the mids and high response. Think of Mids as MALE'S VOCAL around 3-4khz freq., trumpets, etc. and HIGH AS Female's Vocal that occurs around 7khz freq, treble clef etc, electric guitar (excluding bass guitars), violin or any high sounding instruments. Okay that's out of the way, one thing that's MOSTLY IMPORTANT about any songs are the vocals. Vocals are the KING/QUEEN. Without the presence of Vocals, headphone should be tossed away or sold off of any auction websites/to a friend. Imagine yourself walking into a club or concert and the very first thing you noticed is the vocal presence with a clarity of words and details. This headphone gives you that. Clarity of mids and highs are VERY VERY RESPONSIVE for a headphone that's around 100 dollars. You can't get any better than this. To be honest this headphone should be around 150 dollars from the quality that I've been hearing on these headphones.

NOW THE MOST IMPORTANT PART....THE BASS!!!! Bass sounds full and RICH. It's not some vibrating bass you get from BEATS STUDIO. Let me explain what the bass sounds like. Imagine your head is empty/hollow and having gentle air fill into your head and now your head feels FULL. The bass is almost identical to the music you'd hear from clubs or concerts. It sounds very Full and ALIVE.

Now let's talk about comfort. This headphone has very small round earmuffs/pads and since the whole headphone has aluminum casting and backbone, you could feel a little pressure around your ears. However if you fiddle with the position of the muffs/pads, then it could reduce the pressure around your ear lobes.

Build-quality - IT IS VERY STURDY. Aluminum casting, you could bend the headphone, but it is not likely to break.

ANYWAYS THAT WAS MY REVIEW

SHORT REVIEW:

-Bass is rich and full. DOESN'T VIBRATE, BECAUSE OF DUAL AIR CHAMBER SYSTEM. Mids and highs are very detailed
-build quality is solid, sturdy aluminum casting.
-Value is THE BANG FOR THE BUCK.

review_body: Everyone uses MDF now.  It's because it doesn't resonate like plywood. Plus, MDF is harder on tooling... sparks fly from carbide blades when you're cutting it... that's the carbide coming off your blade.  THEREFORE, unless you're moving the speakers a lot (using them in different venues), MDF is the way to go.  It's sonically \\"dead\\" compared to resonant plywood.  The use of MDF is a choice made not to cut costs -- obviously, Klipsch Heritage speakers are not cheap anyway... and the main cost is in labor, tooling, and components.  The choice is made because MDF sounds better.  Ferraris come with carbon fiber bodies... and some might say \\"that's plastic,\\" but they didn't choose it because it was cheaper than stamped steel.  The same concept applies here, IMO.

product_title: Pyle Home PAMP1000 160 Watt 2 Channel Home Stereo Power Amplifier
review_body:
The Pyle PAMP1000 is working perfectly as a subwoofer amp for an Audiosource 8 inch in wall subwoofer. I have it set up in bridge mode and it is providing plenty of power.

It is connected to my Yamaha RX-V471 by rca cable from the 'subwoofer' out to the line 2 right rca input of the Pyle amp. From there the speaker wires connect to the speaker A Right + and Left - indicated in the manual for use in bridge mode. I set up my 5.1 system using the Yamaha auto set-up. Before I began I turned the Pyle volume for the sub to half (indicated in the Yamaha manual for subwoofer set up). Then I ran the auto-set up. The Yamaha set the level of the subwoofer to +10db. If I find the bass is too much or too little, I turn the Pyle volume for the sub up or down. I've found a little more than half-way is just about perfect.

Auto-on is also working as expected for this amp. When I turn on the TV, the Yamaha turns on then the Pyle turns on a few seconds later and then the bass kicks in. When I power off the TV, the Yamaha turns off and it takes the Pyle about 5 minutes to power down.

This amp was more expensive than a plate amp I was also considering, but this unit fits right in my av cabinet and I can make adjustments easy. I would have put a plate amp in the basement or closet and making adjustments would have been an ordeal. It was worth it to pay more for that convenience. The $84.99 price of this unit seems right on.

For operation, convenience, and price, I give it 5 stars. I wanted this review to provide the information I was looking for when considering this unit as a subwoofer amp.

product_title: Logitech Harmony One Universal Remote with Color Touchscreen (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Harmony One is the one, if you need to restore Harmony in the house.
review_body: Prior to my purchase I read the reviews and really focused on the complaints, there definately was no shortage of them.  I had several friends who loved theirs and I was a little torn after all the product is quite expensive for a remote.  I can definately after my purchase say I was not disappointed in the slightest.  After receiving the product immediately tried to program remote with what little charge it had remaining..... first mistake take the time let it charge fully before attempting to program.  While you are waiting upload/install your software and collect all the model numbers off your equipment (be sure to get them right one number/letter makes a significant difference (as I found out the hard way when it wanted me to manually program my remote and I didn't have the button on my orginal remote it was asking for finally realized my mistake and didn't have to manually program)  I advocate saving in an excel document for later use if neccessary.  I cannot speak to the battery swelling issues although my remote wouldn't take a charge until I removed it(while powered on) and reseated it.  After adding all the devices they all seemed to work very well independently but when they need to work well in conjuction with each other thats where the hiccups began (I suspect this is the reason for most complaints).  It is well worth your time to remedy these in the begining.  For example if you have a digital cable box connected to you're tv through HDMI (in my case)it was important to bring that cable box on first then the TV.  If I changed the order TV would sometimes miss the signal.  Make no mistake, there is a time consuming learning curve particularly for complex setups but after you get it right I was able to hand remote to a \\"technically challenged\\" person and they were able to figure out in a few minutes without any explanation. product_title: CyberPower PFC Compatible Pure Sine Wave Tower UPS
review_body:
I have had the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD UPS in service 24/7 for over 5 months and it has been rock solid. I run two computers on it simultaneously, one running Ubuntu Linux with a Pentium 4 2.8GHZ processor with 2ea 500GB and 1ea 1TB drive and the second an Alienware gaming system running Windows 7 with an Intel i7-3820 4 core processor at 3.6GHZ with 2ea 1TB Seagate drives and an Nvidia GTX 560 TI video card. The CP1500PFCLCD is more than adequate to condition the power of both computers, 22\\" monitor, router and speakers all running simultaneously at moderate load while providing a safe shutdown in the event of a power failure. We have had 3 power failures (we live in a rural area with extremely unstable power) since purchasing this UPS and a graceful shutdown was performed by the UPS each time. The unit's power output level indicator is typically at 1/3 and occasionally 1/2 the output capability of this unit. I deliberately purchased the 900W unit to avoid overtaxing the UPS.

To be fair though I have not run the gaming system at \\"full throttle\\" while the \\"business\\" system is simultaneously banging away at several databases so given the gaming system has a 875W PS and the business system a 380W PS I suppose, and I'm no electrical expert, logically the UPS could be expected to reach or exceed it's limit if both were at maximum power consumption.

OF SPECIAL NOTE: Regarding a \\"line conditioning\\" (pure sine wave) UPS in general. Prior to obtaining this UPS I did without one for years after my APC unit failed. Due to our iffy local public power supply my computers would, on a monthly basis, have strange \\"lock-ups\\", disk crashes and other hardware anomalies. I attributed these failures to the computer gear. Apparently I was wrong because during the time I've owned this UPS I have not had one of these events. Thus especially under such circumstances the line conditioning with this unit has proven to be at least as important as the ability to provide backup power and a clean shut down on power failure.

product_title: Kaito Voyager Pro KA600 Digital Solar/Dynamo AM/FM/LW/SW & NOAA Weather Emergency Radio with Alert & RDS
review_headline: Consumer Emergency radio with the most features
review_body:
The Voyager Pro is a nice radio and not just for emergencies. It also to this date comes with the most features of any Emergency radio I have ever owned. Besides the hand-crank,there is solar power, AC adapter and AA battery options and even charging via your computer's USB port. There is a flashlight and reading light,both which are adequate for what they do.

The radio part is a treat. AM 9 or 10kHz steps,LW (mainly useful in Europe),SW (2300-23000 MHz)and all seven Weatherband channels.

It's all digital readout. Use either tuning dial or keypad entry to get to any station. Store your favorites in to memory presets,5 for LW,10 for AM-MW,50 for SW and FM.

FM comes with an RDS function. If the FM station supports it,the station ID,artist and song being played will show up on the display.

There is a sleep timer (radio shuts off after 90 or less minutes of play),two alarms,snooze and a weather alert which if set will turn on the radio tuned to your local NOAA weather station in case of a emergency.

Nice to have: A temperature display (C or F)/humidity indicator which is accurate when compared against my other thermometers.

Would like to see: A swivel antenna,this one expands expands/collapses straight up.

Caveats: This is basically a home/travel/camping radio. FM and AM reception is fine,you may want to clip on a longwire antenna for shortwave,there are no sideband capabilities. It's a basic receiver,not a dedicated all band portable.

It also can charge a cellphone either by AC adaptor or handcrank. The built-in rechargeable battery should
be disconnected first.

So among the current crop of emergency radios,the Voyager Pro is among the most with features,and should do well when you travel to places where electrical power is spotty.

review_headline: Stunning sound! Difficult for long-term wear
review_body:
I purchased these from a local retailer (Audio Perfection in Minneapolis, MN). Grado is all they carry, so I could have any headphone I wanted, as long it was from Grado :-) Really, they were quite insistent on this point and talked me into a lengthy audition session.

So, I came back to the store with my MacBook Pro (late 2010 model) with NuForce uDac-2 DAC fed by Channel D's Pure Music audio engine and a collection of Apple Lossless tracks (Redbook and high-resolution). I've since upgraded to the asynchronous USB model (which is a surprising improvement - you can read my review of the NuForce uDAC-2SE for details):

[[ASIN:B00688GY6C NuForce Icon uDAC-2 (Red) Special Edition (with Asynchronous USB)]]

The salesman from Audio Perfection in Minneapolis (Eric - a great guy) brought out three Grado models:

1. Prestige Series SR325is Headphones
2. RS-2i
3. RS-1i

Of course, every good salesman knows that the customer will always go for the middle-priced model - which is what I did :-) That aside, I spent about an hour and a half listening to the above headphones with my laptop, while Eric setup a movie for my daughter to watch in another room.

The SR325is cans weren't bad, but they are simply outclassed by the other two models - the difference is immediately obvious and one doesn't need more than a few seconds of listening to pick the winner.

The RS-2i and RS-1i are close in sound quality - both sets have incredible definition, separation of instruments, tight, fast-attacking bass and great sibilance. The clarity of the vocals was something I've never heard before in a headphone. In fact, when friends listen to these, that is usually the comment I hear: \\"...I can really understand the lyrics...\\".

But, as other reviewers have pointed out, the difference just wasn't enough to push me into an additional $200.00 for the RS-1i - so I went for the RS-2i.

This was a few months ago and the headphones sound as great now as they did then - no buyers remorse, whatsoever. However, I've stopped using them at work and went back to my Bose QC-15 cans. For active listening, the Bose models sound like muffled dixie cups - really, it's sad to compare the two, side-by-side. If you are reading this and thinking: \\"...oh, here's another guy bashing Bose...\\", I challenge you to listen and compare with a pair of high-end headphones (Sennheiser, Grado, Audio Technica, whatever).

But I really need the noise canceling at client sites and the Grados are an open air design - all sound comes out and all sound goes in from the surrounding environment. You need to be aware of this if you are going to use these in an office environment for background listening.

Worse, however, is the comfort level - the Grado cans simply hurt after a couple of hours. My ears get sore and the top of my head gets irritated by the headband. The Bose QC-15s are wearable for 8 hours at a time. I've worn these for many overseas flights and wear them for 4 hours at a time while working.

product_title: Pioneer SW-8 100 Watt RMS Subwoofer System (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
I like the design and size of this woofer but I have had a couple problems so far.
I ordered this for $80.00 new and shipped through Newegg on a promo. I'm adding it to my Onkyo Mini-system which I purchased through Amazon and reviewed. I don't feel like I have to have a sub but for the price, why not?
It came in the Pioneer factory box without an overwrap but it arrived in great cosmetic condition, box and all. When I opened it I noticed one minor annoyance, the feet were slightly different heights and caused it to wobble a little on my very flat terrazzo floor. It wobbled about 1/8.\\" I stuck a small felt pad under one of the feet and this solved the wobble. I believe I received a defective sub in a couple ways since, when increasing the bass output level, there was a noticeable buzz that occurred during bassy bumps. Even at low volume levels I could hear it and my wife said,\\"That sounds terrible,\\" from across the room. She is no audio pro, so when she heard it I knew I had a problem. Its almost as if a wire is loose and resting on the speaker.
The build quality seems very solid (despite the problems) for the price and its nicely weighted.

Once I receive my replacement sub I will update again...

3/27/12- The replacement arrived today!

No foot wobble and sounds terrific. Guess I got a bum unit originally, so I'm increasing to 5 stars. Its on less than 1/4 volume level and I set the crossover at less than half up to match the small Onkyo speakers I have. I'm really impressed with the overall build and the sound is great. It's nice to know I have a lot more power to go if I ever need it. For eighty dollars shipped from Newegg I couldn't be more pleased. Even at a little over a hundred this is a deal. There is nothing close in price from what I found. And who wants a 10\\" if you've got little book shelf speakers or other small monitors? Way to go Pioneer.

review_body: I have only had these headphones for a couple of days, but I am already glad I bought them! They arrived on time, and the packaging was not as bad as others have stated at all, and there was not too much so relatively environmentally friendly too!  I bought these because my apple iPod headphones finally gave up and even electrocuted me! The sound of these phillips headphones is noticeable better, though I'm not an expert I definitely can tell there is a difference! I have very small ears, but have had no problems with the earbuds whatsoever as others have mentioned they are uncomfortable. They fit well and comfortably, after a minute I barely notice that they are there at all, and they stay in my ears perfectly whilst I run, where the iPod ones were forever falling from my ears; very much a pain when trying to run!  I do like the colour of them too, it is different and eye-catching without being ghastly to look at, and they look very well-made and professional. The materials are lovely compared to that of the iPod standard ones, with a metal jack piece (i don't know the name, but the bit that holds the jack which enters the device, anyway I'm sure you know what I mean!) which is pleasing to the eye rather than the plastic-y white of apple headphones. The cord is made of fabric which I thought might be strange but I have become very attached to it (not literally!), it works very well and does look good.  Some people have also commented that the tangle-free cord is a joke, but I have so far found it to actually be working quite well. I can pull them out of my bag without having to fiddle around for five minutes trying to un-knot them before leaving the house! Whereas it may be impossible to stop them tangling completely especially if, like me, you throw them around a lot and leave in a bag, they are certainly much better and easier to sort out!  The volume and track control works very well and functions with my latest version of the iPod touch easily. The control maybe slightly too high on the cord for my liking, but is still easy to use, it is in roughly the same place as the iPhone ones have theirs, an is well positioned for use of the microphone easily. It is also in keeping with the lovely design.  I bought these on sale for $20, and would definitely recommend them at this price, especially compared to others on sale for the same price range, far better, a great buy which I am very pleased with!

product_title: Bose SoundLink Bluetooth Wireless Speaker
review_headline: Does not work well with Mac devices.  Terrible UI.
review_body:
I purchased this in September 2011. I use it (or try to use it) with my Macbook Air, my Ipad 2, and my 3G iphone. I've been very exasperated by ongoing problems with the bluetooth connection. First, say, I stream music from my iphone to the soundlink one day, and then try to connect my macbook the next day, the device refuses. I first need to go into my iphone, into the general settings app, and turn disconnect the bluetooth. Only then can I connect the Macbook. If I don't remember which of my devices was last connected to the sounlink, I have to get out both the iphone and the ipad, turn off their bluetooth functions, and then connect the Macbook.

Now, once I have the Macbook Air connected to the speaker, it's only a matter of time before the sound starts breaking up-- stuttering in and out. The support people at Bose claim this is because the Air lacks RAM needed to stream via bluetooth, and suggested i turn off all other apps while using the soundlink. An inconvenient solution, and anyway it doesn't work. Sound still breaks up, even if the only app open is itunes or Chrome.

So at the best of times, this thing is a finicky to use. What makes matters worse is that the device sometimes fails to recognize any device at all. So first I've got t go through the rigamarole described above-- taking out all my devices and switching off bluetooth. Then when that fails, I have to do a hard reset on the sounlink itself, and set up the device pairing anew. I should mention as well that the soundlink's user interface is as unintuitive as can be. To pair a device, you have to hold down the bluetooth button for 5 seconds, and wait for a light to start blinking slowly. If it's blinking more quickly, that signals something else (can't remember what) and the pairing won't work. If you want to reinstall a device you need to hold the button for 10 seconds, and await another blinking pattern. This is single purpose device. I shouldn't need to consult the instruction manual on a monthly basis for a refresher on this code of button-pressing-times and blinking lights.

On a regular basis, I try to turn on a little music while doing chores, and find myself tinkering with this device for longer than the duration of the chore itself. And once I manage to get it connected, it's just a matter of time before the signal starts breaking up. The support people at Bose are nice, but I have to recommend against buying this device if you use Mac devices. It's just a way way way too much of an annoyance.

product_title: ClearStream 5 Indoor/Outdoor HDTV Antenna - 65 Mile Range
review_body:
My wife and I recently decided to drop our satellite TV service. We just didn't feel like we were watching $90/month worth of television. We found a Tivo package deal that came with a Clearstream2 antenna, both for $99. I ordered the Clearstream5 antenna from Amazon to add VHF coverage as the **CS2 only receives UHF channels**. It was on my porch the 2nd day after I ordered it.

I have attached the two antennae to a homemade \\"mast\\" (2x2 wooden beam) in the attic. We now have CBS, ABC, NBC plus Fox and the CW all in crystal clear HD. We also get several other independent stations, about 12 channels/subchannels altogether. A couple of the smaller indies aren't as high in quality but we won't watch those much anyway. I think I may be able to adjust the antenna mast to get at least 1 or 2 more.

We live about 30 miles south of most of the broadcast towers in Atlanta. It's mostly flat in the area but we live in a \\"dip\\" in the surrounding terrain so I was pleasantly surprised with the quality of the picture, on the major channels it's better than we got with satellite!

The hardware (Tivo box, both antennae, extra cabling) cost a total of about $250. We will recoup that amount in less than 3 months by dropping Satellite. Adding Netflix, Hulu Plus, AND Amazon Prime cost only a little over $22/month for all three. This was well worth the investment.

product_title: Optical Quantum 6X 50GB BD-R DL Double Layer White Inkjet Hub Printable - 10 pcs
review_headline: Best BD-R DL Buy Out There!
review_body: I have been using these DL BDR's for quite awhile now and have never had a problem, NEVER! (Knock on wood that this continues to be the case) But these CMCMAG 50GB Disc's are just excellent in the White Inkjet version or the Silver Logo version. I have burned 8 ten packs without a failure at 8x using an LG WH12LS38 BD-RE with current firmware. To the person who is having the \\"UNRECOGNIZED\\" problem with his \\"High-End\\" PC's, sounds like the problem isn't the disc's, I would bet Dollars to Doughnuts its your firmware being in need of updating. You need to go into your Control Panel, then to Device Manager, then DVD/CD Drives and locate in the drop-down your BD-RE Drive, (Not BD-Rom), then determine the manufacturer and under properties get your current Driver identification and at the website of the maker download the current Driver and install it. There will be a download called \\"Firmware\\" which will come with a utility that will identify your current firmware version and assist in the \\"Flashing\\" process of the BD-RE Drive. Note: once you start the Flash process be patient, don't touch ANYTHING on the machine until it reboots or restarts the application/utility; this process sometimes takes quite awhile to complete and interrupting it can ruin your device. Hope this helps. Dan

product_title: Kinivo Mini Portable Speaker with Rechargeable Battery and Enhanced Bass Resonator
review_body:
I've had this for a couple of weeks now and I love it. I purchased it because I like to listen to music from my phone at work, and the volume on my phone only goes up and down like 5 notches, so the volume I prefer is in between two settings, one of which is too quiet and the other too loud so I wanted a speaker that had its own volume adjustment that could provide a wider range of volume and this one works great - it has a really wide range of volumes without too much of a change from one volume setting to another so you can get just the right amount of sound for whatever situation you're in. The music also sounds really great for such a small speaker.

Also, it is not at all difficult to turn this on - I'm not sure why other reviewers are having trouble with it. While it's not immediately clear where the power button is (the power sybmol is on the black part but the actual button is on the red part right underneath it, same with the volume buttons) once you figure out where it is, it's very easy to turn on. There is a clear audible and tactile \\"click\\" when you press on the power button (and the volume buttons on the other side) and it's very easy to tell if the speaker is on or off because when it's on the blue light is on and when it's off it's not. So you just have to press it and hold it and once the blue light comes on, it's on and vice versa for when you're turning it off. I have no idea what the other reviewers are saying when they say they can't tell if the speaker is on or not.

One negative of this speaker though is how short the cord is. It works fine for me because I just have my phone right next to it, but if I wanted to plug it into my desktop at work, it would be too short. The cord is only about 2 ft long. And then, the USB cord for charging (they're actually one cord split in two, not two cords) is only about 5 inches long, which is very annoying when trying to charge it, but it's a small annoyance for me although it might matter a lot more to someone else. Also, one charge has lasted me two weeks now of daily use (on a low volume so it might not last as long on a high volume, but still, it's pretty good).

product_title: Kinivo 501BN Premium 5 port High speed HDMI switch with IR wireless remote and AC Power adapter - supports 3D, 1080p
review_body: I bought this switch because I have an older (6 years or so) plasma tv with only one HDMI input, and I now have multiple gadgets I want to plug in through that port.  After using this switch now for a couple of months, I'm pretty satisfied with it.  I don't notice any loss of picture or sound quality using it, and the auto-switch generally works properly when you first turn a new device on.  It does have a couple of small quirks that I think deserve mention.  First, the auto-switch feature that switches to the device most recently turned on mostly works (for instance, when I turn my Xbox on, it switches to that), but when I then turn the Xbox off I often have to manually switch it back to the cable box to get the tv feed to show up on the screen.  Second, if I turn the Xbox on before the tv, for some reason the sound sometimes doesn't work.  If I turn the Xbox and tv off after that, and turn the tv on first and the Xbox on second, the sound will work fine.  So neither one of these is really a problem, but small quirks that keep the device from performing flawlessly.  It has more ports than I think I'll ever need, which is a nice bonus.  And the price point is pretty fair.  So all in all I'm pretty satisfied with this produce.

product_title: 3 Pairs, Black - fits extra small to small ears - "Squish Fit" memory foam earphone cushions by Earphones Plus - Fits most earbud style earphones (see compatibility details and other available sizes in details below)
review_body:
I prefer noise-isolating to noise-canceling head/earphones, because I find the former to sound better. I wondered once or twice why a company hadn't produces an earphone cushion from the material found in simple foam earplugs -- the kind that slowly returns to form after being compressed. These cushions from Earphones Plus fit the bill, and I like them very much.

I easily put them on my Sony EX-series earphones. Roll the pad/stem in your fingers, place in your ear, and wait a few seconds while the foam expands. I find them to isolate sound as well or better than do silicone cushions, attract less dirt, and be more comfortable. They fit and stay in my ears very well, and I guess I have medium/small ear-holes, because I usually use the smaller-sized cushions that come with earphones.

product_title: Monoprice 100966 Digital Optical TOSLink Splitter Adapter
review_headline: Not perfect, but does what I needed for very little cost
review_body:
I needed to split the audio from a computer to 2 different receivers. The close run was on a 6ft cable and worked flawlessly. The longer run was on a 30ft cable (very low quality cable) and it was finicky.

I found the splitter does not have \\"keyed\\" jacks like toslink cables do, so you can plug the cable in 2 ways. Even though the signal was passing through on the long cable (I could see the red light at the end) it just wasn't strong enough for the receiver to pick up. I unplugged the cable at the splitter, rotated it 180 deg, and plugged it back in - it then worked great.

On that audio run the sound does cut out/flicker once in a while. It's not bad, and it doesn't bother me much as it's only for music - not a movie. I thought it could be due to my old low quality toslink cable but I did see another reviewer mention they have the same issue. Maybe it's the splitter, or maybe the combination of the splitter and a low quality cable. I have not replaced the long cable so I don't know.

I would probably rate this 3 stars, but I would have happily paid $40 or more to split the audio, so I'm giving a bonus star for the $4 price.

product_title: AKG Acoustics K550 Closed-Back Reference Headphones
review_body:
I sampled a pair of these at J&R Electronics in New York City. I only had my mobile phone with a few mp3 on it. Prior to listening to these at the store, I had sampled a myriad of other cans including Senheisers, Denons, and more... I recall that as soon as I had dawned these headphones and played some music through them; I had noticed that the sound was just right. It was light, unforced, and had a just-there feeling on every track. What's more, I knew if they sounded that good with my mobile phone and a portable amp, then they were going to sound even better when driven with better equipment.
What I did notice though, is that they do not like any equalization put through them. I was tooling my sound card to put out more bass, less midrange and other wonderful permutations of sound settings, but they really insisted on sounding their best at a flat setting. Don't get me wrong, the bass is there, IF it is there -- never overstated or booming, just natural!
My overall impression of the sound is it lends to neutrality, lightness and an over all airy feel; it also sparkles with details, but with just enough warmth. Great set! I feel I really got lucky to get this pair, because, I went in to buy the Denons 2000, and while these don't pump out as much bass, I do believe that overall they sound better.

product_title: Logitech Harmony 900 Rechargeable Remote with Color Touch Screen (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body: I owned two Harmony 659 remotes over the last five years or so, and they were excellent, albeit not very durable. When the last one finally stopped working last month, I upgraded to the Harmony 900. The 900 looks and feels a lot more solid and is more ergonomic, including more buttons to cater for newer cable boxes, Bluray players and the like. And the 900 is certainly a lot more attractive in appearance.  The color touch screen is a nice addition too, and I really like the charging dock - no more hunting around for batteries in the middle of a show like I used to with the 659.   The software used to set up the remote has remained largely the same over the last few years: functional but with a rather tired and quirky user interface and workflow. Once used to it, though, it works well enough, and I have not had any real problems setting up my remotes in the past, including the 900. Yes, you cannot migrate your old remote settings to the 900, and apparently the software is not compatible with current versions of Mac OS, but neither of these were issues for me. I got the 900 up and running in about an hour.   The RF feature, which was the primary reason for getting the 900, works very well in my setup. I did have to use one of the included mini blasters on the second shelf of my media cabinet, but setting it up was a breeze. Everything except the TV is behind closed doors and within the 30ft or so range that I've tried, it works flawlessly. And I like the fact that the RF is assigned to devices from the remote itself, so no need to program the RF unit separately.  Time will tell how durable the 900 is, but so far I'm impressed. For the current price I think it is an excellent value.

review_headline: Conflicted review is both four stars and one star!
review_body: Okay, here is the explanation for that somewhat confusing review title.  I purchased this very unit about a year ago through Amazon for my living room home theater and have had nothing but a   great experience with it.  The set up was a breeze, connecting was flawless and the sound and overall performance has been  exemplary.  Needless to say, when I was setting up a home theater in the basement, I figured I would refer to the one review I could   trust the most which would be my own. After running solidly for three to four hours on   the first day, I turned it on the second day only to have a blinking blue light and an \\"Amp Overheat\\"warning greet me.  Mind you,   the receiver was ice cold and had not been running for about 20 hours.  Still, after unplugging, resetting, etc., it would not   turn on and the blinking blue light was all I was getting.  Just for clarification, the AV stand I had it in is almost completely open air with the shelves exposed almost all the way around   so ventilation could not have been an issue.  After investigating some reviews on Amazon, I saw the problem I had being reported by other users.  Their level of success  getting it fixed convinced me that I should probably consider myself lucky with the fist receiver and switch to another  brand for the second.  Again, if it works, it is awesome, but, if it doesn't...well, you get the idea.

product_title: Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10 Noise Isolating Earphones
review_body: I have had these headphones for about 11 months now and use them every day at school, or at the gym. I put them in their case every time I am not using them, and toss them in my backpack, and they have held up very well with no loss in quality. I did add some after market cables since I have read horror stories about the stock cables breaking. I would rate the audio quality in these headphones as excellent, and I do not regret for a second dishing out the extra bucks for a set of quality IEMs. They are great for listening to a wide range of music aside from heavy bass music; however, if you are looking for base IEMs you should look at the higher end monster turbines, a good set of full size cans, or actual speakers and a sub-woofer. It is also important to note that the music quality of most IEMs is influenced by the type of ear tip, as well as the material it is made out of as there is notable difference in the music signature between using gel based ear tips and foam. The foam ear tips are excellent, but do truncate some of the bass. It is very important to have a good seal between the IEM and your ear for optimum music quality. If you do buy these make sure to have all your portable music from good sources, and in the best quality format such as flac or some other lossless format, and get ready to hear some tight bass, excellent mids and crisp highs. Thanks ultimate ears for the great product!

product_title: SPIN-CLEAN - COMPLETE RECORD WASHER SYSTEM Mk2 (PKG)
review_body: I purchased a Spin-clean primarily to clean some old shellac 78s that I wished to do some restoration work and then digitize.  I was concerned that the water would harm the shellac surface, but the records came out clean with no harm to the records, and they were dry shortly after using the cotton cloths that came with the spin-clean.   There is nothing in the spin-clean process that could scratch vinyl records, unless there was hard grit on already on the record surface.  I would suggest that visible surface dirt be brushed off with a soft-bristled brush before immersing the record in the Spin-clean.  I also cleaned a couple of 60-year-old home-recording discs. These discs have a very soft surface, and any grit on them could cause some real damage.  There was already some visible and audible damage to the discs, and I can't say for sure that the spin-clean had actually added to damage already present.  As for being overpriced, the price is high for what you get, but keep in mind that the high cost of the dies used to mold the parts must be amortized over the number actually sold, and this is a limited-volume market. Also, dies wear, and need tweaking and eventual replacement.  I am happy with my Spin-clean.

product_title: Sony S-544 8 GB Walkman Video MP3 Player (Violet)
review_body: [This is a long review, but it is comprehensive.]  All right, so I got this a couple months ago and I think it's time to write up a review. It was a replacement to my Sansa Fuze, which was pretty unreliable and broke often (had to get replacements every couple months).  PROS:  -Sound quality is great, slightly better than the Fuze I had. Now I know a lot of people just use their phones to listen to music, but once you've tasted the Walkman you won't go back. The phone I compared it against, the Nexus 1 (a high-end phone, currently $400), was much worse. Trust me, you need an mp3 player (and not an iPod, sound quality is also lacking there).  -Interface is easy to navigate and intuitive.  -Speakers are handy when you can't use earbuds (e.g. when you need to be able to hear ambient noise, in the bathroom, etc). Their volume and quality are impressive but not amazing.  -Lightweight and portable.  -Its drag-and-drop music download system is really nice.  -Hard volume buttons are useful for control of the player while it's in your pocket.  -Screen is large enough to use efficiently.  -Software of the player is so far flawless. The delay in between songs is very small (.2 sec?).  -Appearance is pleasing.  CONS:  -You can't delete songs directly off the player.  -Battery life is okay, not as good as my Sansa Fuze.  -If you want to see the total length of the song, you need to go onto Options - Detailed Information to view that. The only thing that is given (track length-wise) on the playing screen is the amount of time into the song you are.  -Playlists can not be set up on the player. You need to create the playlist on your computer then paste it into the player's \\"playlists\\" folder.  -Construction is kinda flimsy and slippery. Buttons are also not great and sometimes don't snap back up after you've pressed them (albeit this has only occurred on one button, the Options button, the small circular one on the right). Can be annoying.  -Some more contour for the frontal buttons would be nice. Sometimes it's even hard to use the buttons when you're looking at the player.  -The playlist's master volume could be a little higher.  -Screen gets tiny scratches on it even with gentle care, but hey don't they all.  -If you try and skip back to the previous song and you're 1 second or more into the song currently playing, the skip will only take you back to the beginning of the song (if you're 1 second into the song and skip back, you'll go to 0 sec). Personally I'd like the cutoff to be somewhere around 3 seconds.  ---  Well I think that sums it up pretty well. You might be wondering at my 5-star rating and then recalling my rather long list of complaints, but they're petty really. As you might have realized sound quality is what I really had in mind here, and the tiny little annoyances this player came with didn't make me waver. I got what I wanted.  My more detailed rating is a 4.5/5, but seeing as I have to choose between a 4 and a 5, I would give it a 5. Thanks Sony! product_title: Nuforce ICON-HDP-SILVER High Performance Digital to Analog Converter, Headphone Amp and Pre Amplifier (Silver) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Great Sound, Not So Great Build Quality
review_body: I have used the HDP as a desktop hub for all my computer-based listening for about six months. Its connections and footprint made it the most suitable contender for a high-quality interface to sit on a desktop without taking up too much space. I have it connected to a MacBook Pro and a set of AudioEngine 2 speakers. I use a pair of Sennheiser 535's and Beyerdynamic DT 880' 600 ohm as my primary headphone inputs. All in all, the fidelity of the HDP is excellent given its price point and its size. I own a UDAC2, which is a wonderful and tiny addition to any computer-based music set-up, and the HDP is much better in its sound reproduction. However, my primary reason for giving this device three stars is its build quality, and second, its relatively low power.  At first, the unit appears very well made, with a brushed aluminum cover and solid knobs. However, I often use the device in a darkened environment, and I noticed that light from the internals was leaking from the right side of the faceplate. Upon closer inspection, I could see that the front plate did not align properly with the aluminum case. Moreover, as others have pointed out, the unit stays on, even when the power is turned off. When I powered the unit down, an internal red light came on, and it was clearly visible through the gap in the faceplate. I contacted NuForce service, and they agreed to send out a new unit, but only after they had received my faulty unit. I complied, and had to go without desktop audio for ten days, which is an annoyance, since I use my audio setup for music creation as well as listening. When the second unit arrived, I was dismayed to find that the light bleed was even worse. Back on the phone to customer support, who this time agreed to send me yet a third unit. Guess what? Same problem with the third unit. According to the factory, this known defect is \\"within the factory tolerances\\" of this Taiwan-made unit. The Icon HDP that I own does not have this problem.  The other area ofconcern is the lack of power when it comes to driving high-impedance phones like the DT880's. The unit is a preamp for external speakers, so it either requires active monitors or an amp in the chain. But for headphone use, this device is billed as a Class A amplifier. I don't listen to music that loudly, and I often listen to demanding classical music. There is no doubt that the HDP reproduces sound very well, but it takes turning the volume to well past 3 o'clock on the rotary dial to get the music to that level where it \\"fills\\" the cans. For low impedance phones, this is not an issue, but for high impedance cans such as the DT 880's and others of its caliber, it is a major issue. Even at high volume, I never have the sense that the unit is really bringing out the best that the cans can offer.  While at that level the amplification is sufficient, there is a sense that the unit is really straining. I had a Fio E9 headphone amp for a short period of time, and though a different beast altogether, it handled the impedance of the DT880's with nary a hiccup. Given that the HDP bills itself as an audiophile-grade headphone amp (and one of the reasons I invested in it), and that the company states that it can handle the most demanding headphones, its lack of power is surprising and off putting.  I often get the feeling as I listen to one of my mixes or a demanding piece of music that it is struggling to keep up.   I gave serious thought to returning the third unit, primarily because I believe that a device that bills itself as audiophile quality and costs $450 ought to be constructed sufficiently well so that odd lights and gaps don't reveal themselves. In the end, I kept the unit, primarily because the sound quality is excellent, and primarily because I could not find another device at this price that does what the HDP does in terms of its simple interface and useful connectivity. The combination of its headphone amp quality (though underpowered), its DAC for computer-based applications, and its high quality preamp ultimately compelled me to keep it. Just barely.

product_title: Coby KCD150 Under-the-Cabinet CD Player with AM/FM Radio (Silver) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: NO Documentation, CD Player doesn't work, and Coby's warranty policy SUCKS!
review_body: I thought I was getting a good deal, as these devices seem to be going out of style.  I was afraid of the bad reviews so far, but I decided to take the risk.  I'm writing this to help you understand that you don't need to go through the same hassle as I went through.  For starters, there was NO documentation in the box.  No papers, no instructions, no \\"Register for Warranty\\" postcard, no \\"Safety Disclaimers\\", no user manual, no installation diagram to help drill holes in the right location.  There was nothing to read, except for the words printed on the box and the actual device!!  So, I made my own installation instructions (see below).  Unfortunately, I didn't test the device before installing it!  Don't be the fool I was!  Test your device before installing!  Once it was installed, it took a lot more effort to use the device than I expected.  Its user interface is very poorly designed.  Its almost like they took a dual alarm clock radio and CD player, and just redid the housing to make an under the cabinet device.  The two alarms could be handy if you need multiple timers in the kitchen, but I wasn't impressed.  I agree with another review, in that the radio is a pain to tune.  After a few minutes I finally realized how the two knobs (volume and tuning) worked, so that I knew where they started and stopped, so that I could turn them to the desired locations.  The tuning and volume knobs are not easy to grip (how many decades have we been making these kinds of knobs for??)  The radio sounded fine, once you figured out how to tune it.  The CD player DID NOT WORK.  Since this is what my wife wanted the most (for her Christmas present), this is the most important reason why I rated this item 1 out of 5 stars.  I put the CD in, and after 20-40 seconds of waiting (no vibration nor sound of the CD spinning up), the display simply said \\"no\\".  Pressing the \\"CD Info\\" button (not sure why any CD player has such a button and I didn't have a user manual to explain this), it would just say \\"no\\" again.  When I pressed the CD eject button, the CD was is the same place as when I put it in (it had not been turned).  I repeated this 5-10 times with different CDs, all known to be good, and got the same exact result every time.  I went to Coby's website ([...]) to see if there was an easy way to get a replacement.  I almost snorted when I was reading their warranty fulfillment requirements.  Not only do you have to ship it to the manufacturer (third of five required steps), you also have to include a money order for the return shipping (step 4 of 5).  Thats right, if you buy this, and it does not work, and you want to send it back to the manufacturer to have some warranty replacement/repair work done, you have to: 1. Pay all shipping costs to get the item to Coby, 2. You ALSO have to pay to have it shipped back to you.  This is the other reason why I rated this item 1 out of 5 stars.  Needless to say, I simply returned this item to AMAZON (which was very easy) and wrote this review shortly after printing the return claims.  Obviously, I will never NEVER buy anything with the brand name of COBY again.  BTW, Coby is short for Cowboy (according to wikipedia).  How much do you really want a Cowboy engineering/designing your electronic appliances, only to have them mass-manufactured in China?  Just in case anybody still wants to buy this device, and it didn't come with a drilling diagram, here is what I did:  I had to make my own drill guide by taping two pieces of paper together (one isn't long enough), taping it to the radio on the top, and then using a pencil with lots of back/forth motion over the circles to get outlines of where the circles were, marked cross hairs through the circles, and then transferred that to my cabinet, and drilled the holes.  My cabinet has a trim on the bottom, and the radio did include a mounting kit that can mount to several different distances, for some minor differences in trim.  My trim is about 1/2\\"-3/4\\" (I'm notgoing to measure it...  I was very happy with the mounting kit, as it worked great for my cabinet.  Don't worry about being overly accurate, as the distance of the bolts between the cabinet and the radio allows for a greater margin of error.

review_headline: Great box except for WiFi receiver
review_body: I've had the Squeezebox for almost 2 years now.  Sound is excellent for a table top radio.  User interface is intuitive and complete.  I use it with SqueezeNetwork, but I've never used it with SqueezeCenter.  However I have been using it most of the time on a WiFi, and it frequently stops, stuck in buffering mode.  As it has gotten older this problem seems to be getting worse.  Finally I lost patience and started researching to find the cause of this problem.  I looked at the Logitech support web site and saw that several other people have had similar problems.  Finally I ran across a discussion thread entry saying that WiFi radios in most internet radios are relatively weak.  (I had dismissed this potential cause earlier because my problem seemed to be worse with only a few stations.)  I decided to connect my SqueezeBox to the network using a LAN cable, and voila, my buffering problems disappeared.  My SqueezeBox is about 35 feet away from the WiFi router, through 3 walls.  So be careful--if you're depending on WiFi connectivity for your internet radio, you may be disappointed with SqueezeBox (and quite possibly other internet radios too).

product_title: Koss Pro-4AA Studio Quality Headphones
review_body: I went through countless pairs of earbuds before finally deciding they were uncomfortable and made all my music sound like it was playing through a tin can. Since then I've broken 4-5 pairs of over-the-ear headphones, and this year I decided enough was enough. I spent a little under $100 on a pair of Koss Pro-4AA over-ear headphones plus a Grado adapter in October and haven't looked back. If it ever does break or fail in some way, Koss has a lifetime guarantee for all of their headphones, which is what really sold me on buying Koss. If in 20 years I get an electrical short listening to my old Animal Collective albums, all I have to do is send the headphones back to them along with $9 to cover the return shipping costs and Koss will repair or replace them.  A little bit about the audio quality:   Straight out of the box, they were playing acoustic music beautifully. There were some issues at the beginning with fake/synthetic sounding bass coming through as dull and muted. After making a point to burn them/break them in overnight with bass-heavy recordings, the bass comes in loud and clear. I'd like to note that I don't consider this a design flaw, as a burn in/break in period is normal for most high-quality headphones like these.  As far as the build quality:   These headphones are built to withstand a bomb, made with thick steel, heavy-duty plastic and durable foam rubber. These suckers seal in the music NO PROBLEM. If I put them on and don't play music, I can hardly hear myself talk. I could see this being both a positive and a negative, depending on what you want to use them for.  I've read some other people saying they feel heavy on the head, but I never noticed any heaviness or strain on my neck or anything. I did notice that they felt a little tight on my head at first, and that after a few hours the sides of my head ached a bit. This was easy to fix: I put them on a coffee can and put on a looping playlist of bass-heavy recordings, and left it overnight. Thissolved the tightness in a couple of days, and it solved the bass problems in a few weeks.  A few caveats:   These babies are not super portable by any means. They're bulky, and they weight almost 2 pounds. If you want them for home listening, which is mainly what I use them for, this shouldn't be a problem. If you commute and carry a backpack, this also shouldn't be a problem. If you're looking for something to throw into your pocket, these are not it.  Like I said before, they're bulky. They make you look like an air traffic controller or a helicopter pilot. These headphones are a replica of a model that Koss made in the 70s, and it shows. I like the retro design, although God only knows why they decided to color it like baby vomit, but they're pretty dorky looking by modern standards.  You need to buy an 1/8\\" adapter to plug it into computers and mp3 players.  Lastly, if you're not willing to put in the time to break them in overnight, you'll have to suffer through about 50 hours of muted bass before they loosen up.  TL;DR:   I wish I bought these 6 or 7 years ago instead of going through a dozen pairs of other headphones. They look dumb, they're big and heavy, and they need to be broken in, but they sound great, and they'll last long enough to make your grandkids look like nerds.

product_title: C&E HDMI Splitter Amplifier
review_body: Running a Vista Media Center box to monitors upstairs and downstairs, Vista balks when trying to watch TV on a different monitor (HDCP digital rights error). Extremely complicated to change the primary monitor. Best solution would probably be to install Windows 7 and take advantage of its Windows + P key combination to cycle through local and remote monitors, but I tried this splitter first, with each monitor playing off the same HDMI output instead of two different (HDMI and DVI) independent outputs. The Windows 7 idea is probably more versatile, but I won't ever need the ability to run different things on each monitor - just my recorded TV.  It works, but once in a while Vista will get confused and reset itself to 800x600. Oddly, it seems to work exactly the same way with and without the external power supply - I had a terrible picture on the downstairs monitor and figured I was losing signal through the long run so I reconnected the power supply to no avail. It turned out to be the monitor's fault, unable to recognize that it was a PC signal, and when I connected the splitter to the computer's DVI output through a DVI-HDMI adapter the problem was instantly fixed regardless of whether or not the splitter was plugged into power. On the other hand, my living room monitor always had an intermittent problem \\"waking up\\" when the PC resumed and that issue appears to have gone away, as the splitter seems to \\"wake up\\" the monitor when the monitor is turned on - you can see the splitter's LEDs blinking as it tries to lock onto the monitor.

review_body:
This is an excellent, though pricey, charger. Simply put, its does the job reliably for me, every single time, and with the confidence I have in La Cross' reputation -- my family has used their products for probably 20 years -- the decision to purchase it was easy.

I considered cheaper, less capable chargers (such as BC700, a good, basic charger), but after thorough research, decided that the old but annoying adage, \\"you get what you pay for,\\" which doesn't always hold true of course -- is applicable here. I was tempted by the lower price of the BC700, for example, but decided I wanted the extra features, and upgraded internal electronics, of the BC1000 in lieu of the junior BC700. I was also swayed by the weight of NLee The Engineer's review of the BC700, where he implies that the BC700 is handicapped vis-a-vis the BC900/BC9009/BC1000. And since the BC1000 has more charging-rate headroom, the internal electronics are probably superior overall.

For a moment, I was also tempted by the Maha-brand charger. I use Maha's low self-discharge batteries(IMEDION/Power Ex), which greatly outperform Sanyo newer eneloops for my applications, so I'm partial to their brand), but felt the quirks in the Maha battery charger's interface would be palpable for my uses, and any potential quality difference wouldn't be palpable.

All in all, if you want the best of the best, my advice is to go with the BC1000. I can't imagine anyone being disappointed with this well conceived and engineered battery charger.
