product_title: Coby CVE92 Isolation Stereo Earphones
review_body: This is truly a woeful product. My wife got a pair; first time I tried them on I thought they fit a little awkwardly but once you jam it in your ear, I got some decent bass and mids for earbuds. Nothing to write home about, but better than I expected for six bucks' worth of earbuds. So I ordered a pair for myself at work. Would that it were I had tried them out for more than ten seconds before doing so.  My wife subsequently found that they did not stay in her ear when she jogs, so she bequeathed this pair to me and used a different, even cheaper pair we have. Sound quality is not important to her. So I've been using these at work.  1, they are uncomfortable unless you barely hang them in your ear. In that case they don't really stay in and they sound TERRIBLE. You really do have to wedge this \\"sound tube\\" deep into your ear to get any of the bass. At that point, they become pretty darned uncomfortable. I'm not sure the human ear can accommodate these things in such a way that you can hear any of the 'good sound'.   2, the sound. It's mediocre if you jam them in your ear, poor if you just kind of let it sit loosely in your ear. But the sound quality is abysmal. I've tried them with several computers and three MP3 players and it essentially sounds like either they can't handle the typical headphone jack's power rating, or the drivers are blown. I get this crackly sound from treble and a kind of 'bleed' of bass, exactly as you'd hear if you put a pair of speakers that can only handle 100 watts on a 500W amp, or if you had blown a woofer. All the same computers / MP3 players obviously sound great with a pair of normal headphones. Also, the distortion is present even at very low volumes, which leads me to believe that it is a manufacturing defect and not just power handling. This is pretty frustrating, as the things are less than 2 weeks old and neither my wife nor I listen to music very loud at all.  I may crack open the second pair I ordered just to see if this firstpair is just defective, but what a major failure of an ostensibly very simple product. If you're looking for something that can be comfortable and provide decent bass, this is not it. If you don't want all of your favorite music to be completely washed out with distortion, these won't help you.   ==========  Update: I opened the second pair to find pretty comparable, if perhaps slightly improved performance. It may or may not be a simple perception rather than reality. However, I do have a new baseline for comparison: Skullcandy ink'd earbuds. They absolutely blow these earbuds out of the water.  The Coby earbuds receive a lot of very positive reviews, but I notice one very consistent feature of every positive review: every last one of these fails to make a comparison to competitive products (major brand earbuds under $10). They compare them to very old earbuds; earbuds that came with a cheap MP3 player (worth about 10 cents?); old headphones. All the reviews that contain some reference to comparable, current products are pretty poor. Before you go off and buy these and think you're getting a bargain, do some reading and take that for what it is.  I would absolutely recommend the Skullcandy ink'd over these. The price difference isn't even worth mentioning. The skullcandy earbuds are a good product; these are not. I also just purchased a pair of JBuds J5 earbuds and found them to be clearly superior to Coby, but still inferior to the Skullcandy ink'd. Point being, these Coby earbuds really are at the very bottom of the totem pole.  Go here and buy:   [...]

review_headline: So EASY I Didn't Even Need the Install Disc
review_body: 1. Plugged in power cord and cat5 cable into back of Zoneplayer.  2. Downloaded the iPhone controller app.  3. Ran the iPhone app and followed easy step-by-step instructions to join the iPhone controller to the Zoneplayer (press mute and volume up simultaneously), entered the music share path and username/password into the iPhone controller, and indexed the music files which took a few minutes for my very large music library. That was it! I was up and running!  Need a dedicated controller for the whole family to use (instead of handing over your phone) and don't want to shell out $350 for the Sonos CR500 controller? Buy an iTouch for $200, turn it in a dedicated controller using the free app above, and now you've just saved $150 and gained a whole lot more utility (games & apps) out of the iTouch to boot.  For those that spend hours obsessing over their music tags (metadata), another great thing about the Sonos solution rather than going with DLNA or DAAP solutions is that Sonos seems make use of the ALBUM ARTIST tag. So when you browse by artists, you don't get a bunch of ARTIST and then ARTIST/CAMEO_ARTISTS. That means when you browse by ARTIST, those songs by ARTIST/CAMEO_ARTISTS are also properly included with the originating album rather than separated into its own album. Track numbers are also respected, when browsing and playing back, which is more than I can say for the few DLNA and DAAP solutions I've tried. Embedded album art also displays correctly for the most part, but I do have a few that aren't showing for some reason within the iPhone controller app leaving me mystified.  The only thing lacking is better sound spatialization. To achieve that I may need to buy another Zoneplayer and use the controller app to dedicate one Zoneplayer to the left channel and another to the right channel. Expensive, but until then, the sound quality of the lone Zoneplayer suits my bedroom just fine.  I am also a Verizon FIOS subscriber so I'm not sure what happened to theother reviewer. My modem is an Actiontec MI424WR-GEN2 version F. UPnP is turned on. Unless you hardwire at least one Zoneplayer with a cat5 cable plugged in directly to the back, you will also need [[ASIN:B000X1TS54 Sonos Bridge Instant Setup Solution For Sonos Wireless Network (BR100)]] connected directly to your router to allow you the freedom of moving your Zoneplayer anywhere in the household with a power outlet.

review_headline: If you're thinking about Bose, give these a listen
review_body:
I've never listened to headphones much. As a young man, I always had a pair around for late night listening or when my neighbor might complain. Ten or twelve years ago, I acquired a pair of `phones as a gift from Sharper Image. I was travelling a lot in those days and had my first MP3 player, so those noise cancelling headphones came in handy. They weren't sonically great but they did work well keeping airplane noise out. During my last trip I noticed the plastic leather on the cups started flaking off. While they still work, I figured it was time to get some new gear. I don't travel as much as I used to so I broadened my search beyond noise cancelling types. I listen to a lot of music of different genres and from a variety of sources including vinyl. But it's almost always on traditional equipment (amps, speakers and source component).

I didn't know too much about headphones so did a lot of research and was surprised at what I learned. There are many styles and a range of prices so my first order of business was deciding what my price point was. This will differ with individuals obviously but like most people I'm looking for that magical sweet spot. The style differences will matter in terms of personal comfort, isolation and to a lesser extent, sound quality. If found excellent sound quality from all styles. Here are a few style choices: around the ear, on the ear and in the ear. I was not interested in the in the ear type. Although these can sound excellent and obviously travel well, I find them uncomfortable to wear. In addition I'm not a fan of the cord having to attach to each \\"earplug\\". This is also a consideration for the larger headphones. There are styles that have a cord attached to each \\"can\\" which creates a \\"Y\\" connection to the plug. I find this annoying as well as the cord tends to tickle the cheek if ever so gently. While on this particular point, note that there are also cords that are permanently connected to some headphones and others that are removable. I find removable cords a nice convenience for storage and travel. Some phones even have different lengths and types of cords. For example, many headphones now have cords that work well with i-Pods.

In addition to the types or styles of headphones I considered, my focus was on the ear and around the ear. Within those categories there are additional types. One is closed back which tend to keep the sound in your ears and keeps you somewhat closed off your surroundings. The open back allows sound to escape and enter but also provides an aural component that can improve the sound. Then there are the noise cancelling varieties which essentially manage to block external sound using different methods, all of which generally require the use some form of battery.

I had already tried several headphones in retail stores including the pricy but beautiful B & W P-5, Beats and Skull Candy among them. I liked the P-5's but found them uncomfortable after a while. They are the on the ear type but they put too much pressure on my head and ears. I also tried the Phiaton MS 400 (see my review). After additional analysis and research, I decided to try out 3 models. They were the AKG Q-460, the Sennheiser HD 598 and the Audio-Technica ATH-ANC7. The Q-460's are an on the ear type. What attracted me was their very light weight (abt. 4 oz.) I thought that if they had good sound they might also be good enough for travel even without the noise cancelling feature. The Q-460 is very well balanced sonically which is what I was looking for. Many of the newer and more visable phones out now tend to emphasize the bass. I was looking for a strong lower end without the \\"thump\\". I was surprised that headphones this small could deliver like this. I found them pretty comfortable although I was now concluding that the on the ear style maybe wasn't for me. Still they did a decent job of isolation and the external noise was very low. The problem had been with the cords. The Q-460 comes with 2. Both are lime green by the way. One cord is very short (about .5 meters). I found this essentially useless. Even connecting it to and extension proved problematic because just the weight of the plug-in tended to pull on the headphone. The other cord which is a bit longer is configured for an i-Pod, Touch, Phone or Pad. It has volume and track changing features. Unfortunately this doesn't work with my non-i-Pod MP3 player. Because both have a mic incorporated into the device, this cord shuts down my MP-3 player. It also would not work with a ¼\\" adaptor that connects to a pre-amp or receiver. The bass disappears and the sound is distorted. I contacted AKG about getting a longer standard cord and was essentially told there was not one available. Unfortunately I sent these back. They may be an excellent choice for some but didn't work for me.

I also auditioned the Sennheiser HD 598. These are full size, around the year, open-backed \\"cans\\" with a solid sound across the spectrum. They had deep solid bass, without the boominess, that I was looking for combined with a smooth midrange and excellent highs without any shrill or distortion. I thought I had a winner. These phones have a long removable cord, but they are not for travel. They are large and the open back design allows your neighbors to listen in. But for critical listening these are very satisfying at their price point. I should also warn that the color (cream with burled wood trim) may turn some off. Also, while these are the most comfortable headphones I've found, they may not fit some small heads. Comfort is a big factor for me and these work! The HD 598 may be in the process of being phased out by Sennheiser, but they have other similar styles that are available. I highly recommend these.

Finally, the Audio-Technica ATH-ANC7 which I believe has been replaced with the ATH-ANC7b. I can't talk about any differences but I decided to try the older version because others had commented positively about them and they have a long successful track record. These are around the ear (barely) noise cancelling phones. They come with a removable cord and a variety of connection options in a nice travel case. They are bigger than typical headphones of these type and frankly aren't the prettiest things out there. They would be an ugly step-child next to the Bose or B & W, but boy do they sound good. My teenage son was also listening to all the headphones I've been testing and these were his favorite. The noise cancelling feature works perfectly but...these phones do leak. By that I mean they can be heard when the volume is cranked up. I've not tried them on a plane yet, but I suspect that won't be a problem, but in an office setting I'm not sure. If you want some top notch noise cancelling headphones that sound better than Bose at a fraction of the cost, try these out. I ended up keeping these and the HD 598.ith 2. product_title: Philips HN 110 Folding Noise-Canceling Headphones
review_body:
I fly about 50k miles a year and now I commute by subway 90 minutes a day, so I thought I'd get a new pair of noise-canceling headphones to quiet my days. Two years ago I bought a pair of Sennheiser PXC 150 on-ear headphones for flying, and was reasonably satisfied given its price. My big beef against the PXC 150 and similar models is the external battery pack/sound canceling circuitry thing that you have to find someplace to clip, like on your coat pocket, making you look extra special. I wanted to get some over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones that packed the battery somewhere less conspicuous, like the earpiece or headband. I also thought the noise isolation and sound quality might be better in a model like this.

In these Phillips HN 110's, those two assumptions are both wrong. I have not yet taken these on the subway or a plane, but I've been testing them out in the kitchen with the exhaust fan and the disposall running, and comparing them to my old Sennheisers. Surprisingly, without turning on any noise canceling, these over-the-ear muffs provide no better sound isolation that the Sennheiser on-ears. Even though I have a good seal over my ears, there are other paths for sound to travel -- which I suppose is a good thing to prevent the wearer from missing vital social cues and alerts, like traffic.

Turning on noise canceling, I have to say these do about the same job as the Sennheiser PXC 150 -- noticeable reduction in some hum and roar, but not remarkable. For less than a couple Jacksons, you will arrive at your destination with a little less sound fatigue than your seatmate, so that's probably worth something. These are a bit cheaper than the Sennheisers, and they don't require you to clip a battery pack to your body or have three extra feet of cord to get caught up in.

The music that comes through, noise aside, leaves something to be desired. I've been trying to figure out the best iPod EQ setting to correct for the inherent muddiness of the sound that comes out of the HN 110's. With NC off, music is kind of muddy, with a bit too much in the lower-mid range or upper-low range kind of overpowering the vocals. Applying Bass Reducer just undermines the fullness of the music while only marginally cleaning up the mud, and Treble Booster gives a bit more crispness but still leaving an unappealing bottom end. I've settled on the Acoustic EQ and it's tolerable. But THEN, when you switch on NC, of course you get a volume and a bass bump (same thing happens to a greater extent with my Sennheisers), so you might actually do better with Bass Reducer. No matter what you do, you're going to know you're listening to cheap headphones -- certainly not as bad as that disposal nonsense they sell on airplanes, but bad enough to annoy anyone who likes music enough to read this far into a review of headphones.

For both models that I have, you get what you pay for, so at this price these cans might get you by until someone gets you something awesome for your birthday. Maybe you don't need to spend hundreds more on Bose, but I'm sure you could get better noise reduction and sound quality from something maybe twice as much if you shop around.s of the sound that comes out of the HN 110's. review_headline: Great Discs at a Great Price
review_body: First off, I use a lot of DVD-R 16x over sampling discs as a home consumer.  I use around 6 per day, so that means I use a lot of them per month.  I have used many different recorders and recording methods when burning a DVD.  I have found the machine used is 99% of the success or failure of your recording attempt.  I set my machines to record for 2 and sometimes 4 hours).  I find these Phillips discs to work just great.  I have used close to 400 of them right now and have yet to find a bad one.  However, I have also found hardly a bad one with any other name brand disc I have used in the past with a good machine.  I once had a machine which would only accept one out of four discs, a Lite-On machine).  I get these Phillips discs through Amazon with FREE SHIPPING at a great price.  I cannot say anything but good about these discs.  I read on here some guy said these discs are thinner of more flimsy then another brand.  That is BS and just plain crazy.  They are all the same from brand to brand or for at least all the ones I have tried such as Sony, Verbatim, Kodak, Maxell, Memorex, Panosonic, Phillips, or TDK.  I have never seen one brand a different thickness or made of different material from one brand to another.  I think some people just have a bad recorder or they have some dark reason to suggest these are no good or someone else's are better.  The bottom line is, I have used 400 of these Phillips discs now without one bad disc in the bunch.  They do a great job of recording at a great price and the Free Shipping makes them even a better deal.  You will not be dissappointed buying these discs.  I use Samsung,and Toshiba recorders plus a computer to burn discs).  One last note.  Recording machines need maintenance.  The laser lens needs to be cleaned from time to time with a laser disc cleaner.  Any dust on the lens will cause problems.  When and if this occurs, and it will occur, you have a machine broblem and not a disc problem.  Unfortunately, I think a lot ofpeople with recording problems give the disc manufacturer a bad rap when in actuality it is a machine problem.  I think this is the reason why you find raving reviews from one user and then comes along a guy having all kinds of problems with a certain brand of discs.  If you look at feedback from all the disc manufacturers you will find a few complaining on how bad those discs are yet everyone else loves them.  Most likely the bad feedback should be placed upon their machine and not the disc.    Just to let everyone know,  I am not in any recording business or connected with any manufacturer of recording machines or DVD discs.  I am really into electronics, am a licensed broadcast engineer and a ham radio operator for 58 years with an Extra Class License.  Lee  Houston, Texas

The PS2 was my first console and I used to be a total boss at Star Wars: Battlefront (both 1 and 2) and Burnout 3: Takedown; I have fond memories of playing the original SOCOM: US Navy SEALs every day after work 5 summers ago. Today, I spend most of my gaming time using my XBox 360, but I recently wanted to play some of those classic games again. Only problem? My video device is an HDMI monitor, with no place to plug in composite cables.

The first step to solving this issue was to buy a converter, specifically this one: [[ASIN:B003NS0UUQ New 3 RCA Composite S-video R/L Audio to HDMI Converter]]. When I got it, I excitedly plugged everything in and dialed up a classic from 2004, Star Wars Battlefront. I was quite dismayed to discover that the picture, while displaying in proper scale on my monitor with good audio to accompany it, was incredibly blurry. Now, granted, I realize that the PS2 graphics are not going to be stellar, as it is an old system. However, blocky textures and low resolution were not my concern...the image was so blurry and out of focus that it gave me a headache. After attempting to play on the hardest difficulty, but having forgotten the control scheme, I got frustrated with the game and the terrible picture and gave up.

I checked out the \\"blurry image\\" issue on some internet forums, but the consensus there was that there was no solution; however, most people attributed the problem to the built-in upscaling in HDTV's. Since I am using an upscaling box, which has generally good reviews here on Amazon, I could not understand why my picture was still so bad. Finally, I decided to give S-Video a shot, and if it failed, to simply abandon my plan to play old-school games. The Sony S-Video cable is somewhat costly, but I ran across this Monster one and figured that, for the price and the hyped brand name, it was a good deal even if it did not solve my dilemma.

I plugged everything in to the S-video port on the upscaling box and fired up Battlefront again. To my relief and delight, my picture quality is exactly as I would expect from a PS2! Sure, the graphics are still rather poor, but the blurriness is COMPLETELY gone. It's just like playing on my old SDTV. I can't say that the S-Video looks BETTER than standard composite used to look on the old tube TV, but I can say that it looks just as good, and makes gaming on an HD screen completely possible.

While the blue color of the cable might clash with most electronics, mine is hidden under a shelf and thus hardly visible. The thick cables and gold-plated terminals on this adapter are really nice and have a quality feel. The \\"turbine-cut\\" R/L audio plugs seem a little excessive, as I can't imagine there is any benefit to their notches, but they look cool...that was probably the main goal.

I know that Monster cables are often regarded as overpriced, but considering that this is cheaper than Sony's lesser-looking offering, and as I can testify works EXCELLENTLY, I think it is actually a great deal.

This is a definite must-have for anyone who wants to play PS2 games on a PS2 (as the PS3 sometimes has glitches due to backward compatibility problems) but has upgraded to some form of HD screen. I would definitely recommend getting an upscaling box like the one I have, because I have read many reports of built-in upscaling working quite poorly. review_headline: Stay away unless you love your bass
review_body: I recently bought these on amazon after reading reviews on both Amazon and head-fi and honestly, these are an over-hyped waste of money. I \\"burned\\" them in for over 60 hours and they stil sound pretty terrible.      The bass is so strong that if you listen to any song with even a bit of bass, the bass overcrowds everything else. All you will hear is bass and it's a pretty muddy bass too.   Vocals, when present, sound like they're singing behind a screen; it's far from crisp or clear.   Instruments are too heavily bassed and muddy/unclear as with everything else.   When the music gets louder, it becomes ever more unclear and indistinctive; everything just gets mashed together. (studio recordings w/ AAC @320Kbs; doesn't happen on my other earphones)     ALthough on the side note, I am not a bass-head and I like my music as close to flat and clear as possible. I'm comparing them to JBL 220 Reference earbuds I bought several years ago for $35 and truthfully, relative to these, they sound crystal clear.      If you are looking for even a slightly balanced IEM, then definitely look elsewhere. If you love your bass and love it to the point where that's all you want to hear, then these headphones are for you, even then, you might have to EQ the bass down...     On the side note, the case it comes with is pretty nice and honestly, they look pretty cool...but too bad it doesn't outweigh the massively skewed sound signature.     Overall, the sound quality just isn't there especially for what all the reviews online say. So if you're like me and read the reviews on audiophile websites, be aware that theses earphones are EXTREMELY over hyped and don't sound nearly as good as the reviewers make them out to be.     ---NOT recommended---

product_title: Cables To Go 18 AWG Universal Power Cord, IEC320C13 to NEMA 5-15P
review_headline: Be sure to check the cable's temperature...
review_body: I got a couple of these power cords for use on some PCs. These machines had sat further away from their UPSs than the power cords provided by the manufacturer would stretch, so I figured I'd buy a few of these and not have to move the UPSs closer to the computers. I was totally stoked! I used them on two PCs and luckily I was rummaging around behind the computers and brushed up against the power cord. That sucker was HOT...as in burn your skin hot. They were limp and smelled like melting plastic. And it's not like those machines are power hogs. I immediately shut down the boxes and moved my UPSs closer and swapped out the cords for the ones included by the manufacturer. I didn't feel safe leaving this product plugged into my computer and I certainly didn't want to deal with the fire hazard it represents. I should've known: Resistance in a wire gets higher the longer the wire, and since resistance produces heat... I really needed a thicker gauge power cord for it to run cool. Perhaps these cords would be good for really light duty applications.    A word of advice: Be sure to check the cords after using them on whatever device you're plugging them into after a few minutes, a few hours, etc., to see how hot they're running. These cables could be a fire hazard.      UPDATE: I was just getting the cords ready to send back and I noticed something interesting where the cord touched itself. The sheathing was brittle, and the cord sort of fell apart. (It actually broke in half.) Perhaps I should say that this product is a DEFINITE fire hazard. (See photos)

product_title: Logitech Harmony 1100 Universal Remote with Color Touch Screen (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body: While I love the idea of this remote and find it to be overall useful I have other Harmony remotes that don't depend so much on the touch screen for common functions. For instance using a DVR you wind up using the touch screen constantly which is difficult to do without looking at the display to get your fingers oriented correctly. This is a common problem with touch screen remotes.    I have to say up Until Windows 7 and Mac OS X Lion it was pretty easy to program this remote with only a few exceptions. With Mac OS X Lion you have to boot your computer into 32-bit mode and hope for the best. By default Lion will boot in 64-bit mode and Logitech has no 64-bit driver. Many compatibility problems on Windows 7 as well and I would up having to install Windows XP mode to get it to work at all. Windows XP mode is basically installing a mini install of Windows XP and running it in a virtual machine. A clumsy solution. This however was not the final way I wound up getting it to work. I wound up installing Snow Leopard on my Mac on another partition so I could get consistent behavior that was acceptable.    As much as I'm not a fan of the Harmony One (due to over sensitive touch display and battery life) I'm less a fan of this remote. I remain a fan of Harmony remotes however and hope that Logitech produces some more useful remotes rather than going for flashy and expensive.    Note if you have an older Harmony Remote and you want to upgrade to this new remote and take all of your changes... TOUGH! You have to create a new Harmony account and manage that remote separately and start your programming from scratch. This nearly made me return the remote out of pure frustration since I already had to jump through hoops to get the device recognized and the Harmony software running.    If you are running Mac OS X Lion or Windows 7 I would recommend you hold off buying any Harmony remotes until Logitech comes up with updated software the properly support those platforms without jumping through hoops.

product_title: Nationite N2 4GB Hi-Fi MP3 Player
review_body: My N2 is paired with a set of Brainwavz M2's and nothing but WAV music files.    The Nationite N2 right out of the box is very impressive. Eventhough it is made in China it has a very strong build to it. Doestn feel flimsy or cheap, actually feels very rugged and durable. As you can see in the product pictures it somewhat flashy (but not overly so)with a hidden simple led display that becomes visible when powered on. The controls are very simple to operate and the menues are simple and plain.    GOOD: The N2 comes with 4 or 8 gigs of internal memory depending on the model and has an expansion slot accomodating up to a 32gig micro SD card. The main features of the N2 would have to be the built in music AMP and the BBE Audio enhancement features (EQ's). The AMP is amazing for such a small thing, more than capable of driving the most demanding high impedence IEM's. Ive yet to raise the volume all the way out of fear of damaging my IEM's. I would say very impressive. The BBE Audio Enhacement to me are a big plus. If you hate standard manufacture EQ's than this is the one for you. Has several BBE EQ's and even some user customizable ones. The N2 blows my ipod nano, ipod touch, and my brothers iphone 4 out of the water when it comes to sound quality and clarity. If your looking for something to play just music and nothing more (and you want it done well) then the Nationite Nanite N2 is for you. Coupled with a decent pair of headphones its sure to impress when compared to other music players. Now to the BAD: The BBE EQ's will not funtion with FLAC files but the will with WAV (so convert, its simple) if you'll be using LOSSLESS MUSIC. The screen is horrible in direct sunlight, almost impossible to see. The screen only displays two lines of info, will take some time to navigate when my music library increases. Everytime its turned on the player must INITIALIZE the info on the external memory card if one is used. . . .depending on size and file type in can take a minute or two.    PROS:VERY WELL BUILT, RUGGED, GREAT SOUND QUALITY, BUILT IN AMP, EXPANDABLE MEMORY VIA MICRO SD SLOT UP TO 32GIG, BBE EQ'S ADD A CERTAIN \\"UMPH\\" TO THE MUSIC DEPENDING ON YOUR TASTE, VOICE RECORDER, SIMPLE CONTROLS, LIGHT AND PORTABLE, VERY WELL PRICED.    CONS:SCREEN IS POORLY VISIBLE IN SUNLIGHT, BBE EQ'S WILL NOT FUNCTION WITH FLAC FILES, TAKES A MIN TO INITIALIZE SD CARD.    Overall i still give it FIVE STARS and would greatly recomend it to anyone looking for a simple to use music player with exceptional quality.

product_title: Philips Fidelio DS7700 30-Pin iPod/iPhone/iPad Speaker Dock
review_headline: Elegant Design, Excellent Sound, Extremely Practical!
review_body:
The Philips DS7700 is a truly exceptional sound dock that matches my iPad2 and iPod Touch very well. While not cheap, I think it is a very good value compared to other premium portable sound options with bluetooth.

The good stuff:

- Elegant and Practical Form Factor. I have used quite a few iPod docks, of all sizes. This is the first highly portable one I have tried that sounds good. About 1 foot long, but only an inch thick, its cover and rounded design make it simple to throw into a suitcase or laptop/messenger bag to enjoy on trips. It has an aluminum shell, and when closed, has no overhanging switches to get caught on stuff. Its beautifully finished metal case feels solid and matches the elegant design of the iPad/Pod itself.

- Sounds very good, and plays amazingly loud for its size. For my purposes, the DS7700 has the best combination of small size and good volume, clarity, and bass performance I have seen in any iPod dock. I am sure it would not satisfy those who must have earsplitting bass or theater level volume, but for me, it is the smallest dock I have seen that has excellent sound and enough volume to fill a medium sized room (hotel room for example). At lower volumes it has really excellent sound....crank it up and the high frequencies get a little strident and the bass gets thin. I rate it 5 stars for sound for my purposes.

- Great charging dock design. It unfolds to provide a sturdy support for iPod/iPhone, and an acceptable support for my iPad 2. (Acceptable only because its small size would make it a bit tippy if you had kids knocking it around). The connector should work well with iPods/Pads/Phones without removing them from most cases, and requires no adjustments for different devices. It charges both my low current iPod and high current iPad just great, but must be plugged in to AC power to do so.

-Bluetooth works great, and from well across the room. It pairs almost instantly and remembers its pairing the next time you use it. I have not exhausted the battery, but have used it several hours without it running down.

- the free iPod/iPad apps are fine. They provide easy access to tune-in internet radio, as well as equalizer functions and battery level indicators. It works fine without the app too.

Could be better:

- Owners manual is terrible. Ignore it. After you get the hang of the DS7700 it is easy to operate, but getting there is more confusing than it should be for such a simple device. Things like what flashing - and + mean (charging I think) and how bluetooth paring works are not mentioned. After 15 minutes of fiddling, you should get it all, but that is 15 minutes that could be saved.

- The AC adapter brick is pretty big - about the size of a large bar of soap, and lacks fold down plugs or way to wind up the cord that would make it more travel friendly. With all the thought that went into the DS7700, they just threw in a generic wall wart. For the premium price asked, it would have been thoughtful if they had included a travel sack that would hold both the speakers and the adapter.

- The DS7700 looks great with an iPod/Pad docked into it...but not so great when used remotely via bluetooth. The iPod back support will not fold flat with the rear panel support extended, it spoils the look on your desk. You fold back the support, and the rear brace retracts so the DS7700 rolls back on your desk. The stylish cover can only be used with the speakers off....if they had put speaker vents in it, you could use the DS7700 it on bluetooth with the cover on. That would be perfect! The cover looks nice, but I would have rather had a sack that carried both the AC adapter and the Speakers for normal travel.

- No Battery Level Indicator on the unit itself. You can see battery level when the player is docked and the Philip's App is visible, but that's not too convenient.

I really like the DS7700, and think it well worth the price. Sound and construction rate 5 stars, but I am judging it 4 stars because the manual could be much improved, and the portability enhanced with a better designed AC Adapter, cover, and an included case.ion rate 5 stars, but I am judging it 4 stars because the manual could be much improved, and the portability enhanced with a better designed AC Adapter, cover, and an included case.

product_title: Comply  Isolation PLUS Earphone Tips
review_headline: Very comfortable, though performance is questionable.
review_body:
I picked up the S/M/L three-pack to go with my [[ASIN:B003NSBKT6 Shure SE535-V earphones]], hoping to squeeze a bit more bass out of them, and to get a better fit than the included foam tips.

With the tips that came with my 535's, I found that I was somewhere in between Medium and Large, where Large gave the best seal, but medium was more comfortable. With the S/M/L pack, I immediately discovered that the large tips were much smaller than I had expected -- maybe just a touch bigger than the Medium tips I had before. Feeling as though the \\"perfect\\" sized tip for me would be between the M / L sizes that came with my 535's, I would have liked the TX-100 Large tips to have been just a tiny bit larger. I didn't need to bother with the smaller sizes.

Despite that, the Comply tips are incredibly comfortable. Hands down, the most comfortable tips I've ever used. I can keep my 535's in for hours, without the slightest discomfort. For that reason alone, I'd recommend these to anyone.

As for sound quality, I know there's been some debate as to whether or not the earwax guard changes the sound. I can't say that I noticed a substaantial difference in volume or clarity. By the same token, I also can't say that these sealed my ear canal any better than the Shure OEM tips. So, there wasn't a discernable difference in bass response, either.

If I had it to do over again, I would still buy these -- though, I'd go with the three-pack of Large.

review_body:
[UPDATE - 02/15/2014]
The MH-C808M charger is still working great, no problems at all.
I've since added to my battery charger collection by purchasing:
[[ASIN:B000NLUSLM Maha PowerEx MH-C9000 WizardOne Charger-Analyzer for 4 AA/AAA Batteries]],
[[ASIN:B004J6DLD4 La Crosse Technology BC1000 Alpha Power Battery Charger]],
and a couple of [[ASIN:B007S9P3BC NiteCore Sysmax Intellicharge i4 V.2 Li-ion/NiMH Battery Charger, Black]] for my 18650 batteries,
all of those are working well also.

[ORIGINAL REVIEW]
My Maha Powerex MH-C808M 8 Cell Multi-Charger is 2+ years old and has been working perfectly.

I purchased my unit from a local Batteries Plus store because I urgently needed a high quality battery charger for my collection of NiMH AAA, AA, C & D cells.
The charger that comes with the [[ASIN:B000WD3IR2 Energizer® Rechargeable Batteries & Charger -- 8 rechargeble AA batteries and 4 rechargeble AAA batteries]] works but it's too aggressive, the batteries are almost too hot to hold right after a full charge, this really shortens the useable life of the cells.

I've since moved away from the regular [[ASIN:B00000J47L Energizer NH15BP-4 Rechargeable AA Battery 4 Pack]] NiMH cells and switched to the low self-discharge Sanyo's [[ASIN:B004UG41XW Sanyo NEW 1500 eneloop 8 Pack AA Ni-MH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries]] and have never looked back.

There were issues with this charger with near fires and actual fires, please read Keith Hillman's & M. Chaffee's 1 star reviews, but more importantly I urge you to read the comment from \\"rwizzard\\" on Keith Hillman's review (I think it's comment #16).

In that comment rwizzard explains that a deeply discharged rechargeable battery will allow it's own polarity to be REVERSED, this is a bad thing, battery chargers don't like it and may overheat and melt/burn. If you suspect your batteries are completely dead pull out a meter and test the battery's polarity (each one) before attempting to recharge them.

All in all, I've had zero problems with my Maha Powerex MH-C808M, it saves me money and I like that.

product_title: Sharp SPC800 Quartz Analog Twin Bell Alarm Clock (Silver)
review_headline: A fine little backup clock, albeit noisy
review_body:
This appears to be a totally decent old-fashioned alarm clock. I've had it as an occasional-use backup for the last six or seven weeks.

Some characteristics:

* The single alarm is loud. Damn loud. Not to fire-alarm levels, but I wouldn't expect a sleeping partner to ignore it.
* The alarm is set by a twist dial on the back. There are two dials; the other one sets the time. You have to be careful which you grab.
* There's no snooze capacity here. The alarm is either activated or not, as set by a small switch on the back.
* It ticks audibly. I sleep with earplugs so I don't care. If your sheep can't stand a fixed rhythm, you won't like this.
* There's a small button on the back to activate a side light. The face is otherwise invisible in the dark.
* It appears to hold time. The first few days I used it, it seemed to lose time, but it's been steady for the last month.
* It really is a pretty clock, especially for the $8 WM wanted for it.

The only question mark for me is the battery wear rate. This clock uses a single AA rather than a proper AC adapter. I've erred on the side of caution with a 1.5V Alkaline rather than the usual 1.2V Eneloop.

product_title: SONOS P3 Color
review_headline: Does what it says, with a few limitations
review_body: I love this system. It does what it says and sounds really good for its size, but there are a couple things in the advertising could be a bit misleading:  1. The Zoneplayer itself is not an \\"all in one\\" solution unless your router is in the same room as the Zoneplayer; to stream wirelessly you need the Bridge ($50).   2. It doesn't exactly stream iTunes, it streams your iTunes playlist FROM YOUR COMPUTER. That means that you have to have your iTunes playlist/library shared on a computer on your network, but more importantly, it means that you can't directly stream from an iPad or iPhone with just the Zoneplayer and Bridge (though they sell a wireless dock to let you stream from your iPhone for an additional price); it seems that the iPhone pictured prominently in the advertising is meant primarily as a remote control(the iPad remote control app works well, haven't tried the iphone).    Technical note: After my initial setup I moved the Zoneplayer into a different room (fewer than 10 feet away from the first) and the control software could no longer find it (even when connected over ethernet); the zoneplayer was totally unresponsive after the move. If this happens to you, I suggest unplugging it, holding down the \\"mute\\" button and plugging it back in... this resets the Zoneplayer back to factory default and made it possible for the control software to find it again. I spent a few hours troubleshooting my firewall when the firewall had nothing to do with it, and the reset I just described was buried on the Sonos website and is the only thing that fixed the problem. Hopefully that saves someone some time someday.  Overall, I'm very happy with it so far. The intial setup was VERY easy, and, like I said, the sound is impressive; just don't expect wireless streaming without the bridge or to stream iTunes without a networked computer.

product_title: Pioneer VSX-1021-K 7.1 Home Theater Receiver, Glossy Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body: I had been trying to decide between the VSX-1021-K and the Onkyo TX-NR609. Depending on the review, I had found reasons for and against both.  I upgraded from a Sony DA3ES, which even though it's 10+ years old, is still a great unit, but was built well before HDMI and the new HD sound formats.    Finally I decided on the Pioneer. It arrived solidly packed, and setup was easy.  I plugged into my router and grabbed an IP address with no problem.  Speaker connections are all binding posts that also accomodate banana plugs (no spring-loaded jacks here.)      Inputs can be renamed from either the receiver menu or the iPad control app.  You can also turn off inputs you don't use so they won't appear when turning the input knob.    After making my speaker and input connections, I connected the included setup microphone, and started the full-auto MDACC setup.  It proceeded to run a series of test tones to test each speaker.  It came back and told me I had a speaker out of phase, and sure enough, I had connected one set of wires backwards.  After correcting, it continued on and set the levels, balance and distance on all speakers.  I've used Video Essentials and a sound level meter in the past, and I have to say that the auto-setup did a great job.    Sound and video quality are great. The 1021-K is 90 watts per channel compared to my Sony's 100, but it puts out good clean sound at all volumes and I haven't noticed any loss of power.  Previously all my sources were plugged directly into the TV's HDMI inputs, but the additional video processing the receiver performs definitely gives HD images a pop and clarity they didn't have before. I have it set to upscale everything to 1080, and while it makes things look a little better, it's never going to look as good as a true HD image.    One negative I do have about the video processing: When changing sources or changing from SD to HD channels, it sometimes takes several seconds to decode the video signal. For example, when turningon my XBox360, it takes long enough that I miss most of the startup screen.  Not a huge deal I suppose, but it's something that I wasn't used to before. I also have a DirecTV DVR and have had a couple of cases where the picture just flashes off and on repeatedly, until I turn the DVR off and back on. I suppose it could be an issue with upscaling, so I may turn off that feature to see if the issue goes away.    I have an iPad, and I do like the remote control app, though I do agree with those that have said certain aspects of the app are gimmicky. Airplay works well, and though the 1021-K doesn't support Pandora natively, that can also be streamed using Airplay.      The included remote is not laid out the greatest, there are a lot of buttons and most are the same shape and size, so working it in the dark isn't the easiest.  A backlit remote would've helped quite a bit.  I've had limited success with programming codes for other devices into the remote, but the learning feature (putting remotes face to face) works just fine.    All in all, I'm very satisfied with this unit.  I feel I definitely got my money's worth and would recommend it to others.

product_title: Logitech Harmony 650 Infrared All in One Remote Control, Universal Remote, Programmable Remote (Silver)
review_body:
I have owned this remote for about 9 months. VERY PLEASED...but PLEASE READ

Use for :TV , DVR, Bluray(w/Netflix), soundbar

so basically its 4 items, each with various advanced features.

I had no issues with set-up.
I did have to do a customized button function for the DVR 'recorded shows' button, and I had to manually sync my sound bar following the pretty easy directions...but, let me just say it was easy for *me* , maybe a little too complex for say, my parents who are not gadget savvy. Or even my wife (hope she doesnt read this)

This remote CAN and WILL simplify your remote control experience, but it does require some level of geek savvy when it comes to programming and especially troubleshooting.
It helps GREATLY to UNDERSTAND how the remote operates.

example:
when you press DVD ON, understand everything that goes on in order for you to switch from TV watch mode to DVD watch.

The remote will, step by step, and in order, send a different signal to each component. Not simultaneously. Step by step.

You need to keep the remote *aiming* at your component(s) through the entire process..as it will..power on dvd....set input...etc. It could be as many as 4 successive steps with just 1 button being pressed...So, it could take about 10 LONG seconds (I'm used to it now)

You have to keep remote aiming properly during this time...So often I have seen people press the WATCH TV button and then put the remote down once the TV turn on...NOPE...thats asking for trouble...you SHOULD KEEP AIMING IT for about 10 long seconds....and hopefully all your components are roughly in the same direction of where u are aiming. For most people thats not an issue. But worth noting.

If all of this makes sense to you, thats a BIG PLUS !!!

The HELP menu on the remote is pretty handy if a component 'missed' a command.

Logitech has done a super job making this remote ALMOST easy. A little patience and understanding go a LONG way.

Here is my CONS:

everything is backlit (love that) EXCEPT the top buttons above the lcd screen!!!...such as the Watch TV button and ALL OFF button. I don't understand why.

CON #2
I tend to drop my remote...a LOT.
No, it hasn't broken, despite some pretty bad falls onto a hard wood floor...Thats actually a good thing, its DURABLE....but what I can almost guarantee is with any JOLT to the remote, it will RESET out of whatever mode it was in.

Here's what happens and the quickest solution :

I'm watching TV (so I'm in the watch TV mode)
I drop the remote.
Remote then resets (due to the JOLT of hitting the floor) to the main screen (where I choose what I want to do)

The remote will not function until I re-tell it to go to Watch TV mode...HOWEVER, since I am presently *actually watching TV* when I press the Watch TV button, its not smart enough to realize my tv is *already* ON...it assumes the TV is OFF, so it sends the power TV signal to the TV...thus turning it OFF.

Solution:
I hit the Watch TV button while I cup my hand and cover the front of the remote (blocking the signal) so that the \\"remote\\" goes into the correct mode, but the \\"signal\\" to power the TV doesn't reach the TV....thus I'm back in the correct watch TV mode without disrupting my TV viewing.

If the above doesn't make sense, from a conceptional point of view, than \\"maybe\\" this remote isn't for you.
Its not magical, but it CAN be a great convenience once you understand it.

However, once you actually see the instructions, you learn that the impedance for each speaker zone is based in the number of speakers hooked up. The words \\"automatic impedance matching\\" are misleading. If you want 8 ohms, you have to have six pairs of speakers connected. Less speakers, higher resistance per zone. product_title: Sennheiser CX 215 Earphones - Blue
review_body: I have been a long-time fan of Sennheiser ear-buds and was eagerly awaiting the arrival of the new CX215s.  I was concerned when I received them given the slightly smaller build compared to my venerable CX300s.  My worries were unfounded.  In addition to having a comparable cost to my CX300s, the clarity of mid- and high-range frequencies actually excelled the CX300s a little.  In the bass department, they were the CX300s' equal; the bass is delivered cleanly, with no distortion that usually accompanies some of the cheaper offerings out there (yes, KOSS and JBL ... I'm looking at you).  In addition, the CX215 model features a very welcome ergonomic improvement.  Putting these earbuds in is unbelievably comfortable...which unfortunately leads to a minor con.  The CX300s are definitely better in the noise-isolation department.  It's not noise-cancelling, mind you, but the snug fit is as good as any ear plug.  The CX215s don't isolate sound quite as well because of the extremely comfortable fit.  Take it with a grain of salt, but if you plan on air travel then don't rely on the CX215s to do the job.  The CX300s are not completely perfect for air travel either, but if you're looking at spending the same money, the CX300s are a better buy.  That said, for casual use, I still find the CX215's ability to isolate outside noise to be satisfactory enough for listening in an office environment, grocery store, etc., where a lot of white noise may otherwise hinder an enjoyable listening experience.  Otherwise, despite that minor gripe, these ear buds are definitely better than some other ear buds that cost anywhere from 20 - 30 dollars more.  Highly recommended!

review_body:
I bought this as a carry-on for my photography gear while traveling. The main compartment can carry a camera with attached zoom lens and four other lenses. However, for my 5'7\\" frame it felt slightly small.

Its strength is its design quality. With a 15\\" laptop in the side slit I was able to carry everything in one bag. (A 17\\" does not fit in the slot) The laptop was secure and well-padded. I also fit a textbook in the side slot. My bag was heavy and dense, but comfy while on my back. My only complaint is that it should come in a medium and large length; three more inches would have been ideal for me.

There's a lot that can go into this small bag. Even when it's stuffed to the seams this bag fits comfortably under an airline seat (at least in a Southwest plane). The outside pockets can hide flight documents, sunglasses or boarding passes that are quickly needed at the airport.

This is a well-made bag. The red canvas matches my red carry-on bag and both carry enough for a week-long get-away.
