product_title: JVC Everio GZ-MS110 - Camcorder - widescreen - 800 Kpix - optical zoom: 39 x - supported memory: SD, SDHC - flash card - black
review_headline: GREAT Image Stabilizer, Sound & Zoom...OK picture
review_body:
I found this one for an excellent price, and I had to give it a shot. I have been looking for one that records to flash media, so I don't have to worry about DVD formats etc.

THE GOOD
This little camcorder has OUTSTANDING image stabilization. I used the 45x optical zoom to focus on something more than 200 yards away, and it was rock solid in the frame, simply hand held. There are limits to everything, however. If you get goofy and want to use the 800x digital zoom you will definitely need a tripod. But to have 45x zoom without a needing a tripod was pretty darn good, in my book.

The sound quality was also VERY GOOD. The mic is on the front, which is always best, and the audio quality was crystal clear, recorded with plenty of volume.

As far as the digital video file goes, Windows Movie Maker live (which is free) was able to open the files without any trouble at all. From there, I'd imagine you could produce whatever kind of home movie you wish.

THE BAD
Unfortunately (or maybe not) we now live in an HD (high definition) world, and this camera does not produce HD quality picture. The picture on my 32\\" 720p television was quite disappointing. Even on my small laptop computer screen, the quality did not seem much better. This was on the \\"ultra fine\\" video quality setting of the camera.
Ultimately, this was the deal breaker for me, and led to its return.

THE UGLY
Not a big deal, but I haven't had a camcorder for years, and maybe this is just me. But this unit felt very light and \\"plastic-y\\". The battery, in particular was so light, it amazed me that it even worked. I have no basis, however, for saying that this affects quality in any way. It just felt a little weird to me, that's all.

THE CONCLUSION
If you like the price, and you aren't particular about crisp, clear picture quality, this could be a good purchase for you. It's hard not to love the image stabilizer, zoom and sound. If only it had HD quality picture, this camcorder would be terrific. As it is, I have to leave it with three stars.

product_title: Pioneer VSX-1020-K 7.1 Home Theater Receiver (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Outstanding Bang for the Buck, Future Proof (7.1 & 3D), iPhone App is Great, Buy an Airport Express Too
review_body:
I tend to do a lot of research before making large purchasing decisions and so far this receiver is receiving a pretty rosy reception! Its predecessor, the 1019, was CNET's and Gizmodo's top mid-range receiver. Both reviewers had just as high hopes for the 1020, and Gizmodo already called it the best receiver $550 can buy, saying the 1020 \\"hit the sweet spot\\" that gave the most bang for buyer's buck.

The critics I read all raved about the excellent sound quality, but the 1020 brings some new offerings to the table for a mid-range receiver.

In short, the most valuable features you get with this model that you don't get with the next step down are:

1. A fifth HDMI port in back, an extra sixth in front (for digital cameras, computers, etc.).
2. Analog video upscaling (which I don't care too much about since most of my content is HD already or played through an upscaling player).
3. The iContolAV iPhone app. Very cool for controlling volume and switching inputs. Works simply by having your receiver connected to ethernet and your iPhone connected to the network via WiFi. A few times the app has had trouble properly connecting, but it usually works well.
4. Internet radio with programmable stations, which is cool, though you can't currently control the station selections from the iPhone App, unfortunately.
5. A color configuration interface output to your TV via the HDMI output. I can't imagine trying to configure all my speakers without seeing a graphical representation of their location on screen.

That last feature feature, the HDMI 1.4 ports that support 3D, the 7.1 surround capabilities, excellent sound quality and the iPhone App are what made the VSX-1020 the clear choice for me. I also appreciated the automatic calibration with the included microphone and the included iPod cable/compatibility, but those weren't as strong of selling points.

The only negatives of note for me is that the little front port cover is a little cheap. It's not even a door, simply a little plastic piece that pops out if you push one side. I, like others, have also experienced the issue where the receiver switches to TV/Sat when first turned on, but I've yet to determine whether that's a problem with the receiver itself or my Harmony universal remote (I'll update the review as I get more information).

One last tip to buyers, however. If you're considering listening to your phone's music over Bluetooth by buying the $99 AS-BT100 adapter, I'd consider buying a $99 [[ASIN:B0015YJOK2 Apple Airport Express]] instead (assuming your music is managed through iTunes). It lets you stream music from your computer to the receiver over WiFi and control what's playing via iTunes or Apple's robust \\"Remote\\" iPhone app, but more importantly the Airport Express acts as a USB print server and a one port wireless bridge (something that lets you connect wired devices to a wireless network).

That wireless bridge capability is especially valuable, since you'll need it or something similar for internet radio and iControlAV iPhone app support if your VSX-1020 receiver isn't close to your wireless router (mine isn't). Buying the Airport Express kills two birds with one stone.

UPDATE:

A few ideas have been thrown out by other Amazon posters to help alleviate the issue with the receiver switching to TV/Sat when it first turns on. The first idea is to change the receiver's settings thusly:
\\"1 Press Receiver , then press Home Menu.
2 Select `System Setup', then press ENTER.
3 Select `Other Setup', then press ENTER.
4 Select `HDMI Setup', then press ENTER.
5. Set Control to 'Off'.\\"

The second idea is to adjust your TV settings like so.
\\"Go into Menu under HDMI-CEC and turn it Off. If the set is a Samsung look for AnyNet+ (default is normally On) and turn it Off.\\"

I'm still having issues going directly to a given HDMI input when the unit first power on (going to \\"HDMI Input 1\\" simply toggles the current HDMI input instead of going directly to the one you want), but I've made the quirk tolerable by programming one of the buttons on my universal remote to toggle inputs, so it's easy to fix.to the one you want), but I've made the quirk tolerable by programming one of the buttons on my universal remote to toggle inputs, so it's easy to fix.

They are built well (a cable that you won't find on other inexpensive IEMs, which is good), and with a little run-in, can compete with higher priced IEMs. I have compared them (listening A/B), for example, to the Phiathon 210s, and they are close (the 210s cost $95 and are a little crisper in the treble range, but it's not a massive gap).    At first, as the other reviewer noted, the M9's bass is a bit sloppy. Mids are fine, but treble also needs some run-in. Just hook them up to your PC or stereo and let them play for 50+ hours at normal volume, and those issues will dissipate. Then, sit back and enjoy the music, no EQ required. These are \\"fun\\" phones, not analytic, and better than most other competitors and close if not better than some higher-priced IEMs I have heard/ownerd. I also owned the Klipsch S4s, and believe the M9 is a better value (the S4s are $79). The M9s are bass-forward, but it's not bothersome like on most low-cost IEMs.    Accessories are also very good, as is the case with most Meelec phones. However, I believe I had to shift to a nonm-Meelec bi-flange tip to get the best sound (I wound up giving my M9s to a good friend whose iBuds broke. He is very happy now). review_headline: This is a pretty good product.
review_body: This product is very user friendly, affordable, light weight, and easy to carry. It feels like the knobs and body of the device are made of solid durable plastic. It comes with a limited addition of Virtual DJ and will play WMA and MP3 files. I've used the controller on Windows7 and XP without a problem. All controls work with Virtual DJ controls without any delay except when scratching. It does not have the same response time as a turntable or CDJ tables, so if you're a Professional DJ into Turtablism, transforming, and other scratching techniques, this may not be the device for you. However, if you like Mixing Music this device works great and will get the job done! The controller is USB powered, so no cords are needed. I have not figured out how to configure the (LOOPS/FX)  to work for hot cue's , or if it is even possible,  but hot cues (multiple cue points)  can be set on the virtual DJ program.  If your computer or Laptop does not have more than 1 sound card or device, you will need to buy an external sound adapter. They are very inexpensive on Amazon, and are needed if want to cue up music on 1 side while music plays for the crowd on the other. Before using the external sound card you will have to configure the outputs on the virtual DJ program. The controller allows you to scroll, and load music files right from the device for quick access. This product is pretty good and I definitely recommend it for beginners or PRO DJs who love to mix and play music.

review_body: I primarily work with Macs. I've been using these blanks with my MacBook Pro and some slim external CD writers.    It works very well and the write speed is very good. AMAZON! Hope you are reading this. You have a great product, but the label surface is extremely poor in quality.

product_title: FINIGO 3.5mm In-Ear Stereo Earphones w/ On-off & Mic For Apple iPhone 6 / 6 Plus / 5 / 5S /5C, HTC One (E8), One (M8), Samsung Galaxy S5 Android Smartphone
review_headline: Huge Sound from these Little Guys!
review_body:
When I first opened the packaging I was a bit frustrated because it's not the \\"hassle free\\" packaging that I truly appreciate. You have to pull out the scissors to open this bad boy and be careful about not cutting yourself with the sharp plastic edges of the cut box. Fortunately, my experience with the BOSE IE2 ear buds gets better from there.

The Medium size, \\"StayHear\\" buds are in place when you get the earphones, and you have S, M, and L for both the StayHear and regular ear buds. I normally wear a size Small in other earbuds, so after trying on the Mediums that were already on, I tried on the Smalls. They both fit me, which was unusual for me. So after spending about 5 minutes trying out the various sizes and styles, I opted to stick with the StayHear Medium size ear buds.

They feel a little looser than the traditional ear buds I use from Skull Candy (those Smalls feel truly wedged into my ears when I wear those and it starts to hurt after a while), but they don't seem to fall out after just moving my head around in various directions.

I plugged the IE2s into my iPod first and the sound was much louder than with my other earphones, so I had to scale back the volume. This is helpful on an airplane and in the gym when there's a lot of background noise to have a higher volume ability. Then what shocked me was the actual sound quality. The bass was totally audible without being painful in my ears. The sound was crystal clear. I then switched over to use the earphones on my laptop and again, the sound quality was amazing and much louder at the same setting than my other earphones. I'm not one to listen to things very loudly, but it's still nice to have the ability to listen to it loudly should I so choose.

Aside from the actual earbuds/sounds: There's a little carrying case that comes with it. While it's a nice case, I don't see myself ever truly using it. It's boxy and takes up a lot of space. I'll probably end up just using the satin bag that comes with my old earphones to store them when not in use or traveling as it's much more compact. The wires of the earphones are black and white, which I found to be different. I'm used to the all white from Apple, or all black or all solid color. So I kind of like that it has a distinctive black/white to it...makes me feel kind of \\"hoity toity\\" walking around with earphones that are distinctive to being BOSE and not some other, less expensive brand.

I would highly recommend these earphones. They're a gem once you get past figuring out which size/style ear buds are right for you.g that comes with my old earphones to store them when not in use or traveling as it's much more compact. product_title: Apple iPod classic 160 GB (7th Generation) NEWEST MODEL
review_headline: WARNING!!! WARNING!!! What Apple doesn't want you to know.
review_body: Hello, everyone.    First let me tell you I had the 2007 edition of the 160 GB iPod classic, but my warning still goes with this newer model.    The iPod classic is the only iPod with a MOVING parts hard-drive. Which means that if you walk around or drop your iPod when it's playing, it could break.    I had two of these iPods (one broke within a week of getting it, the second broke recently but it was out of warrenty). The iPod I got was over $300 (old model) and I ended up getting $17 (recylced) for it.    Now you may not get as much memory with the other iPods but if you want to dance, jog/workout, walk around, or just tend to drop things this isn't the iPod for you.    By the way, even if you have 160 GB of music, video, games, etc. how much of it do you REALLY need. I went from a 160 GB classic to a 16 GB nano. Am I as happy? No, I like to carry all my music, but I love my new iPod. Plus I can dance around as much as I want and don't have to worry about it breaking.    And let's face it, if you might have to spend another $100 to $200 in a year or two is the extra memory really worth it?    Am I saying that it's guarrenteed to break? No, but there's a strong possiblity. And if it's out of warrenty, you're on your own.    Hope this helps :).

review_headline: Enjoying it immensely, but problems with set up
review_body: The set up was frustrating.  After setting up my new router and Squeezebox Boom, I immediately got this puzzling \\"wireless encryption failure\\" message on the screen which lead me to 3 hours of call time with techs having me type things on the computer and plugging and unplugging the router and modem until they got the thing to work.  It works great ever since, except for occasional drop outs which are fixed by simply resetting (unplug/plug in) the router.  I have several music stations from sky.fm, which offers excellent audio quality, on my favorites list and have 44 talk radio station presets from radiotime, a preset on the preset button of a Hawaiian music station I found from Shoutcast; excellent audio quality, and other presets of nature sound effects on the other preset buttons I use with the snooze feature before I fall asleep.  These are the apps. I use the most, but have tried several of the other apps.  I often also listen to Pandora, and have set up my own stations, but the audio quality isn't as good as say sky.fm or Shoutcast.  The fun part is all the sampling and finding out what sounds best and what I like to add to my favorites.  I listen to talk radio a lot so I'm happy that I can find who I want to listen to when I want to listen to them.  I also tried plugging in my ipod to the output cable, but found the audio quality just okay, so I keep it docked in my home theater system in the living room for listening there. I just purchased a subwoofer and will test it out with the Squeezebox Boom just as soon as the 3.5 mm to RCA adapter arrives.  The Squeezebox Boom should have this adapter included since subwoofer cables are RCA type, not 3.5 mm.  I'm surprised that nobody else has griped about that connection.  So, overall I'm liking the sound and features, but unit could have some improvements.

product_title: Sony HTCT100 Sound Bar with Subwoofer - Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Not perfect, but great for small rooms...
review_body:
I have a Samsung LN32B550 that has fairly decent sound by itself, but it was severely lacking on the low end. Having had a full home theater in the past, the thought of running a ton of speaker wire, having to work up a bunch of varied inputs to a receiver, retrain my fiance on how to turn on the TV, etc., all made me shudder. Then I found this little setup. One cable for the speaker(s). One cable from each device (pending your devices all support HDMI). You only get 3 inputs, but 3 gives you enough inputs for an HTPC/Cable/Satellite Box, an Xbox, and a Blu-Ray player; if you need more than that you probably should really seek help, you have too much money and too little common sense.

It doesn't get as loud as I would like, but the one thing my living area has is high ceilings and an open floor plan, so its hard to fill with sound from just one speaker and a sub. That said, it gets plenty loud for the average action movie, and doesn't distort easily, at least to my ears.

The remote is terrible, in true Sony fashion. Panasonic is the only manufacturer I know of that actually provides decent remotes and firmware, so this isn't as much a knock against Sony as the entire industry. For a system like this, that shims in between the devices and the display, it is shameful of Sony not to employ some kind of ridiculously simplistic remote and a flush onscreen display. That would probably have doubled the cost of the unit though, so instead they ship with one of those \\"attempts-to-be-universal-but-does-not-quite-do-it\\" remotes. Its restricted to only working with other Sony Devices, and I can't see it excelling at that task either. This system literally requires all of 16 buttons, out of the 51 provided on the remote; this makes the thing overly hard to use and is intimidating to non-technophiles. The good part is nothing I have found that can't be replaced by a decent learning remote, as each source gets its own dedicated button, and that's half the battle when trying to configure these blasted things.

If you're tight on space, cash, or the thought of running speaker wire all over your living room makes you queasy, this is a great unit that will serve you well. Sony, while typically overpriced and underfeatured, is still a good brand, the quality of their stuff is pretty high, even if the R&D and usability investments are not.when trying to configure these blasted things. product_title: Etymotic Research In-Ear Headset with 3-Button Remote Control for iPod, iPhone, iPad
review_headline: Etymotic HF-5 In-Ear Monitors - Not for every ear canal
review_body: The purchase of the Etymotic HF5's taught my band a valuable lesson on buying this kind of device online ... TEST FIT BEFORE PURCHASE. My band was looking for in-ear buds to go with Shure's PSM200 Wireless In-Ear Monitoring system for live vocal monitoring. We bought them online based on reviews and visuals ... bad idea.  Thank you, Amazon, for allowing us to return them.     So, The HF5's sounded great for the money IF you could get them in and get them to stay in. That's the end of the \\"good\\" part of this review.  They had *major* design flaws in my opinion that negatively impacted comfort, usability, and ultimately, the sound quality that you're able to achieve in real-world use.     First, the nozzel is a much larger diameter than my Shure earbuds and inserts into the silicon triple-flange tips all the way to the very end    Second, the nozzel comes straight out from the drivers and is not bent to accomodate seating the driver in the ear    Third, the nozzel is much longer than my Shure earbuds, suspending the driver and cord further away from the ear     The large nozzel led to the triple-flange silicone tips being unable to compress below the diameter of the nozzel. The combination of tip and nozzel was larger by FAR than the Shures I use when the silicone tip is fully compressed around the nozzel.  You essentially have a large unyeilding tube that you have to force into your ear canal.     The length of the nozzel led to the drivers sticking much further out of the ear, whihc made the earbuds extremely uncomfortable (there was a rather large unyielding element in your ear when fully inserted) and almost impossible to fit into smaller ear canals even with the smaller tips. My keyboardist is petite and her ears are small, and she felt almost violated by the fit.      In actual practice, once when you DID get them in, the rigidity of the nozzel/tip, coupled with the leverage created by the drivers and cords being so far away from the tips caused them to fall completely or partially out of the ear canal with almost any head movements. Even a partial break of the seal compromises the bass response, isolation, and apparent volume.    Finally, the trick I use with my Shures to prevent them from coming out (wrapping the cords around my ears and cinching them up at the back of my hairline) is not effective with the HF-5's.  The distance they stick out from your ears and the lack of support for the drivers because the nozzels are not bent to allow the driver to rest inside the ear do not alow easy routing of the cords behind the ears.     Shure has been doing this for years and has really gotten the sound, comfort, and utility down to a science ... haven't tried Ultimate Ears yet, but I have to say that the few extra bucks you pay for the Shures will pay off in comfort, sound, and reliability over these cool looking, but ultimately unusable earbuds.

review_headline: Don't Ever Pay More For An HDMI Cable
review_body:

The best part of this cable is the price. You'd be hard-pressed to find such good quality for anything near as good a price.

Reasons to buy this over other cables on Amazon. Technically speaking, because HDMI is a digital signal, it is not subject to electrical interference like VGA cables. However, the build-up of static electricity in the connections of some cables of lesser quality can cause brief interruptions of picture. This cable's full shielding prevent this. Also, generally speaking, the more you pay for a cable, to a certain point, the better the fit. This cable fits snugly in all of the ports I've used it on.

These reasons make this product, to this reviewer, the ideal HDMI cable. Monster would try to sell you a cable that you need to take out a small mortgage to afford. This cable does everything the Monster Cable does but at 1/10th the price.

product_title: Creative NOMAD Jukebox Zen Xtra 40 GB MP3 Player
review_body: Basically, if you like to tinker and be patient with things, this is your MP3 player.    Its not an ipod, and the music organizer is no iTunes. I actually hate itunes and how it commandeers your music library, reorganizing it. The Creative Music Organizer leaves it alone, and I found importing tracks to be a breeze, and syncing up the device and my computer to be simple as well. Kind of buggy though.     The interface: the side button interface is wonderful, as is the toggle wheel. The best thing about it is that you can press the buttons - track advance, reverse, volume, pause - from outside your pants pocket. So, basically, when I'm in my lab coat, with my gloves on, I can reach down and feel the buttons through all of the material and hit \\"next\\" if I don't like the song. Thats my number one favorite thing about this player.    As for the actual menu and operating system, I can honestly tell you I finally figured out how to make a playlist after 2 years of owning the thing. I just never bothered, and it wasn't that intuitive. But for listening to 40+ gigs of music on random, hitting \\"next\\" is all you need.     My number two favorite thing is that you can upgrade the storage capacity. I read some of the 1 star reviews (and it sounds like some of them were for the \\"touch\\" model, not the \\"nomad jukebox Zen Xtra\\") and these poor bastards are having hard drive problems and they send them back to Creative and get charged 100's of dollars to fix a hard drive problem.     Its amazing how little people know.    So, here's the story. I had the original device for about 2 years, and I had dropped it one too many times, and it finally stopped working. I figured the only thing that could break is the thing that moves - I.e., the hard drive. So, I get a tiny screwdriver, and 10 minutes later I discover that inside this thing is a laptop hard drive - standard, 2.5 incher. So, I order a new hard drive (80 gig, twice the size) and badabing - after a reinstall of the software, I now have an 80 gig MP3 player.     So, basically, you can upgrade this device to the largest size IDE interface 2.5 inch hard drive you can find. And, an added bonus of my upgrade, the newer hard drive had a lower power consumption, so I extended my battery life too.     A con, however, is that its big. But you can probably store 320 gigs of music (largest size IDE HD available) on this thing.     For this, creative gets credit for designing a quality product that has an incredible lifetime due to its upgradability and replacability.

product_title: Philips SA6145 4GB Flash Video MP3 Player With 3.5-Inch Full Color Display & SuperScroll (Black)
review_headline: Not Bad, But Not Really Good Either
review_body:
The concept is a good one, but the execution is not quite up to par.
The Phillips SA61 portable media player is one of those \\"jack of all trades, master of none\\" players.

It's music function is okay, if lacking.
It's video function is okay, if lacking.
It's picture viewer is okay, if lacking.
It's radio function is okay, if lacking.
I never made use of the voice recording program.

In fact, it's biggest issues are the features it lacks.

For example, with video play, your movies have to be converted over with the Phillips Media Converter, or 3/4 of the time it won't play. There are also no skip functions for in movie viewing, just fast forward and rewind, so if you're watching a long movie and want to move ahead a chapter or two, you can move at 4x or 8x fast forward.

The music function is alright, but lacks real controls as well. For example, playing a song is fine, but there is no stop button. You can only pause or play, and if you're not on the music menu function, you can't stop a song at all or skip ahead. You have to go back to the music menu, find the album, find the song, and then pause it or skip to the next song.

The picture viewer is just that, a picture viewer. You can turn the image sideways, which is nice if you need to do so, but there is no zoom, no other options. Just next and turning your image to the side on the screen.

The radio function works okay, there's not much to it but I guess there doesn't have to be. You can scan up and down the radio dial and save presets.

As for the voice recording option, I didn't make use of it. Your mileage may vary on that one.

Finally, the settings. It's the most bareboned settings menu I've seen in any kind of electronic interface of it's type. I mean, there are a list of options, but there's very little that you can really change. You can change the \\"screensaver\\" time, you can change your video and music playing settings, but even those are very limited. In fact, I would describe the whole setup as limited.

It's about as basic as it gets. iPod, Zune, even the first edition PSPs, these media players are well ahead of the Philips GoGear. If you're looking for absolute bare bone essentials, with just enough to barely get the job done, then I guess you could get this player, although I'm certain you can find something more feature equipped and just better able to handle slightly more complex functions other than \\"Play/Pause/Next\\".

Overall, 3 out of 5 stars, and I'm being a bit generous with the 3.he whole setup as limited. It's about as basic as it gets. iPod, Zune, even the first edition PSPs, these media players are well ahead of the Philips GoGear. If you're looking for absolute bare bone essentials, with just enough to barely get the job done, then I guess you could get this player, although I'm certain you can find something more feature equipped and just better able to handle slightly more complex functions other than \\"Play/Pause/Next\\". Overall, 3 out of 5 stars, and I'm being a bit generous with the 3.

Eventually, the right channel died in both pair I owned. The first pair lasted me a year, which, while frustrating, I was willing to look past. The second pair, though, only lasted four months. I took great care of these headphones, always storing them in their hard protective case. The problem seems to be where the cord attaches to the plug-in; I was able to get snippets of sound out of the right ear by wriggling the cord around at this spot. Unless you're willing to buy a new pair every few months or so, I would look elsewhere.

It comes with a remote that's well layed out (including bass/treble functions) and AM&FM antennas that do an ok job; its reception is kind of all-or-nothing.  The sound is pretty nice (I have it hooked up to a set of [[ASIN:B000OG6I6A Sony SS-B3000 Bookshelf Speakers with 8\\" Woofer (Pair)]] that at its prefered load of 8 ohms compliment it well) and its got enough oomph to really fill an 11x11' room at about 30% volume.

review_body:

Of course, at 107 decibels (volume adjustable), it's loud, but if you don't want to wake the neighbors the vibration disk (under your pillow) is FANTASTIC. I will warn you, it WILL scare you for the first couple of days, but you quickly adjust. Not only that, but it flashes yellow lights when the alarm goes off! Only a video will do it justice- google \\"Sonic Bomb\\" and you'll find some good examples.

I haven't had any issues with build quality, alarms not going off (it's a hard switch, not soft- so it's easy to see), etc.

Minor cons: Wish it was atomic (self setting with time), must make sure that switch is in the right position (if you put it on the 12h 50hz switch and you're running on 60hz US power, you're going to be several minutes off within 24 hours), somewhat bright screen, even when the switch is in the \\"low\\" position. No timeout on alarm (make sure you disable the alarm is off when you leave your room for more than a day, or you're going to get your neighbors busting down your door to turn it out)

Fantastic alarm, highly recommended for any heavy sleeper. It's well priced and I can't thank Sonic Alert enough for making it.

product_title: Sony Mdr-Ex75/Blk Ex Earbuds Headphones with 9mm Hi-Sensitivity Driver
review_body: having used the sony ex71 for a few years the differences of the ex75 are apparent and overall for the worst.  using no EQ, the bass is about neutral, trebles sound a little sharp maybe slightly boosted- this may smooth out over time but has the benefit of showing more detail, but most annoyingly im hearing a narrow dip in the mids which unfortunately gives a slightly boxy and unnatural sound and narrower stereo separation, i cant see this flattening out with use.    in contrast although the ex71's werent perfect with a slightly muddeying and noticeable boosted bass but they had  a flater spectrum in the mids and trebles, giving the music more impact, wider stereo spread and overall more musical.  the ex75 are crisp but thinner sounding (although the thinness can probably be equalized), narrower stereo spread like the music is more in front than to the sides when sounds are panned, slightly boxy and slightly unnatural sounding particularly on electric guitar and being less musical some passages of music pass you by without any impact.  theyre not terrible, most people probably wont even notice unless they A/B test with other/better earbuds, but right now i think id take the older ex71's over them.    personally ive always found the ex series comfortable with the soft earbuds, although watch out as the rubbery tips are easily lost. personally ive always liked the cord length too as i wear my player on my arm and the short lead is perfect for this.  the cable is however unreassuringly thinner than the ex71's which always suffered from one earbud going dead in under a year so im not confident these will hold up for more than say 9 months of daily use. thin cable, although light ,also means they will twist and tangle easily.    overall theyre cheap everyday expendable earbuds with an ok/passable sound, but the slight boxyness of the sound and lack of openness is a backward step compared to older sony earbuds so id rather take a different pair of similarly priced earbudsover these.

product_title: Barnes & Noble NOOK ebook reader (WiFi + 3G)[B&W]
review_body: I will make this review a quick and dirty reference of the pros and cons of this awesome device to make things easier for potential buyers to make their decision.    PROS:  -Can read the .epub file, making it possible to read the files from most other e-book stores and public domain sites with ease...just load it onto the nook via USB cable by dragging and dropping the book into the My Documents folder.    -LCD touch screen powered by the Android OS makes for quick and logical navigation of all aspects of the device...need to search for a specific book?  The screen will become a responsive QWERTY keyboard.  While you're actually reading a book, the screen becomes your means of navigation through the book, your on-hand dictionary, your way of changing the font type/size, etc.  It's a brilliant design.    -The recently released 1.3.0 firmware really speeds up the device in all regards.  It also added chess and sudoku, though anyone buying a device for playing games probably should look elsewhere.  Also a web browser, but again, nothing to write home about.  This thing is meant to read, and read it does.    -Truly beautiful e-ink screen which is just the perfect size for reading (about the size of a trade paperback).  It astounds everyone who sees it for the first time.    -User-replace battery and expandable memory by microSD card.  This was the real deal-breaker for me, as I am bothered by companies who force you to send the product to them and give them $100 for something you can do yourself in 5 minutes for $20 when the Li-Ion battery inevitably loses its charge.  It seems completely illogical and the nook addresses this problem.    All other aspects are at least equal with the competition (the Kindle) and aren't necessarily worth mentioning.  Overall I would recommend this to absolutely anyone looking for an e-reader, as it is the same exact price as the Kindle but offers so much more.  It's a no-brainer, really.

product_title: Zune 120 GB Clamshell Digital Media Player Red/SilverBack
review_body:
I bought this in December and loved it. Playlists are a snap, loading is automatic, updating is a breeze, podcasts are easy to find and subscribe to. I knew I'd made the right choice to get this rather than an iPod.

Then my hard drive died in Feb. I sent it back and took a month to get a replacement. The replacement (new not refurb) had a battery that wouldn't hold a charge and the operating system was 2 full #'s out of date. I fully charged it, turned it off, and by morning, it was only half charged. I charged it fully the first Friday and turned it off, by Sunday morning it didn't even have enough charge to turn on when I plugged it into my computer. Again, I had to send it back and do without for a month.

In short, I love it when I have it, but I am getting very tired of returning it and doing without for weeks at a time. If the 2nd replacement (due to arrive next week) doesn't work correctly, I will demand my money back.

I took a gamble when I bought this since I'd seen lots of reviews like this one, but it seemed that if you got one that worked, it was great. That's true, just understand you are gambling for a good one if you buy a Zune...so good luck to you!!!

EDIT:
The 3rd Zune I got was a black one instead of red, which didn't matter to me at all. It has been working beautifully for over a year now. I listen to it almost all day at work, virtually every day, so it gets a workout. Perhaps it was just the red ones that had issues. Now, I am very glad I purchased the Zune. It is worth the hassle to get one that works, since they do replace it when needed and once you get one that works, you've got a GREAT product! It holds my whole music collection, lots of podcasts, Audible books as well as the FM radio. I never run out of things to listen to and it is so easy to sync. Love it!

product_title: Antennas Direct C2 ClearStream Television Antenna
review_headline: Did I say this antenna is very ATTRACTIVE ! ;-)
review_body:
Hi,

Tech Challenged Senior Female here, so keep that in mind.

Not only tech challenged, but financially challenged too.

Which is why, when my cable company offered me a digital package for only $20/mth, and HD for $40 mth ) I declined. After all, all i had was an old zenith large screen TV, hooked to a VCR and old DVD player and the basic cable from my cable company, hooked through an entry level Yamaha Home Theater receiver ( Trust me i had to learn all this as i went along, but I do sound techy, eh? lol )

This changed, when I won a TCD648250B model Tivo on Ebay, that records HD, and has THX sound capability.
I started to long for the idea of recording shows that I couldn't get.

When trying to hook through the TiVO to the VCR, I noticed that instead of a cable in and cable out jack on the TiVO unit that it had a cable in and ALSO an ANTENNA IN. So i thought, why not give the HD antenna a shot, before, perhaps, breaking down and ordering digital cable that I could ill afford.

Hence the search for an antenna

I received this antenna in the afternoon, it took me all of 10 minutes to put it together with a Phillips screwdriver, using this short cable, the type the cable company uses, that I happened to have around, who remembers why?

I then screwed it onto the back of my TiVO to the antenna jack in.

Stuffed it behind the big screen TV, so it wouldn't show to the room, ( another 10 minutes ) did a channel scan...( that took the longest time )

and VOILA !! 128 channels found !

I then proceeded to look up some HD movies and told the TiVO to record them, and now enjoy HD THX movies at night.

Bravo Clearstream!! You're my Heroes !

Except for the fact that now i am longing for an HD TV ~ ;-)

UPDATE ON THIS REVIEW -> FAST FORWARD TO AUGUST 2012

I have since gotten an HD TV AND a projector HD TV and anHDMI THX home theater unit... I can't tell you how wonderful it is to see the HD shows that the antenna pulls in. Nicer looking than anything coming over a cable.

In addition, i took the antenna out of my south facing window and we put it on the roof, and now we get 153 !!!! channels.

Meanwhile... before putting this on the roof, we got an expensive Orca antenna with rotary capability and supposedly is good for 150 miles !!!
The rotation unit was DOA... and the very few stations pulled in had weak signals...

So we put this up there in the interim of finding something else.

However, this works so very well, and almost every station is pulled in with a strong signal, we are not going to get anything else !

I do have to mention that we added a Clearstream CV 2 reflector assembly, a week after we put it up. ( Costs $19.95) for VHF stations.

Before we did that, it only got 142 stations, not 153 ;[)

product_title: Altec Lansing iMT620 inMotion Classic Portable iPod Dock with Rechargeable Battery and FM Tuner - 30 Pin Connector
review_headline: The Auto-Shutoff is a MAJOR diappointment.
review_body: Two of my favorite apps on my iPhone 3GS are Pandora and iHeartRadio.  Now that these apps are able to run in the background, allowing me to do other things on the iPhone while listening, I use my iPhone to listen to music and talk radio a lot more.  So, I started looking for a portable docking system for my iPhone.  I like to listen while I am working in the garage or outside.  I found the Altec Lansing iMT620 at a retail store.  It looked like exactly what I needed, so I bought it.  After I charged it up, I was really looking forward to docking my iPhone and listening to Pandora while doing some work around the house.  Imagine my surprise when the music stopped, and I figured out that the Altec was cutting out after a couple of minutes!  Turns out that, when you dock an iPhone, the Altec thinks you have paused an \\"iPod\\".  When the pause hits the limit, it cuts out.  The workaround is getting the proper cord (iPhone plug on one end, aux input plug on the other) and using the Aux input port on the back to connect the iPhone.  Thus, the docking port is useless, unless you want to listen to the iPod app on the iPhone.  I am inclined to keep the Altec, even though I just bought it yesterday, and I could return it.  I figure it is as good as any other portable boom box with an Aux input port.  I'll give it 2 stars.  It would get 5 stars if it were really compatible with the iPhone, as it advertises.

product_title: Onkyo TX-SR608 7.2-Channel Home Theater Receiver (Black) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_headline: Incredible Value, but HDMI Video Issues mar an otherwise perfect Entry-Level Receiver
review_body: Unlike a lot of CEs, Onkyo may have indavertantly cannibalized its own model lineup by pushing so much featureset into an entry level receiver that it might deter buyers from their higher end models. I recently did a thorough comparison of the Pioneer VSX-1020 and Denon AVR-791 and the Onkyo nudged out the Pioneer due to its beefier amp section and OSD capabilities. That said, I must caution users that its value is marred by what appears to be a bug with its ability to pass through HDMI video signals unmolested, even in \\"Through\\" modes. This bug manifests itself in two ways: 1. 24 bit sources (like cable hdtv) are upconverted to 30 bit when output on a display; AND 2. for some inexplicable reason, 1080p 24fps sources stutter intermittently as if a frame is dropped. The latter might be more noticeable to plasma owners whereas 120hz and 240hz LCDs might compensate for the frame stuttering with their interpolation software (ie the soap opera effect).    With that caveat, the Onkyo is a terrific performer offering strong power (power consumption is up from the 607 to a very grown up 756 watts), terrific flexibility (four speaker terminals can be assigned to wide, height or zone 2). The Denon is limited to merely 7 speaker terminals and the Pioneer has only a pair of assignable terminals. The Audyssey auto-callibration (2EQ) is a notch behind Denon, but the inclusion of Audyssey DSX (for wide arrangements) is a feature that the Denon does not offer. While it lacks the USB terminal for Ipod playback of the Pioneer and the Denon, it does offer a computer input which might resolve the HDMI handshake nightmare many face with htpcs.     Onkyo rather smartly included a fan atop of the receiver, which is silent and all but eliminates the historical Onkyo toaster oven effect.     I really enjoy this receiver, but found the HDMI video molestation issues to quite problematic and what mar an otherwise incredible buy. Hopefully Onkyo can issue a firmware update.

product_title: Sennheiser In-Ear Stereo Headphone
review_body:
I bought these so I could have a set of earphones that sounded good and were comfortable enough to wear for a straight hour while I'm at the gym, nothing more, nothing less.
When I first received them I was pretty excited.
So I hooked them up to my MP3 player and started to check them out.
If you get them in your ear just right they sound great, a little much on the bass though.
On electronic based music (rap, techno, R&B, etc.) the bass is great, on instrument based music (rock, classical, etc) the bass is a little much.
If you have a good player, you can adjust the bass but not all players allow that.
My biggest gripe with these headphones is the cord splits and gives like 8 inches to go to your left ear and then like 16 inches to go to your right ear.
I don't like the offset design but I understand that some do.
Even so, what's with this huge difference in length?
Unless your head is like 2 feet wide, the cable going over to your right ear will be dangling all limp and goofy looking.
Also, the length to the end where the mini plug is is really too short for anyone my height.
I'm 6'2\\" and I can't keep my MP3 player in my pocket because THE CORD IS TOO SHORT.
So I have to place it in my waist band while I'm working out, which I guess works but is not ideal.
I just gave them to my wife and she likes to use them with her laptop.
Works great for her, sucks for me.
Bottom line, THEY SOUND GREAT BUT IF YOU ARE 6 FOOT OR TALLER DO NOT BUY THESE.

So, in conclusion:    Pros:    - Comfortable    - Great Sound    - Secure (while running)    Cons:    - Sweaty ear pieces    - Tendency to fall off while lifting weights    - Doesn't come with a pouch (purchased separately)    Overall, we are both very satisfied with this. product_title: SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player
review_headline: you're lucky if you get one that works!
review_body:
Im the last 4 years I've purchased 3 sansa players. The first, an older 2g model, for my husband. It worked just fine for about three months then the screen stopped working and he was no longer able to add songs. He still uses the device for work commutes but cannot choose what he wants to hear, as he cannot use the screen to navigate his music.

I bought the pink 4g fuze earlier this year, have absolutely no complaints on that one. Never froze up or malfunctioned. I loved it, it was a fair price too. It was stolen from my car this summer, unfortunately.

I repurchased the same pink 4g fuze....not so lucky with this one....sigh....nothing but freezing up and not being able to shut it off. Every time i try to add new music it freaks out and freezes up. It won't tell me if i've added bad tracks or not. Not sure what to do, but would really like to chuck it ut the window! The purpose of a portable music device it to be able to hear what you want to when you want to, but all i get to hear is what the dumb thing allows me to...that is when its not frozen! I find it so terribly ironic that the only sansa that worked well was the one that got stolen. I will not be buying any more sansa players, despite the ease of sync-ing and how well it adapts to windows media player....its just too much to ask that at roughly $80 a pop, you might get a good one, or get a rediculously bad one!

I purchased the zune 30g today for my husband for christmas, I'm keeping my fingers crossed til they almost fall off that the zune won't be a waste of my hard-earned money like a sansa!!!

product_title: Homedics HMDX-C30 Speaker Dock for iPod with AM/FM Clock Radio with Nature Sounds, Silver/Grey
review_body: Had to buy another dock for my second ipod, and after my jensen spectra, i think badly of this dock in comparison. This dock has a lot of features that really no dock should have, or features that are never really used. For one, there's bass and treble controls on the remote. You really only need this the first time your listening to the dock, if anything. I've only used it once. Also, the nature sounds. Sometimes i listen to them if there is absolutely nothing on the radio. Then there are 3 separate buttons for alarm functions, which is a lot, but could live with that. Then there are things that my other dock had that this doesn't. First, there is a sleep button, BUT that is not the sleep function i am accustomed to. My idea of the sleep button is where the radio is on for a certain amount of time, then turns off so if you are sleeping already, you don't waste energy. Not the case here, in fact its the opposite.It's more of a nap alarm. you set it for like 2 hours, and go to sleep then it sounds an alarm to wake you up. But seriously, you could just set the second alarm (yes it has two which is cool) to whenever instead. And i wish the projector thing was more maneuverable instead of only going in one direction. And also, this doesn't really matter, but on my other dock, i could set favorites for my radio stations, but here, i have to search all over the frequency spectrum for my desired station. Then there is the fact that the buttons sorta don't work anymore after like 8 months. But there are good things for this thing. There is the fact that is does its job, listening to ipod radio, has good alarm, two in fact. And the fact taht it has a remote was a deciding factor. I can only honestly say taht there are more con's than pro's for this one.

product_title: ACCESS HD 1080D NTIA-APPROVED DIGITAL-TO-ANALOG TV CONVERTER [Electronics]
review_body: I got this convertor box with the government coupon. After installing, I noticed a constant humming noise (not bad if TV was loud enough) and faint diagonal strobing. I thought: Well, so much for the \\"wonderful new digital TV signal.\\" One evening in early August, just 3½ months after installing, I turned the TV on, and had no digital picture. I checked to make sure that nothing on the box had been turned off or unplugged and that there were no loose connections between it and the TV, or antenna. Everything was fine. The box, usually quite warm to the touch, was colder than an icecube! I unhooked everything, and plugged the box into a different outlet: Nothing... dead. I had bought a Phillip's convertor box to hook up to my VCR so I could watch one channel/record another. I hadn't hooked it up yet, so unpacked it and hooked it up to the TV. Guess what?- NO humming noise, NO diagonal strobing..... PERFECT picture. The Access HD boxes were, I believe, created to fill an underestimated demand. People ordered them when there was little else available and got ripped off, in my opinion. Some might say that folks shouldn't complain if they got them with a coupon, but- the changeover was NOT supposed to incur fees/charges to the consumer. Now, I have to purchase a new box for my VCR at full cost to me. I think Amazon should feel embarrassed to be associated with the Access HD products!
